name: RobinHood (tail-latency-aware cache repartitioning)
baseline: OneRFpolicy: a single shared off-the-shelf memcached cache per application server, matching Microsoft OneRF's production configuration. Also compared: TAO++ (static per-backend allocation) and emulated LAMA++, Cliffhanger++ and FAIR++.
workload: Testbed of 16 application servers and 34 backend servers across 50 Azure VMs. The servers host 20 backend services (KV store, MySQL cluster, matrix-multiply recommender) modeled on OneRF's 20 most-queried backends. Each application server has a local 32GB memcached. Traffic comes from OneRF production statistics, averaging ~200k queries/s (500k peak), with injected backend load and latency spikes. The metric is the fraction of time a 150ms P99 request-latency SLO is met.
claimed_speedup: Under backend load spikes on the OneRF-modeled testbed, RobinHood meets a 150ms P99 request-latency goal 99.7% of the time, whereas the next best policy meets it only 70% of the time. Sec. 5.2 names the next best policy as OneRFpolicy, a single shared memcached cache matching Microsoft OneRF's production setup: it violates the 150ms P99 SLO 30% of the time vs <0.3% for RobinHood.
hardware: 50 Microsoft Azure D16 v3 VMs: 2.4 GHz Intel E5-2673v3 (8 cores), 64GB memory, 400GB SSD, 8Gbit/s network
tradeoffs: Optimizes cross-backend cache-space allocation, not the per-cache eviction policy itself; requires a central resource-allocation (RBC) controller polling all backend caches, adding a coordination layer on top of plain memcached; reallocation decisions are rate-limited to avoid thrashing (ignores reallocations faster than 5s)
caveats: The metric is SLO attainment (share of time meeting a 150ms P99), not a throughput or speed ratio. The next-best baseline is a caching policy (one shared memcached cache without partitioning), not a slower memcached. RobinHood repartitions off-the-shelf memcached, so it is a cache resource-allocation system, not a new eviction algorithm. The testbed is Go plus a Python controller, last touched in 2019. No compiler or flags are stated.
found_via: gh api repos/dasebe/robinhoodcache/readme; OSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed OSDI'18 paper. It states the 99.7% vs 70% result for meeting a 150ms P99 goal (abstract, Fig. 3) and compares against two production policies (OneRFpolicy, which is a single shared off-the-shelf memcached cache, and TAO++) plus emulated LAMA, Cliffhanger and FAIR. The testbed code is public in the repo and the CPU is given (Azure D16 v3, E5-2673v3), but no compiler or flags are stated, so it is not A.
verification.notes: All metadata matched gh (BSD-3-Clause, 95 stars, last commit 2019-07-08, not archived, not a fork). The main fix is that the 70% 'next best' policy is OneRFpolicy (single shared cache), not a static-partitioning policy. Static partitioning is TAO++.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: RobinHood meets a 150ms P99 latency goal 99.7% of the time during load spikes, versus only 70% of the time for the next-best static cache-partitioning policy tested
corrected_fields.baseline: memcached-style per-backend caching without dynamic repartitioning
corrected_fields.hardware: Servers provisioned with 2.4GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673v3
corrected_fields.workload: 50-server production-trace testbed emulating a large web service (20 backend systems, memcached-compatible per-backend caches) under load spikes, measuring P99 request latency against a 150ms SLO
corrected_fields.caveats: Baseline is 'next best' static/off-the-shelf cache partitioning across memcached-like backends, not literally raw memcached itself, so baseline_in_list is false and confidence is reduced accordingly; this is a cache resource-allocation system rather than a new eviction algorithm

name: S3-FIFO
baseline: LRU (Meta CacheLib's optimized LRU; also CacheLib's optimized 2Q and TinyLFU, plus Segcache)
workload: Throughput: an S3-FIFO prototype in Meta CacheLib replays only a synthetic Zipf (alpha=1.0) trace. The trace is 100*n million requests over n million 4KB objects (n = thread count), run at 1-16 threads with a large cache (LRU miss ratio 0.02) and a small one (0.21). Miss ratio: libCacheSim simulation over 6594 production traces from 14 datasets (MSR, FIU, CloudPhysics, CDN1/2, Tencent, Wikimedia, Alibaba, Twitter, Meta KV/CDN, ...).
claimed_speedup: S3-FIFO achieves more than 6x higher throughput than the highly-optimized LRU in Meta's CacheLib with 16 threads, at both small and large cache sizes (synthetic Zipf trace). The throughput gap is larger still vs CacheLib's optimized 2Q and TinyLFU. Separately, in libCacheSim simulation over 6594 traces from 14 datasets, S3-FIFO has lower miss ratios than state-of-the-art algorithms and the lowest mean miss ratio on 10 of the 14 datasets.
compiler_and_flags: Artifact build script (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 mybench/build.sh) uses CMake build type RelWithDebInfo with Ninja; compiler not named
hardware: CloudLab Clemson c6420 nodes for the prototype (the paper does not name the CPU model). Turbo boost off, one thread pinned per core, all memory allocated on the same NUMA node with numactl.
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (1a1a11a/libCacheSim, simulator home of S3FIFO.c); artifact repo Thesys-lab/sosp23-s3fifo 145 stars; CacheLib prototype in Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23
tradeoffs: Uses three FIFO queues (small, main, ghost) instead of one list; ghost-queue metadata adds memory overhead; small-queue size ratio (S) needs tuning per workload
caveats: The throughput numbers come from a single synthetic Zipf(1.0) workload in a modified CacheLib, not from production traces. The miss-ratio results come from simulation. The paper names no CPU model (only CloudLab c6420 nodes) and no compiler, so this stays at tier B. The S3-FIFO simulator code is in libCacheSim (libCacheSim/cache/eviction/S3FIFO.c). The throughput prototype is in a separate CacheLib fork snapshot (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23, Apache-2.0).
found_via: gh search repos 'S3-FIFO cache'; junchengyang.com publication page; arXiv search 'S3-FIFO cache eviction'

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'23 paper. It states S3-FIFO in CacheLib reaches >6x the throughput of CacheLib's optimized LRU at 16 threads, with a larger gap vs 2Q and TinyLFU (Sec. 1, Sec. 5.3, Fig. 8). The prototype benchmark code is public (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 mybench/, CMake RelWithDebInfo), but the paper names only CloudLab c6420 nodes, not a CPU model or compiler, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The record's '1559 evaluated traces' does not appear in the paper, which says 6594 traces from 14 datasets. The record also said the throughput test replayed CDN/Twitter/Meta traces, but the paper says it used only a synthetic Zipf trace. Both are fixed. gh metadata matches the record: Apache-2.0, 347 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, active (GitHub lists the repo language as C++, while S3FIFO.c is C).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: S3-FIFO achieves more than 6x higher throughput than the highly-optimized LRU implementation in Meta's CacheLib at 16 cores; the gap widens further versus 2Q and TinyLFU; also reduces FIFO's miss ratio across most of the 1559 evaluated traces (see the paper's Fig.6-7 percentile plots)
corrected_fields.workload: CacheLib-based KV-cache prototype replaying synthetic Zipf and production CDN/KV traces (CDN1, CDN2, Twitter, Meta), throughput scaling measured across 1-16 cores
corrected_fields.hardware: CloudLab testbed nodes; the paper cites an AMD EPYC 9654P only as an example of a modern many-core CPU, not confirmed in the extracted text as the exact throughput-test machine
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); implemented inside Meta's CacheLib per the paper
corrected_fields.caveats: Exact CPU model for the throughput experiment and compiler/flags are not pinned down in the text we could extract, so capped at tier B not A

name: SIEVE
workload: 1559 traces from 7 datasets (247,017 million requests, 14,852 million objects; Twitter, Meta, Wikimedia, TencentPhoto and two proprietary CDNs) replayed in libCacheSim for miss ratio. Separately, a Cachelib (C++) prototype replays two production KV traces (Meta, Twitter) with 1-16 threads, with cache size 4 x nthreads GB, to measure throughput.
claimed_speedup: Cachelib-based prototype: SIEVE is 16% faster than Cachelib's optimized LRU (17% vs TwoQ) at 1 thread on both the Meta and Twitter KV traces. At 16 threads it has more than 2x the throughput of optimized LRU and TwoQ on the Meta trace (the contributions list says 125% higher than optimized LRU). Optimized LRU itself scales about 6x from 1 to 16 threads on Twitter; only the unoptimized LRU plateaus at 4 threads. Miss ratio in libCacheSim: on CDN1 at the large cache size, SIEVE reduces FIFO's miss ratio by a mean of 21%, and by more than 42% on 10% of traces (p90 whisker). Over 1559 traces it reduces ARC's miss ratio by up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%). The paper frames that 1.5% mean as significant next to ARC's own mean 6.3% reduction over LRU; the 1.5% is smaller than the 6.3%, not larger.
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6142 @ 2.6GHz, 384GB DDR4 DRAM (CloudLab c6420 node), turbo boost off, threads pinned within one NUMA node
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); sievecache.com (redirects to cachemon.github.io/SIEVE-website) lists adopters including Immudb, TiDB, Pelikan, DragonFly, DNSCrypt-proxy, PostgREST and Ceph
tradeoffs: Needs a per-object 'visited' bit like CLOCK; underperforms TwoQ/LHD/ARC at very small cache sizes because new objects can't demonstrate popularity before being evicted
caveats: The paper states the CPU model, NUMA pinning and turbo-boost setting for the throughput prototype but not the compiler or optimization flags, so it is capped at tier B. The miss-ratio numbers come from the libCacheSim simulator. The throughput numbers come from a separate Cachelib-based C++ prototype (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23), not from libCacheSim. The >2x throughput result at 16 threads is reported for the Meta trace only. The paper is internally inconsistent about ARC's mean reduction over LRU: the introduction says 6.7% (up to 33.7%) and Section 4.2 says 6.3%. libCacheSim's Sieve.c is a simulator policy, not a drop-in production cache.
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for 'SIEVE cache eviction'; junchengyang.com publication page; gh search repos 'SIEVE cache eviction'

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'24 paper compares SIEVE against LRU (Cachelib's optimized LRU for throughput) plus FIFO, ARC and 7 other policies for miss ratio. The code is public (cacheMon/NSDI24-SIEVE simulator snapshot; Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 prototype) and the CPU model is stated (c6420, Intel Gold 6142 @ 2.6 GHz, turbo off, one NUMA node), but the compiler and flags are not, so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: The original claim misattributed the 4-thread plateau to the optimized LRU; in the paper it applies only to the unoptimized LRU. The claim also inverted the 1.5% vs 6.3% comparison. The core >2x-at-16-threads and 63.2%-vs-ARC numbers are on the page. The metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 347 stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-26 (active). The phrase 'production-ready' does not appear on sievecache.com; the site lists adopters, so stars_or_usage was reworded.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Prototype throughput is >2x an optimized 16-thread LRU (LRU plateaus at 4 threads while SIEVE keeps scaling); reduces mean miss ratio vs FIFO by 21% (up to 42% at p90) on CDN1 at large cache size, and vs ARC by up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%, itself more than the 6.3% mean reduction ARC gets over LRU)
corrected_fields.workload: 1559 CDN/KV traces (247B requests, Twitter/Meta/Wikimedia/proprietary CDN) replayed in libCacheSim for miss-ratio, plus a multi-threaded prototype cache replaying KV-cache workloads for throughput scaling from 1-16 threads
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim, the reference implementation); promoted as production-ready on sievecache.com
corrected_fields.caveats: Paper states CPU model, NUMA pinning and turbo-boost setting for the throughput prototype but not the compiler or optimization flags, so capped at tier B; miss-ratio numbers come from libCacheSim simulation while the throughput numbers come from a separate hand-built prototype

name: Skytable
workload: GET/SET requests via redis-benchmark/memtier/sky-bench, 30 threads with 1 client per thread, run against Redis, KeyDB, Dragonfly and Skytable on two AWS m5.4xlarge instances (one server, one client)
claimed_speedup: GET/SET ops/sec (30 threads, 1 client per thread): Skytable 619,992/676,091 vs Redis 112,100/99,892, about 5.5x GET and 6.8x SET (derived from page data); KeyDB 288,931/282,997 and Dragonfly 408,322/392,446 in the same post
hardware: 2x AWS m5.4xlarge (one running the k/v store, one running the benchmark client)
tradeoffs: Skytable answers queries in BlueQL (a small SQL-like language) rather than plain GET/SET, so it does strictly more parsing/validation work per request than Redis/KeyDB yet still came out ahead in this benchmark; this 0.8.x line is single-node only (clustering was still WIP at the time); Skytable is also the only one of the four that runs natively on Windows.
caveats: The post does NOT state that the benchmarker has no affiliation, and its independence is doubtful. The HN account johnwoods also submitted 'Skytable - A realtime NoSQL Database written in Rust' (2022-08-26), 'Skytable NoSQL Database: Even with BlueQL, Skytable Outperforms Redis and KeyDB' (2023-12-05, linking ohsayan/sky-benches) and 'Skytable's new NoSQL engine released' (2023-12-09). The post gives no payload size, server versions, build flags or scripts, and does not say which of redis-benchmark/memtier/sky-bench produced the table. The author says Skytable was 'a little inconsistent at times' and that they could not reproduce Dragonfly's claimed 25x. Dragonfly's author replied in the thread with his own m5.4xlarge memtier run (about 1.02M SET ops/s at 28 threads x 20 connections), and the poster objected to the differing connection count. The numbers are from June 2022, before Skytable 0.8 moved to BlueQL. Skytable's own sky-benches repo (first-party, chart only, Tiger Lake 6C/12T, no compiler or flags) is not stronger evidence.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'Redis KeyDB Dragonfly Skytable' -> HN item 31796311 'Redis vs. KeyDB vs. Dragonfly vs. Skytable' (independent shootout, 130 points)

verification.tier_reason: The HN Ask post (item 31796311, 2022-06-19) does list GET/SET ops/sec for Redis 112,100/99,892 and Skytable 619,992/676,091 at 30 threads x 1 client on 2x m5.4xlarge. It is not a well-known benchmark suite: it is one post by an anonymous account, with no payload size, no server versions, no statement of which tool produced which number, and no scripts. Commenters asked for the missing methodology. So these are numbers without methodology, which is C.
verification.notes: I downgraded B to C: an anonymous HN post with no methodology does not count as an independent third-party suite, and the poster's history is heavily Skytable-promotional. The record's 'states no affiliation' claim was unsupported, so I rewrote the caveats. I read the HN item through the Algolia items API mirror. The repo metadata matches: AGPL-3.0, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-26.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: GET/SET ops/sec: Skytable 619,992/676,091 vs Redis 112,100/99,892 (~5.5-6.8x); also ahead of KeyDB (288,931/282,997) and Dragonfly (408,322/392,446)
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmarker states no affiliation with any of the four projects and ran the tests themselves (redis-benchmark, memtier_benchmark, sky-bench) on 2x m5.4xlarge, but reports Skytable's numbers were 'a little inconsistent at times' and that they could NOT reproduce Dragonfly's own claimed 25x-over-Redis speedup. Compiler/build flags for the four server binaries are not stated. Skytable's own first-party benchmark repo (github.com/ohsayan/sky-benches, same author as Skytable) shows a similar Redis/KeyDB/Skytable comparison on a 6C/12T Tiger Lake box with hardware specified but is first-party, not used as the primary citation here.

name: Valkey
workload: valkey-benchmark -t SET,GET -r 3000000 -d 1024 --threads 6: each iteration is 50M SETs followed by 50M GETs, with 1KB values and a 3M-key keyspace. Connection count was tuned per system: Valkey peaked at 400 connections, Redis at 384. Both servers ran in Docker with --io-threads 6 and persistence off (--save '' --appendonly no), pinned to 6 cores with NIC IRQs pinned to the other 2.
claimed_speedup: Valkey 8.1.1 999.8K RPS on SET at 0.8ms p99 vs Redis 8.0 729.4K RPS on SET at 0.99ms p99. The page itself states '37% higher on SET and 16% higher on GET, alongside 30% faster p99 latencies for SET and 60%+ faster on GET' (these are stated, not derived). Absolute GET RPS is not printed in the text.
compiler_and_flags: Official Docker images valkey/valkey:8.1.1 and redis:8.0, run with --io-threads 6 --save '' --appendonly no --maxmemory 10gb; client was valkey-benchmark with --threads 6. Compiler/build flags of the images are not stated.
hardware: AWS Graviton4-based c8g.2xlarge (8 vCPU) server in an EC2 cluster placement group; c8g.8xlarge (32 vCPU) load generator
tradeoffs: Valkey originated as a community fork of Redis (created when Redis relicensed away from BSD) and has since added its own multi-threaded I/O path in the 8.x line, which is the source of this speedup; API/RESP-protocol compatible so migration cost from Redis is low, but as with any fork it can diverge over time from upstream Redis modules and Redis Enterprise-only features.
caveats: Momento (the blog's publisher) is a caching-as-a-service vendor that also sells Valkey-based products (valkey-router, valkey-operator), so it is not a fully neutral third party even though it is independent of the Valkey project itself; the article includes a 'Try it Yourself' reproduction section but does not link a public benchmark-code repository, so it falls short of tier A. A secondary aggregator blog (andrewbaker.ninja, 2026-01-04) cites the same 37%/999.8K-RPS figures, corroborating they were not altered in transmission. [retier] Evidence is a blog by Momento, a vendor selling hosted Valkey (not independent).
found_via: HN Algolia search 'valkey benchmark redis' -> 'Valkey is now outperforming Redis in benchmarks: 37% higher write throughput' (andrewbaker.ninja) -> traced to primary source gomomento.com/blog/valkey-turns-one-how-the-community-fork-left-redis-in-the-dust/

verification.tier_reason: Momento's blog (Khawaja Shams, 2025-05-07) is independent of the Valkey project and runs Valkey 8.1.1 against Redis 8.0 on the same c8g.2xlarge. It gives the exact docker and valkey-benchmark commands and states 999.8K vs 729.4K SET RPS, '37% higher on SET and 16% higher on GET', and 30%/60%+ faster p99. It falls short of A because the servers are official Docker images with unstated compiler/flags, and no benchmark repo is linked. B follows the batch-39 precedent that an independent vendor blog counts as B.
verification.notes: I verified every figure on the page. One small fix: the 16%/60%+ figures are printed on the page, not derived. The page's headline has a typo, 'Redis 8.0 got as high as 729.4 RPS'; the connection-tuning section confirms 729.4K. Valkey is a hard fork of Redis per its README (GitHub fork flag false), so I set is_fork_of. Metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 27,299 stars, last commit 2026-09-26. The author is at Momento, which sells Valkey-based services, so the tier holds only if interested-vendor blogs count as B; otherwise it is C.

retier.reason: Orchestrator consistency retier: the only numbers come from a Momento blog, and Momento sells a managed Valkey service, so the source is a vendor, not an independent suite or peer-reviewed paper. Same rule as other vendor-blog evidence in waves 5-6: tier C.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Valkey 8.1.1 999.8K RPS on SET @0.8ms p99 vs Redis 8.0 729.4K RPS on SET @0.99ms p99 (37% higher SET throughput); ~16% higher GET throughput and '60%+ faster' p99 read latencies vs Redis (derived from page data)
corrected_fields.workload: valkey-benchmark: 50M SET operations followed by 50M GET operations, 1KB item values, 3,000,000-key keyspace, ~500 connections (tuned per system), single node, --threads 6
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: valkey-benchmark run with --threads 6; compiler/build flags for the Valkey and Redis server binaries themselves are not stated
corrected_fields.caveats: Momento (the blog's publisher) is a caching-as-a-service vendor that also sells Valkey-based products (valkey-router, valkey-operator), so it is not a fully neutral third party even though it is independent of the Valkey project itself; the article includes a 'Try it Yourself' reproduction section but does not link a public benchmark-code repository, so it falls short of tier A. A secondary aggregator blog (andrewbaker.ninja, 2026-01-04) cites the same 37%/999.8K-RPS figures, corroborating they were not altered in transmission.

name: Cachelot
workload: A Python script (test/memory_consumption.py) generates 2GB of random keys (10-60 chars) and values in four size ranges: 10B-1KB, 1-4KB, 4KB-1MB, and 10B-1MB. It fills cachelotd and Memcached, each limited to 2GB, over 10 shuffled runs and measures 'effective memory', the total bytes of surviving keys and values.
claimed_speedup: The page says Cachelot 'keeps more items in the same amount of RAM than Memcached (saves up to 15% RAM, depending on the data and store patterns)', with 5-7% metadata overhead. The chart data (benchmarks.js, 2048MB budget, 10 runs) shows effective memory of 91.2-93.9% vs 79.5% for Memcached on small values (10B-1KB), 94.2-98.6% vs 86.7% on 1-4KB, 93.3-96.9% vs 87.2-87.3% on 4KB-1MB, and 93.4-97.4% vs 86.9-87.0% on mixed. That is up to about 14.4 points of the budget, or 7-18% more stored data (derived from page data). The README says Cachelot 'is faster in terms of latency' but gives no numbers.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded server design (scales via sharding/multiple processes, not one multithreaded process); fixed pre-allocated memory pool; only a subset of the memcached wire protocol
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, flags or Memcached version are stated for the vs-Memcached test. It measures memory efficiency only; the latency claim has no numbers, and a memslap throughput script (src/benchmark/memslap_benchmark.sh) exists with no published results. The current script's MEMORY_LIMIT is 4GB while the page reports 2GB runs. There is no independent verification. The last commit on master was 2023-04-12 (pushed_at 2024-08-07 is not a commit), over 3 years ago.
found_via: GitHub: search 'cachelot memcached' -> README's 'What is Cachelot Distributed Cache Server' section linking to the cachelot.io benchmarks page

verification.tier_reason: First-party cachelot.io chart compares Cachelot vs Memcached effective memory under a 2GB limit across four value-size datasets. The benchmark script (test/memory_consumption.py) is public, but no CPU, compiler, flags or Memcached version are stated, so it is C.
verification.notes: The page shows a real vs-Memcached memory comparison. The '15%' is the page's own 'saves up to 15% RAM' wording, not 'more usable data'; the chart implies 7-18% more stored bytes. last_commit was the pushed_at date; the real last commit is 2023-04-12, which makes the project abandoned rather than stale. BSD-2-Clause and 376 stars confirmed.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Cachelot keeps up to 15% more usable data than Memcached in the same RAM budget (per the cachelot.io benchmark page, with ~5-7% metadata overhead); README also states Cachelot 'is faster in terms of latency' but gives no latency numbers on the pages checked
corrected_fields.workload: LRU cache benchmark: 2GB of random keys/values (1-4KB range) loaded into both Cachelot and Memcached under a 2GB memory limit each, measuring total 'effective memory' (surviving key/value bytes) retained
corrected_fields.caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or flags stated for the vs-Memcached benchmark; only a memory-efficiency percentage and a qualitative latency claim are given, with no independent verification; project has been stale since mid-2024

name: Dragonfly
workload: memtier_benchmark SET/GET ops (-d 256) against Redis on m5.large/m5.xlarge, and against Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge; also idle/peak memory usage during BGSAVE-equivalent snapshot
claimed_speedup: Vendor README: on c6gn.16xlarge, 25x the throughput of a single single-threaded Redis process, crossing 3.8M QPS. Vs Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge: SET 3,844K vs 806K QPS (~4.8x) and GET 3,717K vs 2,100K QPS (~1.8x) (ratios derived from page data); Memcached had the lower GET p99 (0.34 ms vs 1 ms). Vs Redis on m5.large: about parity (SET 173K vs 159K; GET 191K vs 194K). Vs Redis on m5.xlarge: SET 279K vs 190K, GET 305K vs 220K. Memory: ~30% lower idle memory than Redis, and Redis peak during BGSAVE was almost 3x Dragonfly's. The 25x is contested. Redis's June 2022 rebuttal ran a 40-shard Redis 7.0 Cluster on the same c6gn.16xlarge and reported 18-40% MORE throughput than Dragonfly (e.g. GET pipeline 1: 4.43M vs 3.8M reproduced). The third-party tidwall/cache-benchmarks (c8g.8xlarge; Dragonfly 1.30.3 vs Redis 8.2.1 with io-threads) shows mixed results. Redis is faster at 8 server threads (GET 1.51M vs 1.41M), and Dragonfly is ~2.2x faster at 16 threads (GET 2.94M vs 1.32M). Memcached beats Dragonfly on GET at every thread count and pipeline depth.
hardware: AWS m5.large, m5.xlarge, c6gn.16xlarge, r6g/c7g (instance types stated; CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Business Source License restricts running it as a competing hosted service (converts to Apache-2.0 on 2030-11-01); single shared-nothing multi-threaded architecture differs operationally from Redis single-thread model
caveats: The 25x headline is a vendor claim against one single-threaded Redis process on a 64-vCPU instance, which is not how Redis is scaled. Redis's own 2022 test on the same c6gn.16xlarge with a 40-shard Redis 7.0 Cluster measured 18-40% higher throughput than Dragonfly. That test is also vendor-run and dates from 2022, against Dragonfly built on 2022-06-03. The README states no CPU model, compiler, flags or baseline versions, and publishes no benchmark code. The earlier caveat that tidwall/cache-benchmarks 'corroborates Dragonfly beating Redis/Memcached' is wrong. In that suite Dragonfly beats Redis 8.2.1 (io-threads) only at higher thread counts, loses to it at 8 server threads, and loses to memcached on GET in every configuration; that suite's author also makes the competing Pogocache. License is BUSL-1.1 (not OSI; Apache-2.0 on the Change Date of 2030-11-01, and production use is restricted for competing in-memory data store services).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/dragonflydb/dragonfly (seeded from prior knowledge of 'modern replacement for Redis and Memcached'); README benchmarks section opened directly

verification.tier_reason: First-party README numbers only. It gives memtier command lines and AWS instance types, but no CPU model, compiler, flags, Redis/Memcached versions or server configs, and no benchmark code is published. Redis's own 2022 reproduction on the same instance contradicts the headline.
verification.notes: The README numbers are transcribed accurately, but the headline overstates the win against a fairly configured Redis. Evidence from independent or third-party sources is contradictory or mixed. Tier stays C. The verdict is downgrade because the claim is overstated and the corroboration caveat was wrong. Metadata checks out: LICENSE.md is BSL 1.1 (gh reports NOASSERTION), 31,688 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, active.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: up to 25x throughput vs a single Redis process on c6gn.16xlarge (3.8M QPS); ~4.8x SET QPS vs Memcached (3844K vs 806K) on c6gn.16xlarge; ~30% more memory efficient than Redis at idle
corrected_fields.caveats: First-party README benchmark; AWS instance type given but exact CPU model, compiler, and build flags are not stated, so numbers cannot be independently reproduced from the README alone. A separate independent-ish suite (tidwall/cache-benchmarks) corroborates Dragonfly beating Redis/Memcached on AWS c8g.8xlarge with stated versions (see the Pogocache entry in this file).

name: EloqKV
workload: memtier_benchmark write-only (ratio 1:0), read-only (ratio 0:1), and mixed (ratio 1:10 put:get) workloads against a single-node in-memory-only (persistence/WAL disabled) instance, 128-byte values, 5,000,000-key keyspace, concurrency swept from 128 to 1024 (32 threads x 4/8/16/32 clients), 300s test runs
claimed_speedup: Text: 'EloqKV and DragonflyDB both outperform Redis due to their support for multiple worker threads' and 'both significantly outperform Redis, both in throughput and in latency'. The chart images (read by eye, approximate) show Redis flat at about 200 KOps at every concurrency. EloqKV is about 950 KOps at 128 connections, about 1,400 at 256, and about 1,600-1,700 at 512-1024, roughly 4.5-8.5x Redis. Redis P999 reaches about 11-12 ms at 1024 connections vs about 3 ms for EloqKV. DragonflyDB is slightly ahead of EloqKV throughout.
hardware: AWS EC2, region us-east-1, Ubuntu 22.04: server = c7g.8xlarge (Graviton, ARM64) running Redis 7.2.5 / DragonflyDB 1.21.2 / EloqKV 0.7.4 one at a time; client = c6gn.8xlarge running memtier_benchmark
tradeoffs: EloqKV splits compute/logging/storage into separate services (TxService + LogService + Storage Service) and enables io_uring by default, requiring --privileged and custom ulimits in Docker; adds full ACID distributed transactions (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, cross-node, no CROSSSLOT) that Redis lacks, at the cost of architectural complexity; for this specific cache-mode benchmark EloqKV had its own persistent storage and WAL turned off to make the comparison to Redis/DragonflyDB fair, so it does not exercise EloqKV's durability path.
caveats: This is a first-party benchmark by EloqData, the company behind EloqKV, not an independent third party. The live URL eloqdata.com/blog/2024/08/17/benchmark-single-node returns HTTP 404 and www.eloqdata.com did not connect as of 2026-09-26; the content comes from a Wayback snapshot dated 2026-06-16. Redis was started as 'redis-server --save "" --appendonly no' with no --io-threads, so single-threaded Redis was compared against multi-threaded servers on a 32-vCPU box. The page itself concedes that Redis would normally be scaled out as a cluster. No compiler or build flags are given for any server. The README cites 'up to 1.6M QPS on AWS c6g.8xlarge' while the blog used c7g.8xlarge. License: the eloqkv repo (the Redis API layer) is dual GPLv2 or AGPLv3 with no 'or later' in LICENSE or the source headers. Its required core submodule eloqdata/tx_service (Data Substrate) is under the Business Source License 2.0 (non-OSI; Change Date 2031-01-08 to Apache-2.0), so a full build is not all-OSI.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'kvrocks' surfaced 'Show HN: EloqKV - Scalable distributed ACID key-value database with Redis API' -> github.com/eloqdata/eloqkv README 'Benchmark' section -> linked blog post (recovered via web.archive.org)

verification.tier_reason: EloqData's own blog (2024-08-17, Wayback 2026-06-16) runs EloqKV 0.7.4 against Redis 7.2.5 and DragonflyDB 1.21.2 on c7g.8xlarge with full memtier commands. It says both 'significantly outperform Redis', with throughput and P999 shown only in chart images. The numbers are first-party, and no compiler, flags or CPU model beyond the instance type are given, so it is C.
verification.notes: Tier C and the claim hold. I corrected the license from '-or-later' to '-only' per the LICENSE and file headers. I changed usability to 'mixed' because the tx_service core submodule is BSL. I read approximate values off the three archived chart images. Metadata matches: 1,501 stars, last commit 2026-09-17, not a fork, not archived.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 'EloqKV and DragonflyDB both outperform Redis due to their support for multiple worker threads' on throughput and p99.9 latency across write-only, read-only and mixed workloads; EloqKV throughput/latency described as 'almost the same' as DragonflyDB and both 'significantly outperform Redis' -- exact ops/sec are shown only as chart images on the source page, not printed as text
corrected_fields.caveats: This is a first-party benchmark authored and run by EloqData (the company behind EloqKV), not an independent third party -- per methodology it is capped at tier C despite detailed hardware/version/command documentation. Live URL eloqdata.com/blog/2024/08/17/benchmark-single-node returns HTTP 404 as of 2026-09-26 (blog appears to have been restructured); content was recovered via a Wayback Machine snapshot dated 2026-06-16. No compiler or build flags are given for any of the three server binaries. License field is NOASSERTION on the GitHub API; the repo's LICENSE file states a dual GPLv2-or-AGPLv3 choice.

name: IKV (Inlined Key-Value Store)
workload: Custom Java multithreaded client (inlinedio/ikv-java-client benchmarks; JedisCluster for Redis) issuing blocking single-field GETs at fixed loads (25K/50K/100K/1M/3M QPS). It used 16 threads, 1M docs (~15 B keys, 3x50 B fields) and a 30 s window, against IKV embedded in the client process and a 16-shard ElastiCache Redis 7.1 cluster in the same AZ. A second test used tiered storage with Zipfian keys, 6000 B values and 16 IKV threads, against a 1-thread, 1-shard ElastiCache Redis.
claimed_speedup: In-memory GET with 16 client threads over 1M docs (150 B values), at 100K QPS: IKV avg 3.13 us / p50 2.89 / p99 5.65 vs a 16-shard AWS ElastiCache Redis 7.1 cluster at avg 319 us / p50 305 / p99 514 (~100x lower latency, derived from page data). IKV also held 1M and 3M QPS, which Redis could not reach from the single client. In the tiered test (1:4 memory:data, Zipfian), IKV averaged 118.25 us vs 225.06 us for in-memory 1-shard Redis (~1.9x, derived from page data), but IKV's p99 was worse (747.65 us vs 348.88 us). The ~100x gap is mostly the network round trip that embedding removes (an in-process lookup vs a remote ElastiCache call over TCP), not a faster storage engine.
hardware: In-memory test: client and embedded IKV on AWS c5.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GiB). Redis was AWS ElastiCache Redis 7.1 with 16 shards (1 primary, 0 replicas each) on cache.r5.xlarge nodes in the same AZ (us-west-2a). Tiered test: client on c5d.4xlarge (400 GiB local SSD) vs 1-shard ElastiCache cache.r6g.xlarge / cache.r6gd.xlarge. CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: IKV is an embedded/in-process library colocated with the application (no network hop) rather than a shared remote cache, so much of the 100x gap is network round-trip elimination rather than a faster core engine; eventual consistency instead of Redis's stronger read-after-write guarantees; requires a separate data-plane (streams/object storage) to keep embedded replicas in sync
caveats: The full report (Google Doc, readable through its txt export) gives instance types but no CPU model, compiler or flags. The comparison is embedded (in-process, no network) vs networked (remote ElastiCache over TCP through the Jedis client). That makes it a valid deployment-architecture comparison for read-heavy, eventually consistent ML feature serving, but not a like-for-like engine comparison. Most of Redis's ~300 us is network round trip plus client overhead. A fair engine test would use Redis over localhost or a Unix socket, or another embedded KV. The tiered '2x faster than Redis' holds for average latency only: p99 is worse for IKV (747.65 vs 348.88 us). The tiered test used 16 IKV threads vs 1 Redis thread, and the report's text and table disagree on thread counts. A single client machine drove the load. The repo is stale (last commit 2024-05-14).
found_via: HN Algolia: query 'faster than redis' -> 'IKV: embedded key-value store, 100x faster than Redis' (github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store); repo README opened directly

verification.tier_reason: First-party numbers. The README table and the linked Google Doc report give AWS instance types, dataset, thread counts and time windows. The benchmark tooling is public in inlinedio/ikv-java-client (src/main/java/io/inlined/benchmarks, MultiThreadedRunner, with a JedisCluster client for Redis), but no CPU model, compiler or flags are stated, so C.
verification.notes: Judgment on the embedded-vs-networked comparison: it is a legitimate real-use-case latency win, but '100x faster than Redis' mostly measures removing the network hop, not IKV's engine against Redis's engine. The claim is overstated as a library-speed claim. Tier stays C. I was able to read the Google Doc report, which fills in hardware and methodology. Metadata checks out: MIT, 227 stars, last commit 2024-05-14, stale, not a fork. Not notable (<1k stars), but it has real numbers against a named baseline, so it is not a reject.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: at 100K QPS: IKV avg 3.13us/p50 2.89us/p99 5.65us vs Redis Cluster avg 319us/p50 305us/p99 514us (roughly 100x lower average latency); README also claims embedded local Flash/SSD-backed IKV is still ~2x faster than an all-in-memory remote Redis cluster
corrected_fields.workload: Multi-threaded client issuing blocking GET calls at fixed QPS levels (25K/50K/100K) against IKV (embedded, in-process) vs a 16-shard Redis Cluster on AWS ElastiCache; measuring avg/p50/p99 response time in microseconds
corrected_fields.caveats: First-party README claim; linked full report is a Google Doc that could not be fully read in this session (only its title, 'IKV Perf Benchmarks | A comparison with Redis', was visible), so hardware/CPU model and compiler flags are unconfirmed; comparing an embedded cache against a networked cache is not entirely apples-to-apples for a 'faster engine' claim, though it is a legitimate real-workload latency win for the intended use case (ML feature serving)

name: KeyDB
workload: memtier_benchmark --tls --threads=32 (op mix/key sizes not stated on page, i.e. memtier defaults); client on AWS m5.8xlarge (32 cores), KeyDB/Redis servers on m5.4xlarge; KeyDB --server-threads 16 --server-thread-affinity true vs Redis 6 TLS (no io-threads in its TLS start command)

hardware: AWS m5.8xlarge (client, 32 cores), m5.4xlarge (server instances) — CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Multithreading changes the concurrency/atomicity model vs Redis (MVCC-style access under a global lock for KEYS/SCAN); staying in sync with upstream Redis features is ongoing maintenance burden for a fork
caveats: First-party blog benchmark (KeyDB's own team); AWS instance types stated but not the CPU model, compiler, or build flags; memtier op mix and key sizes not stated; Redis TLS run was started without io-threads while KeyDB used 16 server threads; repository has had no commits since April 2024 even though the fork's changes are still substantive vs upstream Redis

name: RAMCloud
workload: YCSB workloads A, B, C, D, F (E omitted, no scans), 1 KB objects, 100M operations per client, 24 YCSB clients on 24 nodes against 12 storage-server nodes, triple replication; Redis 2.6.14 and HyperDex 1.0rc4 used kernel sockets over Infiniband, and RAMCloud ran both with kernel sockets and with its kernel-bypass Infiniband Verbs transport at 75% and 90% memory utilisation
claimed_speedup: FAST '14 paper, Figure 12: RAMCloud outperforms Redis on the read-heavy YCSB workloads B, C and D with both kernel sockets and Verbs, and the Verbs transport 'more than doubles read throughput' compared with RAMCloud on kernel sockets. On the write-heavy workloads A and F, RAMCloud with kernel sockets trails Redis, and with Verbs it matches Redis write throughput at 75% utilisation but is 25% slower than Redis on workload A at 90%. Exact per-bar values appear only in the figure. Separately, the project wiki claims reads in as little as 5us and writes under 15us, calling RAMCloud '10-1000x faster than other available alternatives', and contrasts it with memcached only in words.
hardware: 80-node cluster: Xeon X3470 (4x2.93 GHz, 3.6 GHz Turbo), 24 GB DDR3-800, 2x Crucial M4 128 GB SSDs, Mellanox ConnectX-2 Infiniband HCA, Mellanox SX6036 4X FDR switch, Linux 2.6.32
tradeoffs: Requires keeping the whole dataset in DRAM across a cluster (disk/flash used only for backup logging), unlike Memcached's standalone cache-aside model; needs a full cluster (coordinator + masters + backups) rather than a single process; lowest latencies assume InfiniBand/kernel-bypass transport
caveats: The win over Redis holds only for the read-heavy workloads; RAMCloud trails or ties Redis on write-heavy YCSB A/F. The comparison is not like-for-like on durability: RAMCloud waits for synchronous triple replication, while Redis used append-only logging with a 1s fsync and asynchronous replicas. The best RAMCloud numbers need Infiniband kernel bypass (Verbs). The baseline is Redis 2.6.14 from 2013, and the paper is by the RAMCloud authors. Exact values are only in a bar chart, and no compiler or flags are stated. The wiki's 5us/15us and '10-1000x' figures are marketing with no methodology, and the memcached contrast is qualitative only (the TOCS 2015 paper cites ~300us memcached latency at Facebook from a personal communication, not from a benchmark). The project is marked 'No Longer Maintained', with its last commit in 2019. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is plain ISC.
found_via: GitHub: search 'RAMCloud' (cross-referenced from MICA paper's compared-systems list); RAMCloud project wiki 'What is RAMCloud?' overview page

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from C to B on stronger evidence: the peer-reviewed FAST '14 paper (Rumble, Kejriwal, Ousterhout, 'Log-structured Memory for DRAM-based Storage', Section 8.7, Figure 12) measures RAMCloud against Redis 2.6.14 and HyperDex on YCSB and shows RAMCloud ahead on the read-heavy workloads. It is not A because the paper gives no compiler or flags and no YCSB driver path, and the original wiki page only contrasts with memcached in words (5us/15us, '10-1000x faster than other available alternatives'), which alone would be C.
verification.notes: The wiki page does contain the quoted 5us/15us and '10-1000x' text, but it names memcached only in words, so I switched the record's evidence to the FAST '14 YCSB comparison against Redis, which is peer-reviewed. The record's metric should become 'throughput' because the paper compares throughput and metric is not a correctable field. If the orchestrator wants memcached kept as the baseline, the tier falls back to C. Metadata checked: ISC LICENSE file, not a fork, not archived, 503 stars, last commit 2019-10-16, abandoned.

corrected_fields.workload: Remote object read/write over a datacenter network via RAMCloud's own low-latency RPC stack, contrasted qualitatively with Memcached-style caches that must fall back to disk/flash on cache misses
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Project overview states reads complete in as little as 5us and writes in under 15us, describing this as '10-1000x faster than other available alternatives' and explicitly contrasting with Memcached-style caches that must handle misses and disk/flash access
corrected_fields.caveats: The 5us/15us and '10-1000x' figures appear on the project's own wiki overview page without a stated CPU model, compiler, or reproducible benchmark harness on that page (Tier C, not A/B); '10-1000x' reads as a general marketing figure rather than a specific measured ratio against Memcached; project is explicitly marked no longer maintained, last commit 2019

name: RapidKV
workload: memtier_benchmark (8 threads, 25 clients/thread, CPU-pinned via taskset) against RapidKV and Redis on the same machine, with Redis persistence disabled and both servers restarted between runs. Runs: baseline pipeline=1, 1:1 SET:GET, 8B values, 100K keys; mixed pipeline=16, 1:9 SET:GET, 64B values, 200K keys; pipeline-depth sweep (1/10/100/200/500), 1:9 SET:GET, 8B values, 1M keys, 30s runs; plus 2KB-value (pipeline=64), SET-only 128B and GET-only runs
claimed_speedup: At pipeline=1 throughput is within 4% (135,165 vs 130,019 ops/sec) but p99 latency is 49% lower; at pipeline=16 mixed workload RapidKV is +63% ops/sec (1,823,366 vs 1,119,012) with 58% lower p99; at pipeline=100 RapidKV reaches 5,178,742 vs Redis's 1,718,018 ops/sec, a 3.01x speedup; author's headline figure is 'up to ~4.2x faster than Redis on pipelined workloads' (pipeline=500)
compiler_and_flags: Compiler used for the benchmarks not stated (README requires GCC 12+/Clang 15+/MSVC 2022+); the CMakeLists Release build uses -O3 -march=native -flto on GCC/Clang
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 4800H (8C/16T, 2.9GHz base), 16GB RAM, 32KiB L1d/L1i x8, 512KiB L2 x8, 4096KiB L3 x2, Kubuntu 24.04 LTS
tradeoffs: Single-threaded, no multi-core scaling; implements only a small subset of Redis commands (PING/ECHO/SET/GET/DEL/EXISTS/INCR/DECR/INCRBY/DECRBY/EXPIRE/PERSIST/TTL - no lists/hashes/sets/pub-sub/persistence/replication); SIEVE eviction approximates LRU rather than exact LRU
caveats: The benchmark is first-party and self-run with no independent verification. The compiler and Redis version are not stated, Redis io-threads settings are not stated, and the memtier command lines are not scripted in the repo (Tier C). The 4.2x headline is the best case at pipeline=500; at pipeline=1, throughput is at parity (+4% in one run, 0.99x in the sweep). The comparison is not feature-equivalent: RapidKV is single-threaded with string-only values, no persistence, replication, AUTH or TLS, and 13 commands against Redis's 400+. The repo has 1 star, and its first commit was 2026-01-31.
found_via: GitHub: search 'faster than Redis' language:C++

verification.tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section shows first-party memtier_benchmark tables against Redis on an AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, and every quoted number matches (130,019 vs 135,165; 1,119,012 vs 1,823,366; 1,718,018 vs 5,178,742 = 3.01x; 4.23x at pipeline=500). It stays C, not A: the memtier command lines are not scripted in the repo, the compiler and Redis version used are not stated, and benchmarks/ holds only Google Benchmark microbenchmarks.
verification.notes: The README also has Google Benchmark microbenchmarks against std: its FlatMap is 1.5-2.6x faster than std::unordered_map, and CompactString is up to 5.8x faster than std::string on moves. These could matter for the C++-first catalog, but compiler and flags for those runs are not stated either. Metadata checked: MIT, not a fork, not archived, 1 star, last commit 2026-05-10 (active).

name: W-TinyLFU (C++ header-only, based on the TinyLFU paper)
workload: Synthetic Zipf(0.7/0.94) and SPC1-like traces plus real YouTube/Wikipedia/DS1/S3/OLTP traces evaluated for hit ratio, comparing TinyLFU-admission-augmented LRU/Random/LFU against plain LRU, ARC, SLRU, LRU-K and others (algorithm's own paper; this specific repo is an independent C++11 header-only reimplementation)
claimed_speedup: Per the paper (not this port), W-TinyLFU with a 1% window matched or beat every other evaluated policy on the majority of traces, including LRU, ARC and LIRS. It outperformed all other policies on DS1, SPC1-like and the search-engine traces. On OLTP, F1 and F2, the 1% window was not the top performer; a 20-40% window was needed. On P8/P12 it led at all but the largest cache sizes. The ~89% figure is TinyLFU's memory saving over a strawman sliding-window sketch (Zipf 0.9, 1K cache, 9K histogram), not a result against LRU.
tradeoffs: This specific repo explicitly omits thread-safety and hash-collision protection ('barebones' header-only port); the underlying TinyLFU paper's hit-ratio numbers come from a Java prototype and from Caffeine, not from this C++ port directly
caveats: The quantitative hit-ratio results come from the original paper's Java simulator and Caffeine evaluation. They were not re-measured on this C++11 header-only port, so the entry is tier C even though the algorithm's paper is well cited. The README says thread-safety and hash-collision protection are absent. The repo has no LICENSE file. Caffeine itself (the canonical TinyLFU implementation) is already catalogued and excluded.
found_via: gh search repos 'TinyLFU'; arXiv abs/1512.00727 and PDF

verification.tier_reason: The TinyLFU paper (arXiv 1512.00727v2) plots hit ratio against LRU, ARC, LIRS and others, but those results come from the authors' Java simulator and Caffeine, not from this C++ port. The repo has no benchmark of its own, so it stays at C for this entry.
verification.notes: The claim 'best on every tested trace' is overstated: the paper's own OLTP/F1/F2 results show the default 1% window losing, and the abstract's 'equal or better' wording is qualified in Section 5. The metadata checks out: no license (gh license null, no LICENSE file in the root), 64 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2018-10-24 (abandoned). This is a small independent reimplementation.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: W-TinyLFU matches or beats every other evaluated policy's hit ratio on every tested trace ('the only scheme to obtain such good results on all traces' per the paper); e.g. reduces the frequency-sketch memory needed versus a naive counting approach by ~89% in the reported Zipf-0.9 experiment
corrected_fields.caveats: The quantitative hit-ratio claims are from the original paper's Java/Caffeine evaluation, not independently re-measured against this specific C++ header-only port, so this is tier C for this repo despite the algorithm's own paper being well cited; Caffeine itself (the canonical TinyLFU implementation) is already catalogued and excluded

name: ALP (Adaptive Lossless Floating-Point Compression)
baseline: Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas (existing lightweight and general-purpose floating-point compressors)
workload: Single/multi-threaded (1/8/16 thread) SCAN and SUM queries over compressed double/float columns from real-world datasets (food_prices, city_temperature, bitcoin_transactions, gov26, nyc29), plus separate compression-ratio benchmarks over the Public BI float/double corpus.
claimed_speedup: SIGMOD'24 paper Table 5 (Ice Lake micro-benchmark, tuples per cycle, averaged over all datasets): ALP compresses 14x faster than Zstd, 9x faster than Gorilla, 12x faster than Chimp and Chimp128, 8x faster than Patas, 47x faster than Elf and 251x faster than PDE. It decompresses 26x faster than Zstd, 55x than Gorilla, 66x than Chimp, 65x than Chimp128, 17x than Patas, 215x than Elf and 7x than PDE. Figure 1: '1-2 orders of magnitude faster in [de]compression than all competing schemes'. End-to-end in Tectorwise (Table 6, Figure 6): SCAN and SUM on ALP beat every other scheme and even uncompressed data. City-Temp compression is 4x faster than Patas and 7x faster than Gorilla, and Zstd is 11x slower. Compression ratio (Table 4): ALP averages 21.7 bits/value against Zstd's 20.6, so Zstd is slightly better on average; ALP beats all the other schemes.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ (the root CMakeLists allows only Clang; toolchain/i4i_4xlarge.cmake uses /usr/bin/clang++; version not stated). -O3 per the paper. bench_end_to_end CMake adds -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx512dq. Scalar variant: -O3 -fno-slp-vectorize -fno-vectorize. g++ is used only to build the PDE baseline.
hardware: Main results (Figure 1, Table 5, end-to-end Figure 6 and Table 6) on Intel Ice Lake Xeon 8375C at 3.5 GHz (AWS i4i.4xlarge; the end-to-end run used 16 cores / 32 SMT and 256 GB RAM). Decompression was also run on AMD EPYC 7R13 (Zen3), Apple M1, AWS Graviton2 (Neoverse-N1) and Graviton3 (Paper Table 3).
stars_or_usage: 234 stars; integrated into DuckDB, KuzuDB, and liquid-cache
tradeoffs: Targets IEEE754 float/double columns specifically, not general-purpose compression; decimal-heavy data benefits most, high-entropy/high-precision random values compress less well and fall back to a dictionary+FoR split scheme.
caveats: The headline numbers are the authors' own (SIGMOD 2024), backed by the SIGMOD ARI package with all three badges (including Results Reproduced) and the SIGMOD Best Artifact Award. The paper is openly available at ir.cwi.nl/pub/33334/33334.pdf and bronze-OA at ACM. Zstd matches or slightly beats ALP's compression ratio on average (20.6 vs 21.7 bits/value); ALP only wins on ratio when cascaded with other lightweight encodings. The ARI report says the Figure 6 plotting script is missing. The repo CSV publication/end_to_end_bench/result holds raw cycle counts, not ratios.
found_via: Linked from the FastLanes README publications list; repo's availability_reproducibility_initiative_report.md

verification.tier_reason: The SIGMOD 2024 paper (open copy at ir.cwi.nl) compares ALP with Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas, PDE and Elf. It names the CPU model (Intel Xeon 8375C Ice Lake, Table 3) and the -O3 flags, and the repo sets the compiler (toolchain/i4i_4xlarge.cmake uses clang++, and CMake allows only Clang). The benchmark code is public: publication/source_code/bench_speed, bench_end_to_end (-O3 -march=native -mavx512dq) and bench_compression_ratio, run by publication/script/master_script.sh. That meets tier A.
verification.notes: The record's claim that the paper is paywalled with no preprint is wrong: the CWI repository hosts the full PDF, and I read it. I kept tier A. I replaced the vague claimed_speedup with the Table 5 multipliers and softened the compression-ratio claim against Zstd. The raw end-to-end CSV agrees with the paper: summed cycles show SCAN on ALP about 18-20x cheaper than on Zstd with one thread (derived from page data).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ALP is reported superior in decoding speed, compression ratio, and compression speed across every tested scheme (Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas, Zstd, uncompressed, PDE) per the paper's results and the repo's benchmark CSVs; exact multipliers are in the repo's publication/end_to_end_bench results
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Clang++/g++ via CMake (>=3.22); exact build steps and flags documented in BENCHMARKING.md and run by publication/script/master_script.sh
corrected_fields.hardware: Multiple documented target platforms in the reproducibility package: Intel Ice Lake (AVX512, e.g. AWS i4i.4xlarge), AMD Zen 3 (AVX2, AWS M6a/C6a), Apple M1, AWS Graviton 2/3 (NEON)
corrected_fields.caveats: The SIGMOD 2024 paper itself is paywalled and has no arXiv preprint, so the exact headline multiplier was not read from the paper directly. Tier A is justified instead by the repo's ACM SIGMOD Availability & Reproducibility Initiative package (all three badges, including 'Results Reproduced'), which documents hardware, dependencies, and build/run steps end to end, and by the benchmark CSVs present in the repo.

name: Bodo DataFrames
language: Python (JIT-compiled to native code via an MPI-based C++ runtime)
workload: NYC Taxi FHVHV 'monthly trips with precipitation': the 1,036,465,968-row / 24-column Parquet dataset (24.7 GiB, read from S3) is joined with the 5,538-row Central Park weather CSV. A per-row Python UDF assigns hour-of-day buckets, then the job groups by count and mean trip_miles, sorts, and writes Parquet. The README says 'average trip duration', but the code aggregates trip distance. Single-node run on one AWS r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM).
claimed_speedup: Measured with the Bodo JIT path (run_bodo.py --use_jit), not the Bodo DataFrames pandas API. Single r6i.16xlarge (Mar 2025): Bodo 27.71s vs Polars 282.34s (~10.2x) and vs Daft 69.59s (~2.5x). 4x r6i.16xlarge (Dec 2024): Bodo 17s vs PySpark 389s, Dask 915s and Modin+Ray 4155s; the chart labels these 20x / 50x / 250x, while the README text says '20-240x'. 4 nodes vs Daft (Mar 2025): 17.54s vs 37.78s (~2x). The same README's laptop-scale table shows the Bodo DataFrames API slower than Polars: 5.63s vs 1.244s, and 10.221s vs 4.744s on ~20M rows (derived from page data).
hardware: AWS EC2 r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM); cluster variant uses 4x r6i.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Drop-in pandas-API replacement but relies on JIT compilation and MPI for parallelism; the Bodo Platform build used for the cluster run links a forked version of Arrow for faster Parquet reads (bodo-ai/arrow-cpp-feedstock), a deviation from stock Apache Arrow
caveats: First-party benchmark (Bodo's own repo), not an independent suite, and numbers are read from bar-chart PNGs rather than a raw results table. The charts measure the Bodo JIT path: the main README carries a 'TODO: updated graph with Taxi benchmark including Bodo DataFrames Pandas API', and the benchmark README's laptop table shows the Bodo DataFrames API slower than Polars (5.63s vs 1.244s; 10.221s vs 4.744s). The Polars implementation buckets hours with map_elements and a Python UDF (row-by-row Python over ~1B rows), which Bodo JIT compiles to native code, so the ~10x single-node gap largely reflects a non-idiomatic Polars baseline. Bodo ran on the Bodo Platform with a forked Arrow for faster Parquet reads. The package table lists bodo 2025.8.2 while the charts date from Dec 2024 / Mar 2025. No compiler/flags are given, and the CPU is identified only by instance type. The single-node comparison excludes pandas.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/bodo-ai/bodo (README benchmarks section)

The per-system scripts are public (benchmarks/nyc_taxi/bodo/, benchmarks/nyc_taxi/polars/, benchmarks/nyc_taxi/daft/), and the README gives the instance type (r6i.16xlarge) and package versions. But results appear only as PNG bar charts, and no CPU model, compiler or flags are stated, so this falls short of A. It is not an independent suite, so it is C.

name: BtrBlocks
baseline: Apache Parquet (generated/read via the Apache Arrow C++ library) and Apache ORC
workload: In-memory decompression throughput and S3 cold-column-scan dollar-cost, measured on the 5 largest Public BI Benchmark datasets (~2451 columns) and all 22 TPC-H queries.
claimed_speedup: Public BI in-memory decompression: 2.6x, 3.6x and 3.8x faster than Parquet, Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd on average. TPC-H in-memory: 2.6x, 3.9x and 4.2x faster. S3 column scans on Public BI are 9x cheaper than compressed Parquet variants and 20x cheaper than uncompressed Parquet on average. Over all 22 TPC-H queries, Parquet, Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd cost 5.5x, 3.6x and 2.8x more than BtrBlocks.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.1 on Amazon Linux 2, kernel 5.10 (paper). The paper states no optimization flags; the repo CMakeLists adds -march=native -g on top of the CMake build-type defaults.
hardware: AWS c5n.18xlarge: Intel Xeon Platinum 8000 series (Skylake-SP), 36 x 3.5 GHz cores (72 threads, hyperthreading disabled for benchmarks), AVX2/AVX512, 192 GiB RAM, 100 Gbit networking
tradeoffs: README states it 'currently requires an x86 platform' and is only built/tested on Linux and macOS; test suite described as 'rudimentary'; no true random-access-by-row API (would require reimplementation, per a later independent evaluation).
caveats: These are the SIGMOD 2023 authors' own measurements. The Parquet/ORC comparison harness and exact build flags are not published; the repo's engine-comparison directory says it was removed because of DeWitt clauses. A later VLDB 2025 paper by competing FastLanes authors (not independent) re-ran BtrBlocks on an AWS i4i.4xlarge. It found BtrBlocks decoded about 7x slower than FastLanes (encoding was 1.37x slower, derived from that paper's Table 4). BtrBlocks gained nothing from AVX512 and could not do single-value random access without an API reimplementation. On compression ratio BtrBlocks was +18% larger than FastLanes on Public BI, versus +2% for Parquet+Zstd.

name: FastLanes
baseline: Apache Parquet (Snappy and Zstd variants, written and read with DuckDB v1.2's Parquet implementation) and DuckDB v1.2's native storage format; also BtrBlocks
workload: Decoding/encoding throughput (rowgroups/sec) across real-world datasets and a single-value random-access latency micro-benchmark, comparing the FastLanes file format against DuckDB, Parquet+Snappy, Parquet+Zstd, and BtrBlocks.
claimed_speedup: Decoding (Table 4, i4i.4xlarge Ice Lake): on average 29x faster than DuckDB's native format, 43x faster than Parquet+Snappy, 44x faster than Parquet+Zstd and 7x faster than BtrBlocks. Totals: 16.32 ms vs 483.45, 712.55, 731.45 and 115.43 ms. Encoding is not faster: FastLanes v0.1 took 81,341.63 ms against 5,867.07 (Parquet+Snappy), 6,927.52 (Parquet+Zstd) and 20,347.82 (DuckDB). That makes it about 14x, 12x and 4x slower, and only about 1.4x faster than BtrBlocks (111,091.39 ms) (derived from page data). Random access (Table 5; text says 315x/416x/800x/5x): first-value retrieval takes 0.14 ms, 315.62x faster than Parquet+Snappy, 413.66x than Parquet+Zstd, 813.57x than BtrBlocks and 5.96x than DuckDB.
compiler_and_flags: The paper does not name the compiler (the artifact README lists 'gcc / clang'; the current FastLanes CMakeLists defaults to clang++ on non-Windows). FastLanes is built as a CMake Release. The SIMD micro-benchmark (Table 6) used -O3, -O3 -mavx2 and -O3 -mavx512dq.
hardware: All experiments on AWS EC2 i4i.4xlarge: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake), 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM (paper Sec. 4; no CPU model number given). Only the expression-pool micro-benchmark (Table 7, footnote 4) ran on an Apple MacBook Pro M4.
tradeoffs: Encoding (compression) speed in the v0.1 code path is explicitly unoptimized per the paper; the file format only recently reached format-stability (v0.36+), so tooling/ecosystem support lags far behind Parquet; zero external dependencies but currently no true random-access-by-row-position support (block decode still required).
caveats: These are the authors' own VLDB 2025 numbers (Afroozeh & Boncz, CWI). The artifact repo cwida/fastlanes-vldb2025 reproduces them. Parquet was run through DuckDB v1.2's Parquet reader and writer, not parquet-cpp/Arrow. The headline multipliers are decoding-only: FastLanes v0.1 encoding is 4-14x slower than DuckDB and Parquet and beats only BtrBlocks, which the authors attribute to an unoptimized encoder. Random access was simulated with LIMIT 1 queries on Parquet and DuckDB and with full block decoding for BtrBlocks. The table and text multipliers differ slightly (413.66x vs 416x, 813.57x vs 800x).
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for cwida FastLanes VLDB papers; PDF opened directly at vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p4629-afroozeh.pdf

verification.tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper, and its public artifact repo (cwida/fastlanes-vldb2025: master_script.py, scripts/, plus FastLanes CMake targets benchmark_decompression_time and benchmark_random_access) reproduces Tables 3-6 against Parquet, DuckDB and BtrBlocks. verification.notes: The record's '29x faster decoding/encoding' is overstated: the Table 4 multipliers are for decoding, and FastLanes encoding is slower than Parquet and DuckDB. The record also put Table 5 on the M4, but the M4 footnote belongs to the Table 7 expression-pool experiment. Metadata is confirmed: MIT, 713 stars, last commit 2026-04-22 (active, dev branch).

name: Velox
baseline: Presto Java execution engine (stock Presto vs Prestissimo, i.e. Presto with Velox C++ workers)
workload: TPC-H at 3TB (ORC, no zstd compression, lineitem/orders co-partitioned), hand-written query formulations, selected queries Q1, Q6 (CPU-bound) and Q13, Q19 (shuffle/IO-heavy), warm local cache; plus a replay of Meta production interactive-analytics traffic on two clusters with identical hardware

name: Crystal (GPU query-processing library)
baseline: OmniSci (commercial GPU OLAP DBMS, formerly MapD, now HEAVY.AI) on the same GPU. Also the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation, which is itself compared against Hyper and MonetDB.
workload: 13 Star Schema Benchmark queries at scale factor 20 (120M-row lineorder fact table, about 13 GB). String columns are dictionary-encoded to 4-byte integers and the queries are manually rewritten. Data is preloaded into device memory, and each result is the average of 3 runs. Crystal on the GPU (thread block 256, 8 items per thread per tile) is compared with OmniSci on the GPU and with an equivalent CPU implementation; Hyper and MonetDB are compared only with that CPU implementation.
claimed_speedup: Per the SIGMOD 2020 paper (Section 5.2): the Crystal-based Standalone GPU implementation is on average about 16x faster than OmniSci (a commercial GPU OLAP DBMS) on the same V100, and on average 25x faster than the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation across the 13 SSB queries. The 1.17x (vs Hyper) and 2.5x (vs MonetDB) averages belong to the authors' Standalone CPU implementation, not to Crystal on the GPU. The paper does not state direct GPU-vs-Hyper or GPU-vs-MonetDB ratios.

Hyper and MonetDB were compared only against the authors' CPU implementation. The CPU implementation and the baseline-system runs are not in the repo. The ~13 GB SF20 dataset fits in GPU memory. name: cuDF (cudf.pandas)
workload: H2O.ai/DuckDB 'database-like ops' benchmark (join and groupby operations) on a ~5GB dataset, pandas vs cudf.pandas zero-code-change GPU accelerator
claimed_speedup: Headline 'nearly 150x' (body: 'up to 150x faster', 'minutes to 1 or 2 seconds'). Figure 1 on 5GB: Join takes 4 min 27 s with pandas on CPU vs 1 s with cudf.pandas, and Groupby Advanced 4 min 34 s vs 2 s (~267x and ~137x, derived from page data with GPU times rounded to whole seconds)

The blog says some operations fall back to the CPU. Figure 1's CPU totals (4m27s, 4m34s) do not match the per-query charts, which sum to about 169s for join and about 140s for groupby-advanced. On those per-query charts, cudf.pandas takes 1.31s/0.57s (join) and about 2.85s/2.80s (groupby-advanced) over runs 1 and 2, which is about 129-293x and about 50x over pandas. name: Bespoke OLAP
workload: TPC-H (SF20) and CEB, a templated JOB workload on IMDB (SF2, query 8a excluded). An autonomous LLM synthesis pipeline builds a separate workload-specific C++ engine for each benchmark (Bespoke-TPCH, Bespoke-CEB). Headline results compare it single-threaded, pinned to the same core and in memory, against DuckDB 1.4.1 and Umbra 26.02. A 1-64 thread scaling study adds multi-threaded results.
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded, all systems pinned to the same core with data in memory: TPC-H SF20 total 4.4s vs DuckDB 49.2s (11.17x) and CEB SF2 0.4s vs 19.5s (45.33x). Vs Umbra: 7.24x (TPC-H) and 9.56x (CEB). Per-query vs DuckDB: 2.83x-102x on TPC-H and 11.6x-1500x on CEB. Multi-threaded, 1-64 threads: 7.65x vs DuckDB and 6.12x vs Umbra on TPC-H; 23.97x vs DuckDB and 1.87x vs Umbra on CEB.
compiler_and_flags: g++ (default $CXX, version unstated) with -std=c++20 -O3 -flto -fPIC -g for optimized builds (misc/fasttest/compiler.py, tools/fasttest/run.py)
hardware: AMD EPYC 9654P 96-core processor, 768GB RAM (stated in paper)
stars_or_usage: 50 stars (main repo); companion artifacts repo https://github.com/DataManagementLab/BespokeOLAP_Artifacts has 7 stars
tradeoffs: Synthesizes one engine per fixed workload ('one-size-fits-one'); not usable as a drop-in general-purpose replacement for DuckDB; per-query speedup is highly variable (as low as 2.83x, as high as 1500x)
caveats: The GitHub repo is archived (read-only) and was last pushed 2026-07-22, so it is tagged abandoned. name: GenDB
workload: TPC-H SF10 representative subset (Q1, Q3, Q6, Q9, Q18) and SEC-EDGAR: 5 GB of 2022-2024 SEC financial-statement data, with 6 queries sampled from 1,000 SQLSmith-generated ones. LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 4.6 in the paper) generate per-query C++ executables. Baselines are DuckDB v1.4.4, Umbra (February 2026), MonetDB v11.55.1, ClickHouse v26.2.1 and PostgreSQL v18.2, measured on hot, in-memory runs.
claimed_speedup: TPC-H SF10 (Q1, Q3, Q6, Q9, Q18): GenDB 214 ms total vs DuckDB 594 ms and Umbra 590 ms (2.8x), and 11.2x vs ClickHouse. Q9 runs in 38 ms, 6.1x faster than DuckDB. SEC-EDGAR (6 queries): 328 ms, 5.0x vs DuckDB and 3.9x vs Umbra. The 163x figure (TPC-H Q18, 12,147 ms to 74 ms) and the 13.3x / 12.7x figures (SEC-EDGAR Q4 / Q6) are GenDB's own gains between optimization iterations, not speedups over a baseline.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 -fopenmp (src/gendb/orchestrator.mjs; compiler version unstated)
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (2.3 GHz, 32 physical cores total), 384 GB RAM, Ubuntu (stated in paper)
tradeoffs: Generates a bespoke C++ execution program per query/workload/hardware via an LLM agent rather than being one general-purpose engine; synthesis has its own latency/cost the headline numbers don't include; early research prototype (paper: Lao & Trummer, 2026, arXiv:2603.02081)

Only 5 of the 22 TPC-H queries are used, at SF10. The compiler version is unstated. Baselines use their automatically created indexes, and a second variant adds GenDB-generated indexes. The largest multipliers in the paper (163x, 12-13x) are iteration-over-iteration self-improvements, not comparisons with a baseline.

name: JetStream
workload: TPC-H at SF=20 with periodic refreshes, plus a leakage-resistant SEC-EDGAR (SF=3) workload; an agentic pipeline generates query-specific accelerators (optionally with persistent auxiliary state) that extend an existing DBMS
claimed_speedup: Stateful accelerators: 833x geomean read-only speedup over single-threaded DuckDB on TPC-H SF=20 (the Figure 6 legend says 843x) and 3544x over PostgreSQL (the legend says 3554x). The paper compares this with 34.07x for multi-threaded GenDB and 12.35x for single-threaded Bespoke OLAP. Stateless accelerators reach only 1.99x over single-threaded DuckDB. Under TPC-H RF1/RF2 refreshes the geomean is 733x at 300 s, 629x at 120 s and 375x at 60 s. On the unseen SEC-EDGAR workload (SF=3) it is 102x over DuckDB and 486x over PostgreSQL.
hardware: Dual-socket server with 2x Intel Xeon Gold 6230 (40 physical cores, 80 hardware threads), 376 GiB memory and a 1 TB NVMe SSD. Query experiments are single-threaded unless noted.
tradeoffs: Headline number depends on precomputed, query-specific auxiliary state (materialized statistics/range trees), not general query acceleration; drops to a much more modest 1.99x with no persistent state allowed; no public code repository found
caveats: The 833x/375x/102x/486x figures are geomeans over workload-specific accelerators that LLMs generated (GPT-5.6 Terra Pro for analysis, DeepSeek V4 Pro for implementation). The accelerators precompute persistent, query-specific auxiliary state such as per-date aggregates, multidimensional summaries and range trees, so many queries become sub-millisecond lookups. JetStream is not a general-purpose engine replacement, and it costs more memory than stateless execution or the GenDB/Bespoke OLAP baselines. The DuckDB baseline is single-threaded by default. The text and the Figure 6 legend disagree (833x vs 843x, and 3544x vs 3554x for PostgreSQL). Ratios exceed the 50x plausibility threshold and no compiler or flags are given, so the tier is capped at C. This is an arXiv preprint (MIT CSAIL authors including Tim Kraska) with no venue stated. No code or artifact link appears on the arXiv abstract page, in the HTML or in the PDF, and none was found by GitHub search.

name: Lance
baseline: Apache Parquet (the parquet-rs Rust crate, tuned, in the paper). Iceberg is named only in the README/homepage marketing and is not benchmarked in the paper.
workload: Paper (arXiv 2504.15247): parallel 'take' operations of 256 random indices from a single column, run for 10 s and reported as rows fetched per second, over 8 data types (UInt64 scalars through 100 KiB image lists) with 10% nulls. Small types use about 1 billion rows. Parquet uses 8 KiB pages with compression and dictionary encoding off. Full-scan, compression-ratio and struct-packing experiments are also included. All runs are on local NVMe.
claimed_speedup: README/homepage marketing: '100x faster random access than Parquet or Iceberg'. The README's 'Vs. parquet' section attributes this to a preliminary Oxford Pet dataset test ('For batched random access, Lance is 100x better than both parquet and raw files'). The paper (arXiv 2504.15247) states instead that Parquet 'when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' (parquet-rs default 5,500 rows/s vs optimized 350,000 rows/s on small scalars). It also says the Lance 2.1 encoding 'generally tie[s] or beat[s] Parquet' in random access without the scan-performance and RAM trade-offs, but gives no single speedup figure against tuned Parquet.
hardware: Samsung 970 EVO Plus 2TB NVMe drive (measured 850K random 4KiB reads/s, 3,400 MiB/s) with an Intel i7-10700K CPU (8 cores/16 threads), per the paper
tradeoffs: Rust-native with Python/Java bindings (pylance); optimized for AI/ML lakehouse workloads (multimodal blobs, vector indexes, data versioning) rather than general OLAP scans; file format still evolving under a data_storage_version compatibility contract.
caveats: The '100x faster than Parquet or Iceberg' figure comes from README/homepage copy, backed only by a 'preliminary' Oxford Pet dataset test without methodology. The paper, written by LanceDB employees, undercuts it by showing tuned Parquet recovers over 60x versus default Parquet, and it claims only tie-or-beat against tuned Parquet. Lance 2.1 slightly underperforms Lance 2.0 on simple scalar types. The project homepage says the paper was published at VLDB 2025, but arXiv v1 carries no journal reference and a crossref title search found no match, so peer review is unconfirmed. The paper mentions reproduction scripts but gives no link. The paper's metric is throughput (rows/s) rather than latency.

name: QuestDB
workload: Streaming the last 500 million rows of a byte-identical trades table (symbol, side, price, amount, timestamp) out of the database across a 100 Gbps network into Apache Arrow batches in a Python client process, with N parallel reader connections, comparing QuestDB's QWP WebSocket egress (QuestDB 10.0.x) against ClickHouse native TCP (clickhouse-driver execute) and Arrow-over-HTTP (clickhouse-connect query_arrow_stream), with TimescaleDB as a further reference; engines on default settings.
claimed_speedup: 1.55x faster than ClickHouse's fastest configuration of any kind (QuestDB ~220M rows/s at 8 readers vs ClickHouse native TCP 141.9M rows/s at 8 readers) and 2.35x faster than ClickHouse's fastest streaming configuration (Arrow over HTTP, 93.8M rows/s), on 500M rows; on the 2B-row run QuestDB peaked at 291.9M rows/s (12 readers) vs ClickHouse Arrow HTTP 173.8M and native 165.5M rows/s (16 readers), about 1.68x (derived from page data)
hardware: AWS m8gn.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 123GB RAM, 100Gbps) server, c8gn.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 61GB RAM, 100Gbps) client
tradeoffs: Result is specific to result-set egress/streaming into Arrow, not general query execution speed; QuestDB is JVM-based (GC pauses, JIT warm-up) vs ClickHouse's native C++; benchmark measures a narrow protocol (QWP) QuestDB just introduced, so it is inherently favorable framing.
caveats: First-party QuestDB blog (Javier Ramirez); both the post and the harness README say it is 'not a benchmark' but an informal, directional test of the client egress path (Python client, engines on defaults), not an engine ranking. The harness is public but has no license file, pins questdb/questdb:10.0.0 while ClickHouse runs the unversioned clickhouse-server:latest image, and states no CPU model (only m8gn.8xlarge/c8gn.8xlarge instance types) or build flags, so it is capped at C. Separate corroboration: on ClickBench c7a.metal-48xl, QuestDB's hot-run total is 5.40s (2026-09-26 result) vs DuckDB's 15.70s (2026-05-11), but QuestDB is much slower on cold runs (502.2s vs 162.8s) and load (327s vs 98s). These figures are derived from the raw ClickBench JSON.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): questdb.com/blog listing, cross-checked against ClickHouse/ClickBench data.generated.js

verification.tier_reason: First-party QuestDB blog with a public harness (github.com/javier/questdb_qwp_egress_to_arrow_perf: read_bench_questdb.py, read_bench_clickhouse.py, bench.sh) and stated AWS instance types, but no CPU model, no compiler/JVM flags, and ClickHouse pinned only as the unversioned 'latest' Docker image; the post itself calls it 'not a benchmark... an informal test', so C, not A/B.
verification.notes: The numbers match the blog exactly. The only field that was wrong was compared_against_cpp_std_directly: the baseline is ClickHouse, not a C++ std library. The ClickBench aside checks out for hot runs only, so I added the cold-run and load gaps to the caveats.

corrected_fields.workload: Streaming 500 million rows of trades data (symbol, side, price, amount, timestamp) out of the database into Apache Arrow format over the network, using a public reproducible harness, comparing QuestDB's new QWP protocol against ClickHouse's native and Arrow-over-HTTP egress paths.

QuestDB also beats DuckDB on ClickBench itself (5.40s vs 15.70s on c7a.metal-48xl, tier B, derived from page data) as corroborating but separate evidence.

name: Sirius
workload: TPC-H benchmark (22 queries) hot runs at scale factors SF100/300/500/1000 (100GB-1TB), Sirius (a GPU execution engine plugged into DuckDB via Substrait) vs plain DuckDB on CPU
claimed_speedup: 5.5x faster at SF100 (1.71s vs 9.37s), 5.7x at SF300 (4.48s vs 25.72s), 5.2x at SF500 (8.14s vs 42.25s), 2.7x at SF1000 (31.79s vs 85.91s); also 2.1x-5.3x cheaper per run
hardware: Sirius (GPU): best of AWS g7e.2xlarge/4xlarge/8xlarge per scale factor (which size won at each SF is not stated), NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96GB; DuckDB (CPU) v1.5.5: AWS Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Requires an NVIDIA GPU (Turing+, CUDA 12.x/13.x) and Linux with io_uring enabled; plugs into DuckDB via Substrait and falls back silently to CPU for unsupported operators; only DuckDB is a supported target today (StarRocks integration planned)
caveats: First-party benchmark read from a README chart PNG (docs/super-sirius-perf.png); there is no raw results table, and no compiler/build flags are stated. These are hot runs only, and the Sirius time is the best of three g7e instance sizes. The hardware is asymmetric: an RTX PRO 6000 96GB GPU instance against a Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge CPU instance. The chart partly normalizes for this by reporting cost per run (Sirius 2.1-5.3x cheaper). The speedup shrinks from 5.5x at SF100 to 2.7x at SF1000. The page gives no reason, so the earlier explanation (GPU memory/bandwidth bottleneck) is speculation.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "sirius GPU DuckDB"; gh api repos/sirius-db/sirius

verification.tier_reason: The README performance chart (docs/super-sirius-perf.png) is first-party and shows every cited time, speedup and cost ratio for Sirius against DuckDB v1.5.5 on TPC-H SF100-SF1000. The TPC-H harness is public (test/tpch_performance/), but no compiler or flags are stated and the per-SF instance and run configuration are not given, so not A. There is no paper or independent suite behind these TPC-H numbers, so C.
verification.notes: Every number in the record matches the chart. I changed last_commit from pushed_at to the default-branch commit date and removed the unsupported bottleneck explanation. The independent ClickBench suite also has Sirius entries: sirius/results/20260309/p5.4xlarge.json has a hot-run sum of 1.50s, against DuckDB at 11.29s (c8g.metal-48xl) and 17.32s (c6a.metal) in the 2026-05-11 runs. That comparison is cross-hardware (GPU vs CPU) and across dates, all derived; re-pointed to it, the record could support tier B.
