corrected_fields.hardware: Sirius (GPU): AWS g7e.2xl/4xl/8xl instances, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96GB; DuckDB (CPU) v1.5.5: AWS Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge

name: SlothDB
workload: Author-run ClickBench-43 (the DuckDB variant of the queries, verbatim) over hits_typed.parquet queried directly by both engines on the same local machine, compared with DuckDB v1.4.3 (3 trials, min reported, 120s timeout), via bench/clickbench/official_bench.py; plus a bench/run.py mixed suite. The earlier HN claim also named ClickHouse, but the repo has no ClickHouse numbers.
claimed_speedup: Current repo ClickBench-43 run vs DuckDB v1.4.3 (min of 3 runs, one local machine): SlothDB faster on 29 of 40 comparable queries, with a geomean DuckDB/SlothDB time ratio of 1.24x. The total min-of-3 wall time is SlothDB 71.1s vs DuckDB 65.2s, so SlothDB is slower in aggregate. 7 of 40 results differ from DuckDB's, and SlothDB times out on Q19, Q29 and Q33. An earlier HN post (2026-05-01) claimed '1.35X to 5X faster than DuckDB and Clickhouse' on the 14GB/100M-row hits.parquet; the README now calls all numbers anecdotal and query-shape-specific.
hardware: Not stated (author says 'one workstation', no CPU model given)
tradeoffs: Early-stage/experimental per the author; no vendor PR to the real ClickBench is open; the project itself says some benchmark wins come from special-cased per-query handlers rather than the general query engine, which is a materially weaker and more overfit claim than a general engine speedup.
caveats: Self-disclosed low-confidence result: the README 'Status' and 'Performance' sections call the numbers anecdotal ('one workstation against one DuckDB version'). They say some wins come from a per-query handler dispatch rather than the general engine, and the project states no ClickBench vendor PR is planned while that dispatch remains. In the repo's own ClickBench-43 table SlothDB loses on total wall time (71.1s vs 65.2s), returns results that differ from DuckDB's on 7 queries (Q18's 14.81x 'win' among them), and times out on 3. The HN '5x' headline is not supported by any current repo data. No hardware, compiler or flags are stated. Tagged rather than excluded; confidence is low.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia query 'faster than DuckDB' -> 'SlothDB a 5X Faster Alternative to DuckDB, ClickHouse DB' (2026-05-01)

verification.tier_reason: First-party, author-run comparison against DuckDB v1.4.3 with public code (bench/clickbench/official_bench.py plus the 43 verbatim ClickBench queries). No CPU model, compiler or flags are given, and the README itself calls the numbers anecdotal, so it is C.
verification.notes: The README no longer contains any benchmark numbers. The real data is bench/clickbench/official_results.md (last changed 2026-05-19), and it shows only a modest geomean 1.24x win with correctness diffs and an aggregate loss, so I rewrote claimed_speedup. I confirmed the HN 1.35x-5x claim via HN Algolia (item 47971921). Metadata checks out: MIT, 413 stars, last commit 2026-06-03, active.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Originally announced as 1.35x-5x faster than DuckDB and ClickHouse (HN, 2026-05-01); the project's own current README explicitly walks this back, calling README/bench numbers 'anecdotal, not from standardised benchmark hardware' and noting wins are 'query-shape-specific' due to a per-query handler-dispatch path rather than the general engine
corrected_fields.workload: Author-run comparison of SlothDB against a user-supplied DuckDB binary using bench/clickbench (the 43 ClickBench queries verbatim) and a custom bench/run.py harness, plus an earlier HN claim citing a 14GB/100M-row hits.parquet ClickBench-style comparison against DuckDB and ClickHouse.
corrected_fields.caveats: Self-disclosed low-confidence result: the maintainer explicitly warns readers not to treat the numbers as final and flags that they are not from standardized hardware and may reflect query-specific handler dispatch rather than a real architectural win over DuckDB/ClickHouse. Included per the 'tag instead of exclude' rule, but confidence is set low.

name: StarRocks
workload: Star Schema Benchmark flattened into a single wide table (SSB-Flat, 100 GB; the ClickHouse-style denormalized SSB, so no joins), 13 queries, 1 warm-up plus the average of 3 runs. StarRocks 3.5.0 vs ClickHouse 25.3.3.42 (and Apache Druid 33.0.0), all with default configurations.
claimed_speedup: StarRocks docs (SSB Flat-table Benchmarking): on 13 queries over the 100 GB SSB-Flat dataset, 'StarRocks has an overall query performance 1.87x that of ClickHouse' (sum of average latencies 992 ms vs 1,858 ms; per-query ratios 1.12x-2.63x). The earlier StarRocks blog post (Aug 21, 2023; https://www.starrocks.io/blog/benchmark-test) claimed 'ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks' on the same 13 SSB flat-table queries, with no hardware stated.
hardware: AWS m7i.4xlarge hosts (16 vCPU, 64 GiB each; 5 instances listed). StarRocks runs 1 FE + 3 BEs and ClickHouse 3 nodes. CPU model and OS not stated.
tradeoffs: MPP architecture with a separate Java frontend (FE, planner/metadata) and C++ backend (BE, vectorized execution engine) -- heavier operational footprint than embedded engines like DuckDB; MySQL-wire compatible.
caveats: These are vendor-run numbers: default configs, no CPU model, no compiler flags and no linked benchmark scripts. The 2023 blog gave 2.2x; the current docs give 1.87x (StarRocks 3.5.0 vs ClickHouse 25.3.3.42). The claim is contradicted by the independent ClickBench suite on identical single-node c6a.4xlarge hardware. There, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run sums to 18.03 s (best of 3 across 43 queries) versus 44.47 s for StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run, so ClickHouse is about 2.5x faster (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). Both the vendor SSB-Flat test and ClickBench are single-flat-table workloads, not star-schema joins, so the gap cannot be put down to join handling. It more likely reflects cluster vs single-node setup, dataset and query mix, and tuning. The win should be treated as workload- and setup-specific.
found_via: gh api repos/StarRocks/starrocks/contents/README.md; WebFetch starrocks.io/blog/benchmark-test; ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo

The current StarRocks docs page reports 1.87x with instance types, versions and per-query latencies, but gives no CPU model, compiler/flags or public benchmark script, so it is C, not A/B.
verification.notes: Both the 2023 blog's 2.2x and the ClickBench 18.03 s vs 44.47 s figures were verified. The record's caveat wrongly calls the vendor test 'star-schema joins': it is SSB flat tables. benchmark_url was switched to the current docs page, which states instance type, versions and per-query data (1.87x); the old blog is kept in claimed_speedup/caveats. The orchestrator may want to flag this as contested given the independent ClickBench reversal.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: "ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks" on SSB (vendor blog; hardware/compiler not stated in the post)
corrected_fields.workload: Star Schema Benchmark (SSB), 13 queries on flat tables (vendor blog post dated Aug 21, 2023)
corrected_fields.caveats: The 2.2x claim is from StarRocks' own 2023 blog post with no hardware/CPU model or compiler flags stated (tier C). It is directly CONTRADICTED by ClickHouse's own independent, reproducible ClickBench suite: on identical c6a.4xlarge hardware, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run totals 18.03s (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 ClickBench queries) versus StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run at 44.47s -- i.e. ClickHouse is now roughly 2.5x FASTER than StarRocks on ClickBench, the reverse of the vendor's SSB claim (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo, clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). The discrepancy likely reflects ~3 years of ClickHouse improvements plus workload differences (SSB star-schema joins vs. ClickBench's flat-table scans), but it substantially weakens confidence in the vendor claim as a current, general statement.

name: Vortex
workload: First-party CI benchmark dashboard (bench.vortex.dev) covering write and scan throughput (compress-bench), hot and cold random-access take latency over taxi, feature-vectors, nested-lists and nested-structs datasets, ClickBench, TPC-H SF1/10/100 on NVMe and S3, TPC-DS SF1 and others. Each workload runs with both DataFusion and DuckDB as the query engine, against Parquet, Lance, Arrow IPC and DuckDB native formats.
claimed_speedup: bench.vortex.dev (live page, build 737386b as of 2026-09-26). Two figures are geomean throughput ratios to Parquet: write throughput 2.97x (1,756 vs 605 MB/s) and scan throughput 30.73x (84.14 vs 3.20 GB/s). The page's other summary ratios are geomean time ratios to the fastest entry (lower is better), not speedups over Parquet. Random access, hot: Vortex 1.15x (1.85 ms) vs Parquet 627.08x (65.32 s), about 545x (derived from page data). Random access, cold: Vortex 1.35x (3.31 ms) vs Parquet 432.76x (67.10 s), about 321x (derived from page data). ClickBench: DataFusion+Vortex 3.99 s vs DataFusion+Parquet 6.08 s, about 1.52x (derived from page data); DuckDB+Vortex 4.65 s vs DuckDB+Parquet 5.45 s, about 1.17x (derived from page data). TPC-H SF1 NVMe: DuckDB+Vortex 450.40 ms vs DuckDB+Parquet 1.51 s, about 3.35x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. Per the repo's CI workflow: rustc 1.98.0 (rust-toolchain.toml), RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=yes', cargo --profile release_debug.
hardware: Not stated on the page. The repo's CI workflows (.github/workflows/develop-bench.yml, sql-bench-matrix.yml) run benchmarks on an AWS EC2 c8gd.metal-24xl (ARM64); no CPU model is named.
stars_or_usage: 3,225 stars; LF AI & Data incubation-stage project
tradeoffs: Rust-native (needs FFI/bindings for direct C++ use, though it advertises zero-copy Arrow compatibility); file format only reached 'stable' status from v0.36.0 onward; young ecosystem versus Parquet's universal tooling support.
caveats: First-party dashboard whose numbers change with every commit. Most summary 'x' figures are geomean ratios to the fastest entry, not speedups over Parquet, so only the write and scan throughput ratios are direct Parquet comparisons. On the same page, results on S3 are mixed. At TPC-H S3 SF1, DataFusion+Parquet is fastest (6.54 s vs DataFusion+Vortex 8.86 s). At TPC-H S3 SF100, DuckDB+Vortex takes 488.62 s vs 73.45 s for DuckDB+Parquet. The independent ClickHouse/ClickBench results (c6a.4xlarge, sum of best-of-3 over 43 queries, derived from the result JSONs) are also mixed. On 2026-05-11, duckdb-vortex took 40.99 s vs 32.48 s for duckdb-parquet: slower in total because one query is about 20x slower, though it was faster on 26 of 43 queries and about 5% faster by geomean. A 'tuned' duckdb-vortex run on 2026-09-26 took 29.69 s but loaded in 762 s. On 2026-08-20, DataFusion+Vortex took 91.30 s vs 45.57 s for DataFusion+Parquet and was about 1.37x slower by geomean. That contradicts the dashboard's DataFusion ClickBench win, although the engine versions differ (Vortex CLI on DataFusion 53.1.0, Parquet run on 54.0.0). The huge random-access ratios mostly reflect Parquet having no row-level random access.
found_via: gh api repos/vortex-data/vortex; WebFetch of bench.vortex.dev; ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo (duckdb-vortex and duckdb-parquet results/20260511/c6a.4xlarge.json)

verification.tier_reason: bench.vortex.dev is Vortex's own CI dashboard. It compares against Parquet, and the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/compress-bench, random-access-bench, datafusion-bench, duckdb-bench). The page names no hardware or flags. The CI workflows give an AWS instance type (c8gd.metal-24xl), RUSTFLAGS and rustc 1.98.0, but no CPU model, so per precedent this is first-party C.
verification.notes: The record misread the dashboard. Its 1.13x (ClickBench) and 1.32x (TPC-H) figures are ratio-to-fastest scores, not speedups over Parquet, and the Parquet 65.32 s random-access figure is from the hot panel, not a cold/hot mix. I rewrote claimed_speedup with the direct comparisons, marked as derived. I downgraded because the query-engine wins over Parquet are contested by independent ClickBench results, including a new DataFusion+Vortex result that is 2x slower in total. The write and scan throughput wins stand, first-party only.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 2.97x write throughput; 30.73x scan throughput (84.14 GB/s); hot random access 1.15x at 1.85ms vs. Parquet's cold read of 65.32s (~627x, mixed cold/hot comparison); ClickBench-with-DataFusion 1.13x (3.99s vs 6.08s); TPC-H SF1/NVMe 1.32x (450.40ms)
corrected_fields.workload: First-party benchmark suite (bench.vortex.dev) covering write throughput, full-table scan throughput, hot/cold single-row random-access latency, a ClickBench run using DataFusion as the query engine, and a TPC-H SF=1 NVMe run, all vs. Apache Parquet.
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 3.2k stars; Linux Foundation LF AI & Data incubation project
corrected_fields.caveats: bench.vortex.dev does not state a CPU/hardware model or compiler flags on the page itself (only links out to GitHub for 'detailed description'), so this falls short of tier A/B despite the benchmark code being public. More importantly, when the query ENGINE is held constant (DuckDB), ClickHouse/ClickBench's own public results for duckdb-vortex vs duckdb-parquet (2026-05-11 run, c6a.4xlarge) show Vortex was actually SLOWER on the standard ClickBench workload: 40.99s vs 32.48s total (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 queries; derived from page data in ClickHouse/ClickBench's results JSON files), and a later 'tuned' duckdb-vortex run had a much higher load time (762s). This directly contradicts the vendor's 'faster scans' headline for the DuckDB-with-Vortex integration path, even though Vortex's own DataFusion-based ClickBench comparison on bench.vortex.dev shows a (smaller) win.

name: ArceKV (ElasticLSM + Arce)
workload: Dynamic and static read/write-ratio workloads on a RocksDB-based KV store, cgroup-capped memory (75GiB), comparing against RocksDB's own Leveling/1-Leveling/Tiering compaction styles and academic baselines (LazyLeveling, Moose, Ruskey, CAMAL)
claimed_speedup: Paper: average 2.00x and 1.41x over 1-Leveling (RocksDB's default compaction style, the strongest baseline) across the two dynamic workloads; 2.17x-2.92x over Tiering and LazyLeveling; around 3x faster than state-of-the-art compaction strategies in dynamic scenarios; over 10x vs Cassandra and WiredTiger and 3x vs Pebble. Repo README (prod branch, in-memory tmpfs variant vs RocksDB leveling): total latency 282.09s vs 808.85s at read_ratio 0.1 (2.87x) shrinking to 438.04s vs 479.20s at 0.9 (1.09x) (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in paper; repo README lists gcc/g++ (version unstated) with a CMake Release build
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (5.40GHz), 128GB RAM, 1TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 22.04, ext4, memory capped at 75GiB via cgroup
license: GPL-2.0 (GitHub-detected; repo is a modified RocksDB tree that ships both LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb, matching RocksDB's dual Apache-2.0/GPL-2.0 licensing)
tradeoffs: Replaces RocksDB's fixed compaction hierarchy with a workload-adaptive engine (Arce) that expands the compaction/write-stall action space; adds a decision-engine overhead and requires online profiling to adapt to workload shifts, versus RocksDB's simpler static leveling/tiering.
caveats: The paper states no compiler or flags. The 1-Leveling/Leveling/Tiering/LazyLeveling baselines were implemented on the RocksDB-based Moose framework, not stock RocksDB builds. Stock RocksDB appears only in the industrial-system comparison. The default 'prod' branch is explicitly NOT a faithful implementation of the paper: it is an in-memory adaptation for a TikTok recommendation service. An on-disk version was published on the 'dev' branch (2026-04-29), and its README reports a modest gain over leveled compaction: 1.41x total runtime (929.0s vs 1310.5s) and about 10% lower all-op latency, with worse insert latency (2.45us vs 2.15us) and higher compaction I/O. The prod README's cmake line has a typo (-CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE). License: GitHub detects GPL-2.0; the tree carries RocksDB's COPYING (GPLv2), LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb.
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2508.03565; code located in paper text (github.com/NTU-Siqiang-Group/ArceKV)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 19(5):958-972 (2026) paper with public artifact repo (NTU-Siqiang-Group/ArceKV; prod branch tools/arce_bench, dev branch examples/arce_dynamic_compaction_integration.cc) and stated hardware (i9-13900K), but neither the paper nor the READMEs state a compiler version or flags (README only says gcc/g++ with a CMake Release build), so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: The paper is real and peer-reviewed (PVLDB vol 19 issue 5, 2026, not VLDB 2025 as recorded), and the headline numbers match its text. The tier drops from A to B because no compiler or flags are stated anywhere. The public default branch differs from the evaluated system, so treat the repo as a research artifact.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 2.00x-1.41x over RocksDB's default 1-Leveling compaction (its strongest baseline); 2.17x-2.92x over Tiering/LazyLeveling; ~3x faster in dynamic workload-shift scenarios; >10x vs Cassandra/WiredTiger
corrected_fields.caveats: Compiler/flags not explicitly stated in the paper (only hardware and OS); code is public with reproducible build via CMake (inherited RocksDB build system), so tier kept at A given the code+hardware are both confirmed and the build system implies standard GCC/Clang toolchain, but note this is a judgment call absent an explicit compiler line.

name: Badger (BadgerDB)
workload: populate + random-read benchmark: 250M keys with 128-byte values for the read test, and 75M keys with 1KB values for the population/write-time test; Badger's WiscKey-style value log vs RocksDB SSTables.
claimed_speedup: Random reads: Badger is 3.67x faster (32361 ns/op vs 118982 ns/op for RocksDB). Population of 75M x 1KB records: 17m10s (Badger) vs 78m8s (RocksDB), about 4.6x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version not stated anywhere in badger-bench's BENCH-rocks.txt, README or the 2017 blog post (the record's 'Go 1.8' is unsupported). RocksDB v5.1.4 was built with `export USE_RTTI=1 && make shared_lib` (badger-bench README) and called from Go through cgo bindings (badger-bench rdb/).
hardware: Amazon EC2 i3.large dedicated instance: 2 cores, 16GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD (fio measured ~93K random-read IOPS at 4K block size); CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 15.8k stars; used by IPFS, Usenet Express, Decred, Insolar, IoTex, 194+ dependent Go packages
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no Cgo; separates keys from values (WiscKey design) so full-value iteration is much slower than RocksDB's (see companion BENCH-lmdb-bolt.md iterate-with-values numbers); higher resident memory during population (14GB+ RSS) than RocksDB in this test.
caveats: This is Dgraph's own 2017 benchmark against RocksDB v5.1.4, and the badger-bench repo has been archived (last commit 2019-09-20). Tuning was asymmetric: RocksDB was opened read-only with default options, a 16-bit bloom filter and the default block cache, called through cgo, while Badger ran with TableLoadingMode=LoadToRAM so its LSM tree sat in memory. Badger did not win every test. Loading 250M x 128B was slower with Badger (45:26.56 vs 39:10.78 for RocksDB), and the blog post says Badger can be 2-3x slower to load 16-byte values. Go version and CPU model are not stated.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia "badger rocksdb" -> blog.dgraph.io post -> dgraph-io/badger-bench repo (BENCH-rocks.txt)

name: DobLIX
workload: SOSD real-world (WIKI, AMZN, FB, OSM) and synthetic (LOGN, UNI) datasets, 64M pairs with 8-byte keys and 64-byte values; RO/RH/BA/WH read-write mixes plus YCSB A-F macrobenchmarks on RocksDB 8.1.1 (per paper), 4 background threads
claimed_speedup: Average throughput vs stock RocksDB indexing: 2.21x on read-only (RO), 1.22x read-heavy, 1.31x balanced, 1.04x write-heavy; vs TridentKV/Bourbon on RO: 1.41x/1.57x. YCSB B/C/D average 2.02x vs RocksDB; YCSB-E +42.8%. +81% vs RocksDB at 512MB cache (RO, Zipfian, AMZN). RO tail latency 2.13x better than RocksDB. Abstract: 1.19x-2.21x vs state-of-the-art methods within RocksDB. The '2.67x' figure is TridentKV's tail latency relative to DobLIX, not a throughput gain over RocksDB.
compiler_and_flags: C++17, GCC 9.4.0 (paper); optimization flags not stated in paper (repo README uses cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; repo CMakeLists sets -std=c++11)
hardware: 64-core AMD Ryzen Threadripter Pro 5995WX (2.7GHz), 256GB DDR4 RAM, Samsung 980 Pro 2TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 20.04
license: BSD-3-Clause (RocksDB 5.x-era 'BSD License For rocksdb software' LICENSE text; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) plus Facebook PATENTS file (Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2)
tradeoffs: Adds a dual-objective learned index (RadixSpline-based) plus an RL agent for tuning block size/error bound on top of RocksDB; extra training/tuning overhead; RL agent adds runtime complexity vs stock RocksDB.
caveats: GitHub shows NOASSERTION. The LICENSE is RocksDB's old BSD-3-Clause text, shipped with Facebook's PATENTS grant (v2) and its termination clause. The public repo is a RocksDB 5.1.2 tree (include/rocksdb/version.h) with a learned_index/ directory, but the paper evaluates on RocksDB 8.1.1. It has no DobLIX-specific SOSD/YCSB benchmark scripts, and the README's './doblix' binary has no matching CMake target. Several headline ratios (1.19x, 1.41x, 1.57x) are vs other learned-index variants (Bourbon, TridentKV). The direct stock-RocksDB gains are large on read-only work (2.21x) but only 1.04x-1.31x on write-containing mixes.

name: PsiTri (arbtrie)
workload: TPC-B-style bank-transfer benchmark. Each transfer is one atomic transaction of 5 KV ops (2 reads, 2 updates, 1 insert), with triangular-skew access and a fixed seed. The main runs use 1M accounts, 10M transfer attempts, 100 transfers per commit and sync=none. The PsiTriRocks drop-in comparison is a separate April 2026 EPYC run: 1M accounts, 1M transactions, batch=1, sync=none, write-only and write plus one concurrent reader.
claimed_speedup: PsiTriRocks (RocksDB-API drop-in) vs RocksDB, April 2026 AMD EPYC-Turin, batch=1: 2.3x write throughput (369,446 vs 157,588 transfers/sec) and 4.9x reader throughput under concurrent writes (1,416,652 vs 289,627 reads/sec). Native PsiTri vs RocksDB in the batch=100 run: 376,691 vs 126,341 transfers/sec on Apple M5 Max, about 2.98x (derived from page data); 163,614 vs 104,102 transfers/sec on AMD EPYC-Turin, about 1.57x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Apple M5 Max: Clang 17, C++20, -O3 -flto=thin. AMD EPYC-Turin: Clang 20, C++20, -O3 -flto -march=native (AVX-512 enabled)
hardware: Apple M5 Max, 128 GB unified memory (macOS); AMD EPYC-Turin, 8 cores/16 threads at 2.4 GHz with 121 GB RAM (Vultr cloud VM, Linux 6.17, exact SKU not given)
tradeoffs: Also ships PsiTri-SQLite (SQLite drop-in) claiming 1.06x write / 13.5x read vs SQLite in the same bank benchmark, and separately 47x (sync=off) / 3.8x (sync=full) on a TATP telecom benchmark without hardware stated for that specific table. Very new project; README/repo name mismatch (repo is 'arbtrie', product now called 'PsiTri') suggests a recent rename/pivot, so API and durability guarantees may still be in flux.
caveats: Only 4 GitHub stars and no independent replication. All runs use sync=none (no forced durability). On the AMD EPYC-Turin VM, both MDBX (239,041) and TidesDB (167,093) beat native PsiTri (163,614 transfers/sec), so the win over RocksDB is not a win over every engine tested. The 4.9x figure measures reader throughput under a concurrent writer, not a pure read workload. First-party benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/gofractally/arbtrie/readme (found via gh search code "faster than RocksDB"-style crawl of embedded-kv repos), confirmed at https://gofractally.github.io/arbtrie/benchmarks/bank/

verification.tier_reason: The bank benchmark page runs PsiTri against RocksDB (plus MDBX, TidesDB and SQLite) using public code (programs/bank_bench.cpp, driven by bench/suites/bank_tpcb.sh; raw logs and machine.json are in docs/data/bank_tpcb/). It states the CPUs (Apple M5 Max; AMD EPYC-Turin 8c/16t 2.4 GHz), the compilers (Clang 17 / Clang 20) and the flags (-O3 -flto=thin / -O3 -flto -march=native).
verification.notes: All record numbers appear on the page and belong to the right rows. I made clarifying fixes: the workload is TPC-B-style, not TATP, and the 2.3x/4.9x figures come from a separate batch=1 run. Metadata checks out: MIT license, 4 stars, last main commit 2026-04-28, active.

name: CompassDB
workload: YCSB A-F with 16 threads after loading 200M keys (20-byte keys, 1KB values) then 100M operations; O_DIRECT, compression disabled, RocksDB/PebblesDB with 32MB LRU block cache, up to 4x128MB memtables; plus Workload C value-size sweep (50B-50KB) and fill/read/mixed microbenchmarks
claimed_speedup: YCSB (16 threads, 200M keys, 100M ops): 2.5x-4x throughput vs RocksDB and 5x-17x vs PebblesDB on point-lookup/insert workloads A, B, C, D, F. Workload A ~3x, C 2.52x, D 5.5x vs RocksDB. 50%-85% lower average/p99 latency vs RocksDB. Slower than both RocksDB and PebblesDB on scan-heavy YCSB-E. Intro: RocksDB's write amplification about 2x CompassDB's (15x in a 100M-key one-level test), read amplification 3x in pure reads, space amplification 1.2x.
benchmark_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18099 (arXiv v1 preprint, 26 Jun 2024; no journal reference listed)
hardware: Dell PowerEdge T440, Intel Xeon Silver 2.40 GHz (exact model not stated), Samsung PM9A3 3.84TB NVMe SSD, 128GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, ext4 (ordered mode)
tradeoffs: Perfect-hash in-memory index (~6 bytes/KV) instead of RocksDB's default block-based index+bloom filter; claims RocksDB API compatibility for drop-in migration, but no public implementation to verify; perfect-hash structures typically complicate/limit fully dynamic online rebuilds under skewed insert patterns.
caveats: No public repository: GitHub search finds only unrelated 'compassdb' projects. The arXiv preprint (v1, June 2024) has no venue or journal reference. The claimed SIGMOD / Proc. ACM Manag. Data 3(6) Article 294 publication could not be verified: there is no CompassDB entry in Crossref's PACMMOD (ISSN 2836-6573) index, even though vol 3 issue 6 is indexed. The authors are all from DiPeak, the vendor, so these are first-party numbers. The secondary baseline is PebblesDB, not SplinterDB; SplinterDB appears only as related work. Setup is not like-for-like: RocksDB/PebblesDB got a 32MB block cache under O_DIRECT, and CompassDB loses on scan-heavy YCSB-E.

name: DiaLSM
workload: db_bench FillRandom (128B/1KB/8KB values, 10M entries per I/O thread) and ReadRandomWriteRandom (100M 1KB entries preloaded); YCSB A-F with 1KB values; Sysbench OLTP on MariaDB/MyRocks. DiaLSM is built atop RocksDB v8.3.2. Baselines are RocksDB v8.3.2 with Sub-Compaction, and ADOC. For all systems, write throttling (WST), commit logging and block cache were disabled.
claimed_speedup: 8KB FillRandom: up to 2.4x higher throughput and ~50% lower latency than ADOC (a RocksDB-based auto-tuner), not stock RocksDB. 94.3% fewer write stalls: ADOC and RocksDB show up to 17.6x higher stall rates. ~50% lower average/median latency than both RocksDB(16) and ADOC(16) (Fig. 7). ReadRandomWriteRandom: 1.8x vs ADOC. YCSB-E: ~1.7x vs ADOC and RocksDB at the default scan length 128, and 3.3x/5.7x/8.9x at scan lengths 1K/4K/16K; YCSB-C at parity. Sysbench on MariaDB/MyRocks: 2.3x vs ADOC on oltp_insert, up to 9.9x on oltp_write_only, 2.2x vs ADOC on oltp_read_write.
hardware: Two AMD EPYC 7352 24-core CPUs, 256GB RAM, MZSLR3T8HBLS-00A07 NVMe SSD, CentOS 7 with ext4
tradeoffs: Shards the write-flush-compaction pipeline internally to avoid a single monolithic stall path; adds shard-management complexity and per-shard resource overhead.
caveats: Venue is author-reported only. The arXiv comment (v1, 2026-09-13) and the repo README say the paper was accepted to the 43rd IEEE ICDE 2027 (Copenhagen, May 17-21 2027). The date fits ICDE 2027's Round-1 notification (2026-09-10), but there is no public accepted-papers list or proceedings, so peer review cannot be confirmed yet. Tier is held at C; it can go to B once ICDE 2027 lists the paper. The headline 2.4x/1.8x/2.2x/2.3x gains are against ADOC, not stock RocksDB. Against RocksDB the paper shows ~50% lower latency, 94.3% fewer stalls and the YCSB-E range-scan wins. The RocksDB config is non-default: throttling, WAL/commit logging and block cache were all disabled. The paper says the code is 'publicly available' at DISCOS-LAB/DiaLSM, but the repo holds only a README ('will be available soon') and has no license. Compiler/flags are not stated.

name: F2 (FASTER v2)
workload: YCSB (A/B/C/D/F/W) and MixGraph benchmarks, 250M keys (8B key/100B value), Zipfian skew, on CloudLab NVMe RAID-0, memory budget 10% of dataset size
claimed_speedup: 2-11.9x better throughput than existing KV stores (abstract). Fig. 10 (YCSB + MixGraph, 16 cores, memory = 10% of dataset) averages: 11.8x RocksDB v8.11.4, 2.1x FASTER, 2x LeanStore, 4.6x SplinterDB, 11.9x KVell. Average request latency vs RocksDB: 1.4x lower read and 3.5x lower write (Table 1).
hardware: CloudLab sm110p node: 16-core Intel Xeon Silver 4314, 128GiB RAM, 4x Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD (PCIe 4.0) in RAID-0, Linux kernel 5.4, ext4
tradeoffs: Two-tier hash-index + record-log design optimized for skewed, larger-than-memory workloads; latch-free multi-threaded compaction adds implementation complexity; tuned for direct I/O with WAL/compression/checksums disabled in the benchmark, which is not RocksDB's typical durable-by-default configuration.
caveats: The paper is PVLDB 18(12):4910-4923, 2025 (VLDB 2025, doi:10.14778/3750601.3750615), not VLDB 2023; 2023 is the arXiv v1 date. The 11.8x RocksDB average covers YCSB and MixGraph, not YCSB alone. The latency win is 1.4x on reads and 3.5x on writes, not 3.5x on both. All systems ran with Direct I/O and with WAL/persistence, compression and checksums disabled (non-default). RocksDB was further tuned with 10-bit Bloom filters and the data-block hash index via OptimizeForPointLookup(). Memory was capped at 10% of dataset (3GiB YCSB, 4GiB MixGraph). F2's benchmark code is public (cc/benchmark-dir/benchmark_f2.cc; Release builds with -O3 -g), but the compiler/version is unstated and the RocksDB harness is not in the repo, so the tier stays B.

name: HyperLevelDB
workload: InfluxDB storage-engine shootout: 100 million key-value pairs across 500,000 series columns, 24-byte (3-int) keys, protobuf-serialized values, batches of 1,000 writes; write N, query N, delete N/2, compact, query remaining N/2, write N/2 more.
claimed_speedup: Writing 100M values took 10m45.41s with HyperLevelDB vs 36m8.29s with LevelDB (~3.36x faster, derived from page data) and 21m18.60s with RocksDB. HyperLevelDB lost the other steps: querying 100M values took 13m49.01s vs 2m55.37s for LevelDB (~4.7x slower, derived from page data), and it was also slower than LevelDB on delete (6m0.38s vs 3m47.64s) and compaction (6m33.36s vs 3m59.87s).
hardware: DigitalOcean droplet: 4GB RAM, 2 CPU cores, 60GB SSD (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Fork of LevelDB by the now-defunct HyperDex team, adds multi-threaded compaction; abandoned since 2016 so it lacks a decade of LevelDB/RocksDB fixes.
caveats: This is a 2014 benchmark on a 2-core, 4GB DigitalOcean droplet. The author says settings were not tuned per engine, and the page gives no compiler, flags or CPU model. HyperLevelDB wins only on writes and is the slowest engine for range queries. The last three rows of the results image (Query 50M, Write 50M, DB size) match the 30M run in the linked gist, not the 100M run. In the gist's 3M-value SSD run, HyperLevelDB writes were slower than LevelDB's (21.0s vs 18.0s).

name: KVell
workload: YCSB core workloads (uniform and Zipfian key distributions), 1024B items, 100GB(100M keys)/5TB(5B keys) synthetic datasets, plus two Nutanix write-heavy (57:41:2 write:read:scan) production workloads, 250B-1KB items.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: throughput at least 2x the closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads and 5x on write-dominated workloads; on mostly-scan workloads comparable or better; maximum latencies an order of magnitude lower than the best competitor, even on scan-based workloads. Body (Config-Optane, 100M 1KB items): YCSB A 8x RocksDB and 5.8x PebblesDB (next best); YCSB B/C 2.2x/2.7x over existing KVs; Nutanix production workloads ~4x RocksDB (the next best); uniform YCSB E roughly equal to RocksDB (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s).
compiler_and_flags: Paper states none. Repo Makefile defaults: clang with CFLAGS=-O2 -ggdb3 -Wall (clang++ -std=c++11 for index code); README recommends TCMalloc (gperftools). Not confirmed as the build used for the paper runs.
hardware: Config-SSD: 32-core 2.4GHz Intel Xeon, 128GB RAM, 480GB Intel DC S3500 SSD; Config-Amazon-8NVMe: AWS i3.metal, 36x2 (72) cores at 2.3GHz, 488GB RAM, 8x1.9TB NVMe SSDs; Config-Optane: 4-core 4.2GHz Intel i7, 60GB RAM, 480GB Intel Optane 905P
tradeoffs: Shared-nothing architecture can suffer load imbalance; no in-memory sorted global index so scans are relatively weaker; designed around 4KB-atomic-write SSDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper. The paper states no compiler or flags, and the repo Makefile defaults to clang -O2. CPU models are not named. The repo reproduces only the KVell side (scripts/run-aws.sh, sample_results); the RocksDB/PebblesDB/TokuMX/WiredTiger runs have no published harness. Scans are weaker: RocksDB wins with small items, and uniform YCSB E is about equal (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s). The latest commit (2025-12-15) only fixes random-number generation in a workload generator; before that the last commit was 2020-11, and the 'osdi' branch holds KVell+ (OSDI'20).

name: BVLSM
workload: db_bench random and sequential writes with 4KB-64KB values under sync, async and disabled WAL (R-WS/R-WA/R-WO, S-WS/S-WA/S-WO); YCSB workload A (16B keys, 8KB values, 500k preloaded records); 100GB sustained random-write stability test. Baselines are RocksDB v9.7.3 and BlobDB. The comparison is WAL-time vs flush-time key-value separation.
claimed_speedup: 64KB random writes: 7.6x throughput vs RocksDB v9.7.3 and 1.9x vs BlobDB with async WAL (R-WA); ~7x vs RocksDB and ~3x vs BlobDB with sync WAL (R-WS); up to 8x vs RocksDB and 2x vs BlobDB with WAL off (R-WO). Sequential writes: S-WS ~4.1x RocksDB / 9.8x BlobDB, S-WA ~1.3x / 2.2x, S-WO up to 1.3x / 2x. YCSB-A (8KB values): insert/update/read latency is 27.2%/28.4%/19.7% of RocksDB's. 100GB sustained random write: 1.5x RocksDB and 2x BlobDB on average.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (16C/32T, 2.30GHz), 4x32GB DDR4-2933 (128GB), Samsung 990 EVO NVMe SSD (1TB), Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Separates key/value at WAL-write time rather than at flush time so MemTables only hold lightweight metadata; adds a multi-queue BValue store and BVCache; targets big-value (multimedia/embedding) workloads specifically, smaller advantage expected for small-value workloads typical of many RocksDB deployments.

name: CacheAdvance
workload: Appending log messages (a Lorum Ipsum message set) to an on-disk cache file, single-message and batch append, measured with XCTest `measure {}` performance tests against an equivalent SQLite-backed cache.
claimed_speedup: "CacheAdvance persists log events 30x faster than SQLite" (README headline claim).
tradeoffs: No in-memory buffer, every append is a synchronous disk write; not thread-safe (single serial queue only); the SQLite comparison test is disabled on Linux (Apple platforms only).
caveats: The 30x figure is a first-party README claim from April 2020 (commit 6ae0a74 changed an earlier '15x faster while utilizing 40% less memory than SQLite'). The benchmark_url test file measures but prints no stored results and gives no hardware or Xcode/Swift version, and performance tests are disabled on GitHub Actions. The SQLite baseline is naive: every append runs a SELECT COUNT(*), prepares a fresh INSERT and commits it on its own under SQLite's default durability, with no batching, prepared-statement reuse or WAL. CacheAdvance's append path shows no fsync, so the comparison favors it.

name: DBX
workload: Criterion.rs 0.5 bench official_db_comparison.rs: 10,000 string key/value pairs ('key_{i}' / 'value_data_{i}'). INSERT builds a fresh in-memory DB each iteration; GET does 10,000 point lookups; SCAN reads the whole table. DBX (v0.2.0-beta 'Fast-Path', Database::open_in_memory) vs SQLite (rusqlite 0.32 bundled, Connection::open_in_memory, one BLOB-keyed table). Sled 0.34 and Redb 2.1 run on temp dirs in the same suite.
claimed_speedup: 10,000 records, both engines in memory: INSERT 25.21 ms vs SQLite 29.4 ms (about 1.17x; the README rounds this to '1.16x faster, 25ms vs 29ms'). Point GET: 2.84 ms vs 33.8 ms (about 11.9x, derived from page data; the page itself says both '11x' and '13x'). Full SCAN: 51 µs vs 340 µs (about 6.7x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 / Cargo 1.92.0, Cargo release profile, Criterion.rs 0.5; SQLite is rusqlite 0.32 with the bundled feature. No extra flags stated.
hardware: Windows 11 Pro (build 26200) x64 PC, about 16 GB RAM; CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: 0.2.0-beta software; the README's larger '29x' and '4.5x GPU' claims are versus 'traditional B-Tree engines' and CUDA baselines, not versus SQLite directly, so only the 1.16x figure is a real SQLite comparison.
caveats: Very small, very new project (4 stars, created Feb 2026, single first-party report dated 3 Apr 2026). No CPU model, and the sample is only 10,000 records. The benchmarks page contradicts itself: INSERT is called both 14% and 18% faster, GET both 11x and 13x, and the conclusion cites older v0.0.6 numbers (INSERT 44.92 ms, SCAN 1.60 ms). The 'Fast-Path' section says DBX scan fell from 340 µs to 51 µs, and 340 µs is also the figure given for SQLite. The bench code does not match the documented method. The doc says SQLite runs inside a transaction, but the code inserts in autocommit mode. SQLite lookups use conn.query_row, which re-prepares the SQL for every one of the 10,000 lookups; that handicaps the 'GET 11-13x' result. The README says Tier 1 is a BTreeMap, but the benchmarks page says DashMap + SkipMap. The README is marketing-heavy and has an unfilled Ko-fi placeholder link. GitHub reports NOASSERTION because the LICENSE file adds a donation/sponsorship section after the standard MIT text; the grant itself is plain MIT. Low confidence.

tradeoffs: The same page also compares ForestDB server-side against LevelDB v1.15 and RocksDB v3.1 on an Intel Xeon E5-2620 box: ForestDB showed much lower write amplification (7x-20x vs RocksDB's 31x-35x and LevelDB's 166x-387x), but those server-side throughput numbers are only shown as bar-chart images, not text, so they are not quoted as a numeric claim here.

name: LUDA
workload: YCSB-A (0.5/0.5 update-read), 16 B keys, values 128 B-1 KB, 4 MB memtable/SST, 4 KB data blocks. Load 10M pairs (~5 GB), then run another 10M operations, with stress-ng CPU overhead at 0%, 40% and 80%. A separate one-hour latency/robustness run uses 0.1 billion 256 B-value pairs (~50 GB). GPU-accelerated compaction vs stock LevelDB 1.22 and RocksDB 6.4.6.
claimed_speedup: About 2x the YCSB-A throughput of LevelDB and RocksDB, but only when stress-ng takes 80% of the CPU (20% left). With no CPU contention, RocksDB (4 background threads) has the shortest running time on the 5 GB run; LUDA comes second and LevelDB last. The paper also says LUDA's compaction is '1x faster' than LevelDB's and '2x faster' than RocksDB's. At 1 KB values it processes a similar amount of data as LevelDB in 46% less running time. Without CPU overhead it has the lowest and most stable 99th-percentile latency. The abstract's 'up to 2x higher throughput and 2x data processing speed' is the best case under CPU contention.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 10.1; host compiler and flags not stated. Prototype built on LevelDB v1.22 (~1K LOC modified, +2.7K LOC CUDA), with Snappy compression not implemented. Compared against RocksDB v6.4.6 with 4 threads; all stores use default parameters and 10-bit Bloom filters.
hardware: Supermicro X10DAI, Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 (4-core/8-thread), 64GB DRAM, one NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti GPU, one 280GB Intel Optane 900p SSD; Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.15
tradeoffs: Requires a discrete NVIDIA GPU and CUDA; only bloom-filter/compaction sorting is GPU-accelerated, snappy compression is not yet supported; benefits are largest when the host CPU is otherwise busy.
caveats: The win depends on CPU contention. The 2x throughput appears only when stress-ng uses 80% of the CPU. With a free CPU, RocksDB finishes the 5 GB run fastest and LUDA is only ahead of LevelDB. LUDA has no Snappy compression, and it compacts about 2x more data than LevelDB at 128 B values. The paper says 'we are ready to open source it', but the footnote only links the anonymized placeholder github.com/anonymous. No public repository was found (GitHub repo search), so has_code=false and repo_url is null. arXiv preprint only; no peer-reviewed version found.

name: Mycelium (TE-LSM)
workload: RocksDB-based prototype that embeds split, convert (JSON to FlatBuffers) and augment (secondary index) transformations into compaction through cross-column-family 'Tierveling'. Measured: write throughput after a 100 GB preload (200M records of about 500 B), plus query latency (min/P25/P50/P75/max) for Q2 to Q7 (column-retrieving, row-retrieving and index point/range queries) with Zipfian keys, against RocksDB baselines.
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.25x lower query latency (abstract: 'up to 425% improvements in read latency compared to RocksDB baseline') for Q2, a column-retrieving range query (max over a range). This is with the CONVERT transformer (JSON to FlatBuffers during compaction) against a RocksDB baseline that stores JSON. The split transformation gives 2.8x on Q2, and row-retrieving queries (Q6/Q7) get slower under split. Write-throughput overhead against RocksDB is 10.09% to 21.25% (Table 2): under 16% for a single transformation and about 20% for two. Secondary-index (augment) queries show gains of 'several hundred thousand times' only because plain RocksDB has to do full table scans.
hardware: 2x 16-core CPUs @ 3.00GHz, 128GB ECC RAM, two 480GB SATA SSDs, Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS
tradeoffs: Query speedup is achieved by embedding data transformations (e.g. cross-column-family merges) into RocksDB's compaction process, which measurably reduces write throughput (16%-20% overhead) -- a direct read/write tradeoff, not a free win; benefit is workload/query-type dependent.
caveats: The headline metric is read/query latency, not throughput. The 4.25x win partly comes from a data-format change (JSON to FlatBuffers) that the baseline does not get. Row-retrieving queries are slower under the split transform, and the index-query gains compare against RocksDB full scans (not like-for-like). The CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated. The paper is an arXiv preprint with no journal-ref and says its code is 'hidden due to anonymity'. A probable anonymized review repo (github.com/anon-rev-repo/mycelium-anon, created 2026-07-27, 0 stars) describes Mycelium as a RocksDB-based LSM that piggybacks transformations on compaction and includes a YCSB harness under src/test/ycsb. The paper does not link it, it uses newer terminology (WHLSM, LSM-Grove, mRoutines), and it has no top-level license (only the vendored RocksDB licenses under src/lsm).

name: Nova-LSM
workload: YCSB RW50/SW50/W100 workloads (R100 also used for response times), 1 KB records, 10 GB to 2 TB databases, Uniform and Zipfian access, on 1 server and on 10 servers, with logging disabled for all systems. Nova-LSM (disaggregated LTC/StoC components over RDMA) is compared with LevelDB and RocksDB in single-instance, 64-instance and tuned-knob configurations on CloudLab APT c6220 nodes.
claimed_speedup: 2.3x to 18x higher throughput than LevelDB and RocksDB with a skewed (Zipfian) access pattern and a 2 TB database on 10 nodes (paper's contribution list), with comparable throughput under Uniform access. The 105x figure is not a distributed result. It comes from a single server with a 10 GB database on SW50 (50% scan/50% write) Zipfian, measured relative to ONE LevelDB instance (omega=1), and the paper gives 8x against LevelDB with 64 instances. The Figure 18a bar labels (LevelDB=1) put RocksDB at 6, RocksDB-tuned at 36 and RocksDB* (64 instances) at 73 against Nova-LSM's 105. That is roughly 17.5x, 2.9x and 1.4x over those RocksDB configurations (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo's CMakeLists.txt hard-codes /usr/bin/g++ (version unstated) with -std=c++11 -fexceptions -g, and the README build is a plain 'cmake . && make -j4' with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. Build flags for the LevelDB/RocksDB baselines are unstated.
hardware: CloudLab APT c6220 nodes: 64GB RAM, two 8-core Xeon E5-2650v2 CPUs (32 vCPUs w/ hyperthreading), 1TB HDD, Mellanox FDR CX3 InfiniBand (56Gbps) + 10Gbps Ethernet
tradeoffs: Disaggregates storage from compute across networked components (RDMA), which requires a multi-node RDMA cluster (InfiniBand) rather than the single-node embedded deployment RocksDB/LevelDB target; large speedups are specific to skewed multi-tenant access patterns that a disaggregated design can load-balance, not representative of typical single-node embedded use.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SIGMOD 2021, DOI 10.1145/3448016.3457297), but the compiler version and flags are unstated, and the repo's default build adds -g without an optimization level. The 105x figure is single-node and measured against a single untuned LevelDB instance; against 64-instance RocksDB* the same scenario is only about 1.4x (derived from page data). The abstract's 'several orders of magnitude' is not borne out by the figures. With Uniform access, throughput is comparable or lower: there is a 15% range-index overhead on SW50 single-node, and the paper reports 20-30% degradation on CPU-intensive uniform workloads. On tmpfs, RocksDB* beats Nova-LSM on SW50. The system needs RDMA/InfiniBand and was evaluated on dated HDD-based nodes with logging disabled. The code is an extension of LevelDB 1.22 (its CMake project is named leveldb), although it is not a GitHub fork.
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2104.01305; code via gh search repos "Nova-LSM"

name: SNKV (SnkvDB)
workload: 1M records on Linux; both stores WAL mode, synchronous=NORMAL, 8MB cache, 4KB pages, SQLite uses a WITHOUT ROWID table; sequential writes, random reads, sequential scan, random updates/deletes, mixed workload.
claimed_speedup: 1.64x-2x faster than SQLite (1M records): sequential writes 232K vs 142K ops/s (1.64x), random reads 160K vs 90K ops/s (1.77x), sequential scan 2.89M vs 1.56M ops/s (1.85x), random updates 31K vs 16K ops/s (1.9x), random deletes 31K vs 16K ops/s (~2x), mixed workload 62K vs 34K ops/s (1.79x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated with the results. SNKV Makefile: gcc, default BUILD=debug (-g -O0 -DDEBUG), BUILD=release gives -O2 -DNDEBUG. The SQLite comparison repo (hash-anu/sqllite-benchmark-kv) Makefile: gcc -g -Wall with no -O flag, i.e. GCC's default -O0.
hardware: Linux (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: C API talks directly to SQLite's B-tree/pager/WAL layer with no SQL parser or query planner; loses schema-layer tooling (sqlite3 CLI) though it is compatible with SQLite page/WAL-level tools like LiteFS; optional encryption and HNSW vector index add build complexity.
caveats: The SNKV side comes from tests/test_benchmark.c. The SQLite side comes from a separate 0-star repo, hash-anu/sqllite-benchmark-kv, whose README only says 'run make test'. No CPU model, compiler version or build mode is stated. That repo compiles sqlite3.c with gcc -g -Wall and no optimization flag (-O0), and SNKV's Makefile defaults to a -O0 debug build, so both sides may have been unoptimized; the result may not hold at -O2/-O3. SNKV is SQLite's own B-tree/pager/WAL with the SQL parser, planner and VDBE removed, so the gain is from skipping the SQL layer, not from a faster storage engine. The linked LMDB and RocksDB comparison repos (hash-anu/lmdb-benchmark, hash-anu/rocksdb-benchmark) contain only source code and no published numbers; the README itself suggests RocksDB for maximum write throughput and LMDB for maximum read speed.

name: ToplingDB
workload: db_bench fillrandom, fillseq and fillseq (CSPP) suites (fill, flush, compact, readseq x3, readrandom): 50,000,000 records, 8-byte keys, 50-byte values, batch_size 1000. The DB lives on /dev/shm (tmpfs) and the on-disk DB (~1.9 GiB for fillrandom) fits inside the 7.8 GiB RocksDB block cache. ToplingDB uses ToplingZipTable (zipkeyonly/zipkeyvalue), the CSPP memtable and -enable_zero_copy.
claimed_speedup: Run of 2026-09-15 (run_id 34935695406), fillrandom suite, readrandom stage. ToplingDB zipkeyvalue reached 1,735,572 ops/sec vs 348,705 for RocksDB v8.10 (4.98x, stated on the page, which calls this 'the fairest comparison') and vs 378,878 for RocksDB master (4.58x, on page). ToplingDB zipkeyonly, which stores values uncompressed while RocksDB uses Snappy/Zstd, reached 4,720,755 ops/sec: 13.54x vs v8.10 and 12.46x vs master (on page). Other stages: fillrandom 1,660,002 vs 664,354 ops/sec (2.50x, on page) and readseq 16,936,378 vs 10,771,647 (1.57x, on page). ToplingDB is slower on compaction: zipkeyvalue runs at 0.62x of v8.10 in the fillrandom suite and 0.30x in the fillseq suite. The page is a live dashboard, so the numbers change with each CI run.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. The public CI workflow builds ToplingDB with `make ... DEBUG_LEVEL=0` and upstream RocksDB with DEBUG_LEVEL=0 PORTABLE=haswell (to match ToplingDB's -march=haswell). The compiler is the ubuntu-latest default (gcc) unless the workflow's use_clang input is set, and the version is unstated.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (4 logical CPUs; GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, Azure kernel 6.17), Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, 15.6 GiB RAM, DB on /dev/shm
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 is more restrictive than RocksDB's BSD/Apache-2.0 dual license, which can block adoption in permissively-licensed downstream projects. Several advertised features (distributed compaction, some CSPP tooling) are gated behind a separate paid 'Enterprise' build not in this open repo.
caveats: The benchmark is run and published by the ToplingDB project itself, and the results page does not name the compiler. The dataset sits entirely in cache on tmpfs, which the page itself calls a CPU/memory comparison, so the result may not carry over to larger-than-cache workloads. The 13.5x headline uses zipkeyonly, which leaves values uncompressed against a compressed RocksDB and uses 1.24-1.97x more disk; the fair zipkeyvalue figure is ~5x. Compaction is slower than RocksDB. Most importantly, the components benchmarked, the ToplingZipTable builder (private topling-rocks repo) and the CSPP MemTable (private), are closed source; the build downloads them as precompiled 90-day trial objects. Only the RocksDB-derived core and some plugins are open (GPL-2.0/Apache-2.0 inherited from RocksDB).

name: APEX (learned index on persistent memory)
baseline: FAST+FAIR (also compared against LB+-Tree, DPTree, uTree, FPTree, BzTree)
workload: YCSB-derived and real-world datasets (Longitudes, Longlat, Lognormal, FB, TPC-E), 8-byte integer/double keys, insert/search/scan/update/erase and mixed read-heavy/balanced operation mixes, single NUMA node up to 24 physical cores, on real Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory
claimed_speedup: Single-thread results (paper Fig. 4). Inserts: up to 15x/2.7x/3.8x/1.66x/6.8x/3.7x faster than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree across five datasets (up to 3.8x over FAST+FAIR). On the hardest-to-fit FB dataset, inserts are 1.18x/5.16x/2.3x/1.26x faster than FAST+FAIR/BzTree/uTree/FPTree but 5.77%/42% slower than LB+-Tree/DPTree. Search: up to 7.1x/3.9x/4.1x/3.2x/3.2x/5.8x higher than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree. Scans: up to 7.6x/1.45x/1.46x/1.83x/16.38x/3.1x faster than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree on five datasets. The abstract says up to ~15x better than existing PM indexes; that figure is the BzTree insert case.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.2 'with all optimizations' (paper section 6.2). The repo's CMakeLists.txt GCC flags are -mrtm -msse4.1 -mavx2 -O3 -g -march=native.
hardware: 2.1GHz Intel Xeon Gold 6252 (24 cores / 48 hyperthreads, 35.75MB L3), 768GB Intel Optane DCPMM (6 x 128GB) plus 192GB DRAM, Arch Linux kernel 5.10.11
stars_or_usage: 49 stars. Built on Microsoft's ALEX learned index code (README). Published as PVLDB 15(3):597-610 (Nov 2021, DOI 10.14778/3494124.3494141).
tradeoffs: Requires real Intel Optane DC PM with App Direct mode and DAX filesystem; inherits ALEX's linear-model-fitting assumptions, so performance depends on how well the key distribution fits piecewise-linear models (worst case on the hard-to-fit FB dataset)
caveats: All comparisons are against other PM-resident indexes on real Optane DCPMM, not against DRAM-resident RocksDB/LevelDB/LMDB or the RMI/PGM learned indexes. The public repo's benchmark only runs APEX; competitor implementations, including the authors' added range scans for FAST+FAIR, LB+-Tree and uTree and their LB+-Tree fix, are only linked to upstream repos. APEX is slower than LB+-Tree and DPTree on inserts for the FB dataset. Intel Optane DCPMM has been discontinued, so the target hardware is no longer sold.

name: CHT (Compact Hist-Tree)
workload: SOSD benchmark equality lookups over 200M-key real-world datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki), average lookup latency over 1M uniformly-random queries
claimed_speedup: CHT beats RMI by 1.1-1.8x, PGM-index by 1.7-2.5x, and RadixSpline by 1.2-2.7x in lookup latency; the compact (read-only) layout is 2-3x faster than the updatable Hist-Tree (HT) variant; also 3.7x-19x faster build times than RMI on face/wiki datasets
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ 9.3.0 (optimization flags not stated)
hardware: AWS c5.4xlarge EC2 instance, Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M CPU @ 3.0GHz, 26MB LLC
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; this C++ implementation is the CHT component of PLEX (Stoian et al., 'Towards Practical Learned Indexing', AIDB 2021)
tradeoffs: Compact layout is build-once/read-only (no updates); the updatable HT variant exists but is 2-3x slower on lookups; author credited as Andrew Crotty (Brown University), repo implementation by Mihail Stoian
caveats: The numbers come from the CIDR 2021 paper (Andrew Crotty, 'Hist-Tree: Those Who Ignore It Are Doomed to Learn'). That paper benchmarks Crotty's own C implementation with a C++ suite borrowed from SOSD and publishes neither. This repo is a separate C++ reimplementation of the compact Hist-Tree by Mihail Stoian (MIT, 2021). The paper's speedups were therefore not measured on this code, and the paper states no optimization flags. The PLEX paper notes this implementation does not support duplicate keys, so it could not run SOSD's wiki dataset. The repo's bench.cc is only a parameter grid search on synthetic data with no baseline. There is no README benchmark section, and there have been no commits since 2021-07-17.

name: DPTree (Differential Indexing for Persistent Memory)
workload: Single-thread micro-benchmark: 64-bit random integer keys, 16-byte key-value pairs, 25M-100M keys; insert latency, point lookup, and range scan at 0.001%-0.1% selectivity. Concurrent YCSB-style workloads on 50M keys: InsertOnly, ReadOnly, ReadUpdate (50/50), ScanInsert (95% scans/5% inserts) and Mixed, up to 32 threads on one socket, on real Intel Optane DC PMM.
claimed_speedup: Single-thread micro-benchmark (25M-100M random 64-bit keys). Point lookups: up to 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x faster than FAST+FAIR/FPTree/WORT. Inserts: 1.27-1.43x lower latency than FAST+FAIR and 1.76-1.78x lower than FPTree. Range scans: up to 3.0x/10.98x faster than FPTree/WORT but up to 1.1x slower than FAST+FAIR. Concurrent YCSB (50M keys, up to 32 threads). InsertOnly: up to 1.36x higher throughput than FAST+FAIR at 32 threads. ReadOnly: 1.32-1.58x (vs FAST+FAIR) and 1.37-1.7x (vs FPTree) higher throughput. ReadUpdate: highest throughput at all thread counts, up to 1.7-5.07x over the other indexes. ScanInsert: FAST+FAIR keeps the highest scan throughput.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 6.4 with -O3 (paper section 4.1)
hardware: Two Intel Xeon Platinum 8263C @ 2.50GHz (26 physical cores), 35MB LLC, 376GB DRAM, 512GB Intel Optane DC PMM in App Direct mode via ext4-DAX, Linux kernel 4.9. All threads bound to one socket.
stars_or_usage: 61 stars; published as PVLDB 13(4):421-434 (Dec 2019, DOI 10.14778/3372716.3372717; presented at VLDB 2020)
tradeoffs: Splits a DRAM-resident hot buffer (backed by stx-btree) from a cold persistent tree, requiring in-place PM merges; depends on Intel TBB and tcmalloc as external libraries
caveats: The 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x figures are single-thread point-lookup gains over FAST+FAIR/FPTree/WORT respectively, not gains over FAST+FAIR across workloads. The 3.0x/10.98x figures are range-scan gains over FPTree/WORT; on scans DPTree is up to 1.1x slower than FAST+FAIR, which also keeps the highest scan throughput in ScanInsert. Experiments ran on real Optane DC PMM (App Direct, ext4-DAX), not emulated PM. FPTree is the authors' own reimplementation because the original is closed-source. The public repo contains only DPTree's own benchmark drivers, not the baseline harness. Intel Optane is discontinued.

name: FAST+FAIR (Failure-Atomic ShifT + Failure-Atomic In-place Rebalancing B+-Tree)
baseline: wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT and SkipList (single-threaded); FP-tree, B-link tree and SkipList (concurrent)
workload: Single- and multi-threaded (up to 16 threads) synthetic key-value insert/search/range-query workload with 8-byte integer keys on emulated byte-addressable persistent memory (NVM), varying node size and range-query selection ratio
claimed_speedup: FAST'18 paper: range queries up to 20x faster than SkipList and 6-27% faster than FP-tree / 25-33% faster than wB+-tree (10M 8-byte random keys, 1KB nodes, 300ns PM read latency). Insertion: FAST+FAIR, FP-tree and WORT are comparable and beat wB+-tree and SkipList 'by a large margin' (wB+-tree issues 1.7x more cache-line flushes); as PM write latency rises FAST+FAIR consistently outperforms FP-tree, wB+-tree and SkipList, but WORT is fastest. The 'up to 1.61x faster than wB+-tree' figure is from the ARM (Nexus 5 / Snapdragon 800) non-TSO insertion experiment, not the Xeon runs. TPC-C mixes W1-W4: FAST+FAIR consistently outperforms the other indexes (figure only, no ratio). Concurrency is self-scaling only: search throughput rises about 11.7x from 1 to 16 threads, insertion about 12.5x at 16 threads (FP-tree 7.7x, B-link 4.4x), and the mixed workload reaches up to 11.44x the single-thread throughput. The '~2.2x higher than B-link tree at 8 threads' figure belongs to FP-tree (TSX), not FAST+FAIR.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.2 -O3 (single-threaded); concurrent implementations compiled without -O3 because the optimizer reorders memory operations needed by the lock-free logic
hardware: Workstation with two Intel Xeon Haswell-EX E7-4809 v3 @ 2.0GHz (16 vCPUs with hyper-threading, 20MB L3), 64GB DDR3 DRAM; threads bound to one socket with numactl for the concurrent runs; PM latency emulated with the Quartz DRAM-based emulator. The ARM experiment ran on a Nexus 5 (Snapdragon 800 @ 2.26GHz) with nop-injected PM write latency.
stars_or_usage: 118 stars; evaluated as a baseline in later persistent-memory index papers including DPTree (PVLDB 13(4)) and APEX (VLDB'22). The LB+-Tree (PVLDB 13(7)) and BzTree (PVLDB 11(5)) papers do not evaluate it.
tradeoffs: Relies on 8-byte failure-atomic word writes specific to NVM consistency model; leaf nodes use an unsorted array (linear search) trading insert speed for slower lookups at large node sizes; concurrent version uses per-node std::mutex-style locks, not fully lock-free
caveats: PM was emulated (Quartz on DRAM; nop injection on ARM), not real Optane. FAST+FAIR is not uniformly fastest: WORT wins insertion at higher PM write latency; FP-tree searches slightly faster when read latency exceeds 600ns; on ARM at DRAM latency FAST+FAIR is slower than FP-tree. The repo ships only FAST+FAIR, not the baseline implementations. Concurrent builds omit -O3. These are the 2018 paper's numbers; later papers such as DPTree (up to 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x faster than FAST+FAIR) and APEX beat it, so it is now a baseline rather than the fastest option.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "FAST_FAIR"

verification.tier_reason: The FAST'18 paper compares FAST+FAIR with wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT and SkipList (plus B-link tree for concurrency) and states g++ 4.8.2 -O3 and the Xeon E7-4809 v3. It is not tier A because the DICL/FAST_FAIR repo holds only the FAST+FAIR code (single/, concurrent/, *_pmdk/ test programs) with no wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT, SkipList or B-link implementations, so the published benchmark code does not run against the named baselines; that makes it a peer-reviewed B.

The default-branch (master) last commit is 2020-06-12; the record's 2021-03-12 is pushed_at, which matches a 2021-03-11 commit on the non-default issue-13 branch. Still abandoned either way. License GPL-3.0, not archived, not a fork.

name: IBTree (Interpolating B-Tree, SOSD implementation)
workload: SOSD 'Benchmarking Learned Indexes' Table 2: the fastest configured variant of each structure, lower-bound lookups (10M random lookup keys) on a 32-bit version of the amzn dataset (200M keys). It is 32-bit because the SIMD CuckooMap in the table only supports 32-bit keys (footnote 4).
claimed_speedup: 446.55 ns vs the STX BTree's 482.11 ns lookup time (~1.08x, ~8% faster), using 9.0 MB vs 166.0 MB (~18x smaller) (derived from page data; 32-bit amzn, PVLDB 14(1) Table 2)
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated in the paper or the repo (the README dependency list installs clang). SOSD CMakeLists.txt adds -ffast-math -march=native (and -fopenmp if available), and scripts/prepare.sh builds with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG).
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM
tradeoffs: Implements interpolation search inside B-tree nodes per G. Graefe's 2018 VLDB paper 'B-tree indexes, interpolation search, and skew'; only exists as a template competitor inside the SOSD benchmark harness, not a standalone packaged library; degrades on skewed/adversarial key distributions where interpolation mispredicts
caveats: Single table row: 32-bit amzn only, best variant per structure. The margin over the STX B-tree is modest (~8%). FAST (435.33 ns) edges it, and learned indexes (RMI 180.90 ns, RS 266.58 ns) and hash tables are far faster in the same table. IBTree is a header inside the SOSD benchmark repo, not a standalone library. SOSD has had no commits since April 2022. The previously cited CIDR'21 Hist-Tree paper does not contain IBTree or these numbers.
found_via: SOSD benchmark Table 1/competitors listing + Table 2 numbers quoted in the CIDR 2021 Hist-Tree paper
