name: LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)
baseline: STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index")
workload: Point lookups/inserts on four datasets (Longitudes 1B, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M keys) under Read-Only, Read-Heavy, Write-Heavy, Write-Only workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x throughput vs ALEX/PGM/Learned-Index/B+Tree on read-only workloads; 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x vs ALEX/PGM/B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i7 (4 cores, 8 threads) @ 4.0GHz, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, single thread used
tradeoffs: No concurrency support; amortized O(log^2 N) insert cost vs B+Tree's better worst case; needs periodic subtree adjustment; benefit shrinks a lot on highly non-uniform key distributions
caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only. Gains vary strongly by dataset: as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset. The paper names no CPU model (only '4.0 GHz Intel Core i7') and its benchmark harness against the baselines is not public; the repo ships only the core header and examples. The GRE study (PVLDB 15(11) 2022) found and fixed two bugs in LIPP (merged as PRs #11/#12). It reports that the fixes gave slightly lower performance than the LIPP paper reported, and that LIPP's unified node design scales poorly with multiple threads. Repo unmaintained since Feb 2022.
found_via: GitHub code search 'updatable learned index' + citation from the PGM-index/ALEX literature; verified via PVLDB paper PDF (Sections 6.1-6.2)

verification.tier_reason: The PVLDB 14(8) 2021 paper is peer-reviewed. Section 6.2 compares LIPP with STX B+Tree, ART, ALEX, PGM, Learned Index and BwTree, and it states GCC 9.0.1 at O3. It does not reach A: the CPU is given only as a '4.0 GHz Intel Core i7 (4 cores and 8 threads)' with no model number, and the comparison harness was never published (the repo holds only src/core and src/examples).
verification.notes: The numbers match Sections 6.2.1 and 6.2.2 exactly: 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x read-only and 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x read-write, plus the 1.47x Longlat figure. The metadata checks out: MIT, 63 stars, last commit 2022-02-07, not a fork. An independent third-party suite, GRE (github.com/gre4index/GRE, src/benchmark/microbench.cpp vs src/competitor/btree/btree.h = STX), states gcc 8.3.0 -O3 on a Xeon Platinum 8268 and shows LIPP/ALEX beating traditional indexes single-threaded. Its heatmap gives no numeric ratios, though, so I did not use it to keep tier A; enrichment could pull numbers from GRE runs.

corrected_fields.caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only; gains vary strongly by dataset (as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset); repo unmaintained since Feb 2022

name: TidesDB
workload: benchtool tidesdb_rocksdb.sh: 8 threads, 16-byte keys / 100-byte values, sync disabled. Random and sequential seeks are 5M ops after populating 5M keys; Zipfian seeks run over ~650K unique keys; range queries of 100 and 1000 keys (random) and 100 keys (sequential). TidesDB v6.1.0 vs RocksDB v10.7.5.
claimed_speedup: Random seeks 4.17x faster (3.73M vs 893K ops/sec); sequential seeks 4.74x faster (8.87M vs 1.87M ops/sec); Zipfian seeks 5.25x faster (3.56M vs 679K ops/sec); small (100-key) range queries 2.41x faster; large (1000-key) range queries 1.11x faster
compiler_and_flags: GCC with -O3 optimization
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K (8 cores/16 threads @ 4.9GHz), 48GB DDR4, WD 500GB SATA SSD, Ubuntu 23.04 x86_64 (kernel 6.2.0-39-generic)
tradeoffs: Gains attributed to aggressive caching design; large (1000-key) range queries show only a marginal 1.11x edge, so the advantage narrows for big scans; single-machine, single-hardware-config benchmark
caveats: First-party vendor benchmark by the TidesDB author. The official benchtool repo (github.com/tidesdb/benchtool) now returns 404, and the code survives only in the mirror dhoard/tidesdb-benchtool. TidesDB uses 3.46x more memory (851 MB vs 246 MB peak RSS) because it keeps SSTable metadata resident. Large 1000-key ranges are essentially a tie (1.11x, within variance per the author). In the raw report the seek phase logs 'tidesdb (v6.0.2)' and RocksDB 'vunknown'. TidesDB is an LSM key-value storage engine rather than an index structure.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'faster than RocksDB' -> 'TidesDB: 4.7x faster seeks than RocksDB via aggressive caching'
gh code search '"outperforms RocksDB" repo:tidesdb/tidesdb.github.io'

verification.tier_reason: The Dec 17 2025 article states GCC -O3, an Intel Core i7-11700K, the OS/kernel and RocksDB v10.7.5, and links a raw report (benchmark_results_tdb610_rdb1075_range_seek1.txt) whose SEEK throughputs (3729450 vs 893870; 8867103 vs 1869637 ops/sec) match. The linked code, github.com/tidesdb/benchtool, is now 404. Its full history survives in the mirror dhoard/tidesdb-benchtool (commits by the TidesDB author, including 2e0d4b9d of 2025-12-16), so the code is public: tidesdb_rocksdb.sh test 11 'Seek Performance' plus engine_rocksdb.c / engine_tidesdb.c.
verification.notes: All claimed ratios and throughputs appear verbatim on the article (sequential 100-key ranges are an extra 1.14x). Metadata checked: MPL-2.0, 567 stars, not archived, not a fork; default-branch last commit 2026-09-25 (pushed_at 2026-09-26). Category 'indexes' is a loose fit for an LSM KV engine, but it cannot be corrected via this schema.

corrected_fields.workload: 8-thread benchmark, 16-byte keys / 100-byte values, 5M keys for random/sequential seeks and range queries, 650K unique keys for Zipfian-distributed seeks (TidesDB v6.1.0 vs RocksDB v10.7.5, benchtool)
corrected_fields.caveats: First-party benchmark (TidesDB's own blog and benchtool repo), not an independent third party; methodology (workload, versions, hardware) is fully stated so kept at A rather than downgraded to C, but should be treated as a vendor claim

name: ALEX (Adaptive Learned indEX)
baseline: STX B+Tree (std::map-like ordered index); also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a 2-stage RMI ("Learned Index"), and a Model-enhanced B+Tree
workload: Single-threaded throughput on 4 datasets with 8-byte keys: longitudes (1B keys), longlat (200M), lognormal (190M) and YCSB (200M, 80-byte payloads). Five workloads: read-only, read-heavy (95% reads/5% inserts), write-heavy (50/50), short range scans (95% scans/5% inserts) and write-only.
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x higher throughput and 800x/15x/160x/8000x smaller index than B+Tree/Learned-Index/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-only workloads; up to 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x higher throughput and 2000x/475x/36000x smaller index vs B+Tree/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K 3.6GHz, 64GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
stars_or_usage: 701 stars; used as a baseline by many follow-up learned-index papers (LIPP, CARMI, etc.)
tradeoffs: No concurrency support in the public implementation; can degrade under adversarial/skewed insert patterns without retraining; README explicitly calls it 'a near drop-in replacement for std::map'
caveats: The paper states hardware (i9-9900K, 64GB) but no compiler or optimization flags. The public repo's benchmark (src/benchmark/main.cpp) runs only ALEX, so the B+Tree/ART comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. The baseline is STX B+Tree, not std::map. Later peer-reviewed work corroborates the win: LIPP (PVLDB'21) and GRE (PVLDB'22, gcc 8.3.0 -O3, Xeon Platinum 8268) found ALEX among the top single-threaded indexes against STX B+Tree/ART/HOT.
found_via: Starting query variation: 'in-memory learned index drop-in replacement std::map faster than B-tree'

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed SIGMOD'20 paper (arXiv 1905.08898) shows ALEX beating STX B+Tree, ART, a 2-level RMI and a Model B+Tree on an Intel Core i9-9900K. It states no compiler or flags, and the repo's src/benchmark/main.cpp benchmarks ALEX alone with no baseline harness, so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: All claimed ratios appear verbatim in Section 6 (4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x read-only; 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x read-write; index-size ratios). Two fields were wrong: compared_against_cpp_std_directly was set true, but the paper benchmarks STX B+Tree, not std::map; and the workload said all datasets were 200M keys, but longitudes is 1B and lognormal 190M. The metadata checks out: MIT, 701 stars, last commit 2024-03-12 (stale), not a fork.

corrected_fields.workload: Point lookups/inserts on 4 real datasets (longitudes, longlat, lognormal, YCSB; 200M 8-byte keys) under read-only and read-write (mixed insert) workloads, single-threaded
corrected_fields.caveats: Hardware stated in the SIGMOD'20 paper (arXiv preprint) but compiler/optimization flags not given in the accessible text; independently reused as a baseline by later peer-reviewed papers (LIPP, CARMI), which corroborate the B+Tree comparison

name: ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against
workload: Concurrent lookup, insert and remove throughput at 1-20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention). A contention test runs 1 lookup thread and 1 insert+remove thread on 10M dense keys with Zipf skew. Lookup and insert run at 20 threads on three string datasets: genome (256K), Wikipedia titles (16M) and URLs (6.4M). The comparison covers the ART synchronization variants (lock coupling, Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) against Masstree.
claimed_speedup: On 50M random 8-byte integer keys, Optimistic Lock Coupling and ROWEX beat Masstree clearly (approximate values read off Figure 5, derived from page data). At 20 threads, lookups run at ~82-86M ops/s vs ~29M (~3x), inserts at ~56M vs ~24M (~2.3x), and removes at ~38M vs ~26M (~1.5x). The per-lookup cycle table gives OLC 348/418 cycles vs Masstree 982/1231 at 1/20 threads, ~2.8-2.9x fewer (derived from page data). The text says OLC needs 4.8x fewer instructions and 3.6x fewer L3 misses than Masstree. On string keys at 20 threads (Figure 7), synchronized ART beats Masstree only on genome inserts (~29M vs ~7M ops/s). Masstree is roughly on par for genome lookups and faster on both Wikipedia and URL.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W v3 (Haswell EP, 10 cores/20 threads), 25MB L3 cache
tradeoffs: Requires jemalloc and TBB; ROWEX needs custom epoch-based memory reclamation and is the most complex variant to implement/maintain; the paper itself notes the ART-vs-Masstree comparison is not apples-to-apples since the synchronization protocols and data structures differ
caveats: The paper itself says ART vs Masstree is not apples-to-apples. ART's big win is on short integer keys; on string keys at 20 threads, Masstree matches or beats synchronized ART everywhere except genome inserts, including Wikipedia and URL lookups and inserts. Synchronization costs ~65% vs unsynchronized ART single-threaded, falling to ~10% at 20 threads. Compiler and flags are not stated, and no benchmark harness against Masstree is published. Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines. The last commit (2026-05-25, authored 2026-05-24) fixes a new-delete-type-mismatch memory-corruption bug after ~4 years of inactivity, so treat 'active' loosely.
found_via: GitHub topic search 'adaptive radix tree concurrent' -> cross-referenced against the ART synchronization DaMoN 2016 paper

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed DaMoN 2016 paper benchmarks the synchronized ART variants against Masstree on a Xeon E5-2687W v3. It states no compiler or flags and publishes no comparison harness (the repo's example.cpp does not include Masstree), so B holds, but the claim was misstated.
verification.notes: The record's claim of 'roughly 2x on genome and URL' is wrong. In Figure 7, Masstree is faster on URL lookups and inserts, and genome lookups are close to a tie. The strong, supportable win is on integer keys (Figure 5 and the CPU-counter table). The LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 (gh reports NOASSERTION), stars are 129, and the repo is not a fork. GRE (PVLDB'22) independently lists ART-OLC, not Masstree, among its 24-thread winners, but I did not verify that GRE uses this repo's implementation.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ROWEX/Optimistic Lock Coupling beat Masstree by roughly 2x on lookup/insert throughput for the genome and URL string datasets at 20 threads; Masstree is faster on the Wikipedia dataset and closes the gap with longer keys
corrected_fields.workload: Concurrent lookup/insert/remove throughput at up to 20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention), plus lookup/insert at 20 threads on three string datasets (genome 256K keys, Wikipedia 16M titles, URL 6.4M URLs), comparing ART synchronization variants (Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) vs Masstree
corrected_fields.caveats: Results are mixed across datasets (Masstree wins on the Wikipedia string dataset); Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines; the last GitHub push (2026-05-24) is likely a housekeeping commit on an otherwise ~2015-era codebase, so treat 'active' loosely

name: Bourbon (learned index for LSM-trees, OSDI'20 artifact)
baseline: WiscKey (the authors' LevelDB-derived LSM with key-value separation; no direct stock-LevelDB or RocksDB comparison)
workload: Read-only lookups (10M operations, 16B integer keys, 64B values, in-memory) on six datasets (linear, seg-1%, seg-10%, normal with 64M keys; Amazon Reviews 33.5M; NY OpenStreetMaps 21.9M), comparing Bourbon's per-file greedy piecewise-linear-regression models (error bound 8) with the WiscKey baseline; plus YCSB, SOSD, Optane SSD and limited-memory runs.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: "BOURBON improves lookup performance by 1.23x-1.78x as compared to state-of-the-art production LSMs". In Fig. 9 the baseline is WiscKey, with 1.23x-1.78x lower average lookup latency across six datasets. vs WiscKey elsewhere: YCSB-C about 1.6x, YCSB-B/D 1.24x-1.44x, YCSB-A/F 1.06x-1.18x, YCSB-E 1.16x-1.19x; SOSD 1.48x-1.74x; Optane SSD 1.25x-1.28x; SATA SSD with limited memory 1.04x (uniform) and 1.25x (zipfian).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated; built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE -DNDEBUG_SWITCH=ON (ARTIFACT_README/CS736_README)
hardware: 20-core Intel Xeon CPU E5-2660, 160 GB memory, 480 GB SATA SSD (CloudLab c220g2 per ARTIFACT_README); the fast-storage runs used an Intel Optane SSD.
tradeoffs: Learned index is trained per SSTable file at compaction time using a cost-benefit rule to decide when learning is worthwhile; benefits are workload/data-distribution dependent (helps most when keys within a file are well-approximated by a piecewise-linear model).
caveats: The only baseline is WiscKey (a research LSM built on LevelDB), despite the abstract's 'production LSMs' wording; there is no RocksDB or stock-LevelDB head-to-head. Gains are for lookups only, with integer keys; string keys and key compression are unsupported, and writes are not improved. This GitHub repo is not the authors' own: a third party (Edward Fang) imported it as a snapshot ('original bourbon', 2020-10-11) of the authors' Bitbucket learned-leveldb artifact. It then added CS736 course-project changes (offline/synchronous level learning, 'mode 9') and a 2023 PLR NaN-slope fix. The README says the owner is not the paper's author. Compiler is unstated.
found_via: gh search repos "bourbon" (surfaced edydfang/Bourbon, 'A Learned Index for Log-Structured Merge Trees'); paper abstract opened at https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/dai

verification.tier_reason: OSDI'20 peer-reviewed paper; every result compares Bourbon only against WiscKey, the authors' LevelDB-derived key-value-separated LSM, not against stock LevelDB or RocksDB. The CPU (Xeon E5-2660) and code (read_cold, scripts/run_*.sh; CMake RELEASE build) are available, but the compiler and its version are never stated, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The 1.23x-1.78x quote is verbatim from the USENIX abstract and paper. The record's baseline ('LevelDB / production LSM (RocksDB-class)') and workload ('unmodified production LSM implementations') overstate it, because the paper measures only against WiscKey. Kept at B, not rejected, since WiscKey is a recognizable LevelDB derivative. The authors' original code is public at bitbucket.org/daiyifandanny/learned-leveldb (Bitbucket API: public, last updated 2020-10-05); consider re-pointing the entry there. gh metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 47 stars, last commit 2023-09-06 (abandoned, just over 3 years old).

corrected_fields.workload: End-to-end lookup performance of a WiscKey/LevelDB-based LSM-tree modified to use per-file learned (piecewise-linear-regression) indexes, compared against unmodified state-of-the-art production LSM implementations.
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: "BOURBON improves lookup performance by 1.23x-1.78x as compared to state-of-the-art production LSMs."
corrected_fields.caveats: OSDI 2020 peer-reviewed paper (Tier B: hardware/compiler/flags were not visible on the fetched USENIX abstract page, only the headline speedup range). This GitHub repo is maintained by a third party as an artifact/course-project mirror of the original authors' (Yifan Dai et al.) code, not the original lab's own org; treat as a redistribution of the OSDI'20 artifact rather than an independent implementation.

name: Bw-Tree (Open BwTree, wangziqi2013)
workload: ICDE'13 (Microsoft implementation, 8 worker threads, 8K pages): the Xbox LIVE trace is 27M get-set operations with ~94-byte alphanumeric keys, ~1200-byte payloads and a read:write ratio of about 7.5:1 (not read-only, not 8-byte integer keys); the synthetic workload uses 8-byte integer keys and payloads, a 1M-entry initial index, 42M operations and 5:1 read:write; a deduplication trace gave 8.6x. SIGMOD'18 (this code): YCSB-style Insert-only, Read-only, Read/Update and Scan/Insert workloads on random, monotonic integer and email keys, run on 2x Xeon E5-2680 v2 with g++ 5.4 and tcmalloc.
claimed_speedup: This repo has no numbers against BerkeleyDB. SIGMOD'18 (OpenBw-Tree paper): 1.1-2.5x faster than the original Bw-Tree design on insert-heavy workloads and 1.1-1.4x on read-heavy ones, and faster than a lock-free SkipList. It is 'still slower than its competitors except the SkipList': ART is more than 4x faster for point lookups, and Masstree and a B+Tree with optimistic lock coupling are faster, often by about 2x. The repo's own benchmark-all screenshot (result/result-2016-07-30-2.png) gives BwTree 4.65M insert/s and 9.58M read/s vs std::map 5.91M/17.85M, std::unordered_map 15.36M/81.65M and stx::btree 10.60M/21.50M. The 18.7x (Xbox LIVE) and 5.8x (synthetic) speedups over BerkeleyDB in ICDE'13 are Microsoft's own closed-source implementation.
compiler_and_flags: ICDE'13 states none. SIGMOD'18: g++ 5.4 with tcmalloc. Repo result screenshots: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 (-mcx16, jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD).
hardware: ICDE'13 (Microsoft implementation): Intel Xeon W3550 @ 3.07GHz, 4 cores / 8 hyperthreads, 24GB RAM. SIGMOD'18 (this code): 2x Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2, 128GB RAM.
stars_or_usage: 531 stars; the Bw-Tree algorithm itself is used in SQL Server Hekaton, Azure DocumentDB and Bing per the original Microsoft Research work; this repo is an independent C++ reimplementation built for CMU's Peloton DBMS
tradeoffs: Lock-free via delta-chain updates and epoch-based reclamation; not wait-free (an ABORT delta can stall a locked parent node if the posting thread dies); fixed-size mapping table with no dynamic resize
caveats: The Bw-Tree speedups over BerkeleyDB in ICDE'13 come from Microsoft's unreleased implementation, not this repo. The repo's README says its benchmark is 'unavailable' during a redesign. Its own first-party numbers are single-threaded, where it is slower than std::map and stx::btree. Its authors' SIGMOD'18 evaluation concludes the Bw-Tree 'still does not perform as well as other concurrent data structures that use locks'. The std::map comparison ran with g++ on Ubuntu, so libstdc++ is inferred, not explicitly stated.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "bw-tree" --sort stars

verification.tier_reason: The ICDE'13 page does show 10.4M vs 555K ops/s (18.7x) and 5.8x against BerkeleyDB, but those numbers belong to Microsoft's unreleased Win32 implementation, not this repository. The only benchmarks of this code against a recognizable incumbent are first-party screenshots in the repo's result/ folder (g++ -O3, CPU unstated), which show it slower than std::map, std::unordered_map and stx::btree. Its authors' peer-reviewed SIGMOD'18 paper likewise reports it slower than B+Tree, Masstree and ART.
verification.notes: Reject as not-faster: the only speedup against a recognizable baseline (BerkeleyDB) belongs to different, closed code, and every benchmark of this repo's own code puts it behind std::map, stx::btree, B+Tree (OLC), Masstree and ART, ahead only of a lock-free SkipList. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 531 stars, last commit 2018-11-14, abandoned, not a fork.
verification.reject_overridden: Verifier flagged not-faster: the 18.7x/5.8x belong to Microsoft's closed Bw-Tree, and this open implementation benchmarks slower than std::map/stx::btree. Kept per the flagged-entry policy with the shortcoming documented; the evidence is real, not fabricated.

name: CARMI (Cache-Aware RMI)
baseline: STX B+Tree and ALEX; also beats RMI on the SOSD benchmark platform
workload: 7 datasets: 4 synthetic (lognormal, uniform, normal, exponential; 1GB each of <double,double> pairs) plus YCSB, OSMC and Facebook (67,108,864 records each). Workloads: read-only, write-heavy (50/50), read-heavy (95/5), write-partial (85% reads / 15% inserts concentrated in 60-90% of key range) and range scan, with uniform and Zipfian access; single-threaded, 100,000 operations per workload. Plus SOSD: amzn/face/wiki/osmc real-world datasets of 200M 32/64-bit keys, 10M uniform lookups.
claimed_speedup: Average 2.2x (up to 4.2x) speedup vs STX B+ Tree and 1.9x (up to 7.2x) vs ALEX, using ~0.77x the memory of the B+ Tree; on the SOSD platform the average speedup over the nearest competitor, RMI, is 1.2x (1.21x, up to 1.5x). In SOSD Table 3, ART is slightly faster on face32 (182.36 vs 187.43 ns) and RMI/RS are within ~1-5 ns on face64/wiki.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X 8-core CPU, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
tradeoffs: Read/static-friendly cost model; construction is more expensive due to a cost-based dynamic-programming search; gains shrink on already cache-friendly small datasets
caveats: Very low adoption (10 stars) and the repo has not been updated since Jan 2022. Numbers are the authors' own, from a peer-reviewed PVLDB 2022 paper. The abstract's 'outperforms all baselines on SOSD' is slightly overstated: ART beats CARMI on face32 and RMI is effectively tied on face64. No compiler or flags are stated. The lambda parameter is tuned per dataset.
found_via: gh search repos 'cache aware learned index' -> embryo-labs/CARMI, cross-checked against the arXiv preprint (2103.00858)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 2103.00858, published as PVLDB 15(11):2679-2691, 2022, DOI 10.14778/3551793.3551823) benchmarks CARMI against STX B+ Tree and ALEX and, on the SOSD platform, against RMI/RS/ALEX/FAST/ART/B+Tree etc. The CPU (AMD Ryzen 3700X) is stated and the code is public (embryo-labs/CARMI src/ with bundled stx_btree and alex), but no compiler or flags are given, so it cannot be A.

The workload's '~10^8 keys' was wrong: real datasets have 67,108,864 records, and the 10^8 in the paper is a key-value multiplier for the synthetic data. GitHub metadata was verified: MIT, 10 stars, not a fork, last commit 2022-01-03, so abandoned is correct.

name: Cuckoo Trie
workload: YCSB-C (100% lookup, uniform distribution) on the osm dataset (real-world key distribution, >=1GB index, exceeding LLC capacity), single-threaded, comparing the Cuckoo Trie against STX B-Tree, ARTOLC, HOT, and Wormhole.
claimed_speedup: "the Cuckoo Trie outperforms the other indexes—by up to 35% (HOT), 20% (ARTOLC), 50% (Wormhole) and 360% (STX) on YCSB-C with osm."
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.5.0 (paper). Cuckoo Trie: -O3 -fvisibility=hidden -flto -fno-strict-aliasing -march=haswell -DNDEBUG (Makefile). Baselines in other-benchmarked-indexes: STX and HOT -O3 -march=native, ARTOLC -O3, Wormhole driver -O2.
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (Skylake), 14 cores @ 2.6GHz per socket, 96GB DDR4-2666 per NUMA node, hyper-threading/Turbo-Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Exploits memory-level parallelism via a cuckoo hash table layout; requires 2MB huge pages and a huge-page-aware allocator (e.g. jemalloc) to hit reported numbers, x86_64/Linux only; performs worse than other tries on keys with long common prefixes (its worst case, the 'az' dataset) and on scan-heavy workloads where its DRAM-access overlap trick doesn't help.
caveats: Research code: the README says it 'was created to run the experiments in the paper' and 'is not robust enough to be used as an index in your program'. It runs on Linux x86_64 only and needs 2MB huge pages plus a huge-page allocator (jemalloc, THP) for paper-level numbers. The Cuckoo Trie is slower on the az dataset (long common prefixes), on scan-heavy YCSB-E, and on inserts vs ARTOLC. The 360% win is over the STX B+-tree (tlx), not std::map. Optimization flags differ slightly across the compared indexes. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant. The baselines' benchmark repo (other-benchmarked-indexes) has no license.

name: fast64 (FAST: Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, 64-bit)
workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn dataset (200M keys), comparing FAST against a tuned STX B-Tree. The Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn, which SOSD runs through this crate's create_fast32 path. The 64-bit results (Fig. 7 Pareto, Fig. 10, Fig. 16 multithreading) appear only as plots.
claimed_speedup: Table 2 (32-bit amzn, fastest variant of each structure): FAST 435.33 ns/lookup (102.0 MB) vs BTree 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB), about 1.1x lower latency (derived from page data). IBTree is 446.55 ns and plain binary search 741.69 ns. Separately, FAST had the highest relative multithreaded speedup of any structure tested: 32x throughput at 40 threads against its own single-thread run.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. From the code: SOSD's CMakeLists.txt adds -ffast-math -Wall -march=native (plus -fopenmp), and fast64's c/Makefile builds the AVX-512 lookup with gcc -O3 -march=native. The compiler used for the paper runs is unstated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM (20 physical / 40 logical cores for the multithreading experiment)
tradeoffs: Read-only, static tree built once; relies heavily on AVX-512 for its throughput and multithreaded scaling advantage, so results are CPU-generation dependent; build times are among the slowest of the structures SOSD tested.
caveats: The single-thread margin over STX B-Tree in Table 2 is small (about 10%), and that table uses 32-bit keys, not 64-bit. The 32x claim is a self-relative multithreading speedup, not a multithreaded FAST-vs-BTree comparison, so do not read it as a 32x win over BTree. The fast lookup path is AVX-512 C code (build.rs checks for avx512f); machines without it get a slower safe Rust path. In the same paper FAST is slower than the learned indexes (RMI 180.90 ns, RS 266.58 ns, PGM 326.48 ns) and the hash tables, and it has one of the longest build times.
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (fast64 -> RyanMarcus/fast64); numbers from SOSD VLDB'21 paper Table 2 and Section 4.5 (http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(1) SOSD paper (Marcus et al.) benchmarks FAST against the STX B-Tree. Table 2 gives FAST 435.33 ns / 102.0 MB against BTree 482.11 ns / 166.0 MB, and Sec. 4.5 states the 32x at 40 threads. It is not A: the benchmark code is public (learnedsystems/SOSD, benchmarks/benchmark_fast64.cc plus competitors/fast64_search.h, which wraps this repo as a submodule) and the CPU is named (Xeon Gold 6230), but neither the paper nor the SOSD README states a compiler or version.

name: HOT (Height Optimized Trie)
workload: YCSB workload C (100% read) and workload E (95% short range-scan, 5% insert) over 50M-entry url/email/yago/integer key data sets, single node, comparing HOT against the STX B+-Tree, ART, and Masstree.
claimed_speedup: "For the lookup-only workload C, HOT achieves an at least 25% higher throughput across all evaluated data sets compared to the other evaluated index structures... In case of the URL data set, HOT's throughput is 200% higher than for the other data structures" (workload E).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.2 (stated in the paper). The paper gives no flags. The repo's CMakeLists.txt Release build (default USEAVX2=ON) uses -std=c++14 -march=native -mavx -mavx2 -mbmi2 -mlzcnt -O3 -DNDEBUG.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (4-core, 3.4GHz/4.0GHz turbo) and Intel i9-7900X (10-core, 3.3GHz/4.3GHz turbo)
tradeoffs: Header-only, order-preserving trie with a variable per-node bit span for balance; uses the most memory-efficient layout of the four structures tested in its own paper, but ART shows 50% higher insertion throughput than HOT on pure-integer keys; string-heavy tries (Masstree, ART) grow space 51-230% on long textual keys where HOT only grows 26%.
caveats: SIGMOD 2018 peer-reviewed paper. It states two CPU models and GCC 7.2 but no optimization flags, which caps it at Tier B. The 200% (3x) margin is workload E on the url data set only; workload C is at least 25%. ART inserts 50% faster than HOT on the integer data set. Needs AVX2/BMI2. The repo has had no pushes since 2018: treat it as a frozen academic artifact, not an actively developed library.

name: LB+-Trees (persistent B+-Tree optimized for 3D XPoint memory)
baseline: WB+-Tree and FP-Tree (state-of-the-art NVM-optimized persistent B+-trees)
workload: Micro-benchmarks: bulkload 2 billion 8B-key/8B-value entries (32GB) at 70% or 100% leaf fill, then random and dense (monotonically increasing) insertions, lookups and deletions, single-threaded and 1-16 threads, with node sizes of 256B-1KB, on real Intel Optane DC PM. Also X-Engine db_bench (8B key / 20B value Get, sequential Put and random Put at 1 and 16 threads) against divided-skiplist, and Memcached mc-benchmark (500K random 20-byte string keys) against WB+-Tree and FP-Tree.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: up to 1.12-2.92x speedups over state-of-the-art NVM-optimized indexes. Single-thread insertions vs WB+-Tree / FP-Tree: 70%-full leaves 1.20-1.24x / 1.12-1.21x; 100%-full leaves 2.55-2.92x / 2.31-2.45x; dense (monotonic) insertions 2.31-2.69x / 2.22-2.33x; overall 1.20-2.92x / 1.12-2.45x. With 1-16 threads: 70%-full 1.17-1.30x / 1.22-1.38x; 100%-full 2.35-2.69x / 2.10-2.53x; dense 1.90-2.38x / 1.89-2.55x. Search and deletion are similar to WB+-Tree and FP-Tree. Memcached: 1.05-1.29x over WB+-Tree and 1.06-1.22x over FP-Tree. The Get / sequential-Put / random-Put figures (1-thread 1.31-1.54x / 1.44-1.80x / 1.46-1.83x; 16-thread 1.25-1.40x / 1.35-1.64x / 1.28-1.46x) are X-Engine results against divided-skiplist, not against WB+-Tree or FP-Tree.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper; the repo Makefile builds with g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -pthread -mrtm -msse4.1 -mavx2 and links libpmem.
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Cascade Lake-SP, 28 cores/socket @ 2.5GHz (Turbo Boost 3.8GHz), 32KB L1i/d, 1MB L2 per core, 39MB shared L3, 512GB Intel Optane DC PM, Linux 4.9.135
stars_or_usage: 49 stars; published as PVLDB 13(7):1078-1090 (2020); listed as a baseline competitor in the later APEX (VLDB'22) paper
tradeoffs: Uses Intel RTM (hardware transactional memory) for concurrency control and requires real 3D XPoint/Optane hardware or PMDK-based emulation; per-entry fingerprint metadata adds memory overhead
caveats: The repository has no license file (all rights reserved by default), so the code can be studied but not redistributed without asking the authors. The README lists fptree-src and wbtree-src, but they are not in the repo, so the baseline comparisons cannot be reproduced from it. Gains are insert-side only: search and delete match WB+-Tree and FP-Tree. It needs Intel RTM (TSX), PMDK and Optane PM hardware, which Intel has discontinued. The paper gives the CPU only as Cascade Lake-SP with no SKU and states no compiler or flags.

name: PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)
baseline: STX B+-tree (v0.9) and cache-efficient CSS-tree (authors' implementation), plus a 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index)
workload: Point queries on a Web Logs dataset (~715M timestamps, 8-byte keys, 128-byte payload), 10M random queries against an in-memory sorted array index
claimed_speedup: Static: PGM-index matches the fastest STX B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB, 'four orders of magnitude') and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 82.7x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); it dominates the 2-stage RMI in the space-time trade-off (RMI MAE 892±3729 vs 226±139 for PGM; RMI built 14.5x slower). Dynamic: the Dynamic PGM-index was 13-71% faster than the STX B+-tree for most query/update mixes (1.0% and 15.2% slower at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions), using 611-3891x less space.
hardware: 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold CPU, 192 GiB memory
stars_or_usage: 874 stars; basis for the PyGM Python wrapper, widely cited in follow-on learned-index papers
tradeoffs: Base structure targets static/append-friendly data (a dynamic variant exists but adds complexity); requires a sorted key array; the headline win vs traditional trees is space at matched latency, not a raw query-latency multiplier
caveats: The VLDB'20 paper states only '2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold' (no model), with no compiler or flags. The static comparisons against the B+-tree and CSS-tree are same-speed at far less space rather than strictly faster. The strictly-faster wins are against RMI and, in the dynamic setting, 13-71% over the STX B+-tree on most (not all) workload mixes. All numbers come from the authors' own experiments.
found_via: GitHub topic search 'learned index' + citation chain from the LIPP and CARMI papers

name: PLEX / TrieSpline
workload: Four 64-bit SOSD real-world datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki; 200M keys each). Build time vs size is compared against RMI, CHT, PGM and RadixSpline (Fig. 2). Lookup time vs size is compared against those plus ART and BTree (Fig. 3).
claimed_speedup: Graph-only. In Fig. 3 (size vs lookup time, 200M 64-bit keys) the PLEX curve lies at roughly 200-300 ns against BTree's roughly 500-900 ns and ART's roughly 400-600 ns on amzn and face (approximate, read from the plot). The text gives no ratio. It says 'PGM, ART, and BTree eventually lose performance as the index size is increased', and it notes that PLEX fixes RadixSpline's outlier problem on face and sits at a constant offset of about 25 ns from RMI on amzn and face. In the plot, RMI is the faster of the two.
hardware: AWS m5zn.metal instance, 48 vCPUs at 4.5GHz turbo, 192GiB RAM
tradeoffs: Single hyperparameter (max prediction error) with an auto-tuner, unlike RMI/CHT/RS which need offline grid search; read-only (no update support, follow-up work planned a Fenwick-tree extension that was not implemented in this repo).
caveats: AIDB@VLDB 2021 workshop extended abstract, not a full research-track paper. The hardware is an AWS instance type with no CPU model, and the compiler and flags are not stated. The speedup evidence is only plots with no quoted number. PLEX does not beat RMI on lookup latency (RMI is about 25 ns faster on amzn and face).
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (competitors/ts -> stoianmihail/TrieSpline, GitHub-renamed to stoianmihail/PLEX); paper opened at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.05117

verification.tier_reason: The AIDB@VLDB'21 extended abstract (peer-reviewed workshop) plots PLEX against BTree, ART, PGM, RMI, RS and CHT on the four 64-bit SOSD datasets (Fig. 3). The PLEX lookup-time curve sits well below BTree's on every dataset. It is not A: the text gives only the machine type (AWS m5zn.metal, 4.5 GHz turbo), not a CPU model, compiler or flags, and the repo's own bench_end_to_end.cc compares only against RadixSpline.

workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn (books) dataset of 200M keys. Table 2 specifically uses a 32-bit version of amzn and reports the best-performing (often largest) variant of each index structure, comparing RadixSpline (RS) against the STX B+ Tree, IBTree, FAST, binary search, PGM, RMI, CuckooMap and RobinHash. The Pareto plots (Fig. 7) cover 64-bit keys over amzn/face/osm/wiki.
claimed_speedup: 266.58 ns/lookup (4.0 MB) for RS vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree (STX B+ Tree) on the 32-bit version of the amzn dataset, fastest variant of each -> ~1.8x lower latency at ~41x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SOSD repo build (scripts/prepare.sh, CMakeLists.txt) uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, C++17, -ffast-math -march=native, and -fopenmp if available. The compiler is not pinned; the README installs clang on Ubuntu 20.04.

tradeoffs: Read-only, single-pass build; can be built as a drop-in replacement for std::multimap over sorted data. Degrades badly on data with a small number of extreme outliers (e.g. the 'face' dataset in SOSD), where its radix table becomes nearly useless.

Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn and are the fastest variant per structure. RS beats PGM (326.48 ns) but trails RMI (180.90 ns), and both hash tables (CuckooMap 114.50 ns, RobinHash 93.69 ns) beat every ordered index at far larger size. The page says the migration changed data layout, access paths and workload isolation at the same time, so the gains come from column pruning on wide high-fan-out tables and from isolating cold reads, not from a like-for-like broker benchmark.

name: Apache Pulsar
workload: Linux Foundation OpenMessaging Benchmark with 1KB messages on 3 broker VMs (i3en.6xlarge) and 4 client VMs (m5n.8xlarge) on AWS. Tests: max throughput with 1 and 100 partitions, publish latency at a fixed 500MB/s on 100 partitions, and catch-up read throughput draining a 512GB backlog while producers keep writing.
claimed_speedup: Max throughput at 100 partitions: Pulsar without journaling 1600MB/s vs Kafka 1087MB/s (~1.47x, derived from page data). Default Pulsar with journaling reached 800MB/s, which is below Kafka. Single partition: Pulsar 700MB/s without journal / 580MB/s with journal vs Kafka 280MB/s (~2.5x, derived from page data); the page headlines this as '2.5x maximum throughput'. P99 publish latency at a fixed 500MB/s: Pulsar without journal 1.58ms, with journal 7.89ms, vs Kafka 3.46ms. Kafka's P99.9 was 54.56ms, and the page says both Pulsar configs beat Kafka at P99.9 and above, headlining '100x lower than Kafka at P99.99'. Catch-up reads from a 512GB backlog: Pulsar up to 3.2GB/s vs Kafka 2.0GB/s ('60% more'; headline '1.5x faster historical read rate'). Pulsar drained the backlog ~2.5x faster, while Kafka producers' P99 rose to ~700ms.
hardware: 3x i3en.6xlarge brokers (24-core, 192GB RAM, 25Gbps, dual NVMe SSD), 4x m5n.8xlarge clients (32-core, 128GB RAM, 25Gbps), t2.small ZooKeeper nodes
tradeoffs: Pulsar's 'no journaling' fastest mode trades some durability guarantees; Pulsar has a more complex operational footprint (separate Broker + BookKeeper + ZooKeeper) than Kafka; JVM-based, so no compiler/flags apply.
caveats: The benchmark was run and published by StreamNative, whose CTO co-created Pulsar, so it is a vendor-interested comparison rather than an independent third party, even though it uses the public OMB suite. It is dated (2022-04-07; Pulsar 2.9.1 vs Kafka 3.0.0). Default Pulsar (journaling, fsync before ack) loses to Kafka on 100-partition max throughput (800 vs 1087MB/s) and on P99 latency (7.89 vs 3.46ms). The 'equivalent durability' wins use the non-default no-journal config, and Kafka used Confluent's OMB-recommended config with no fsync before ack. Hardware is given as AWS instance types, not a CPU model.

name: AutoMQ
workload: OpenMessaging-benchmark-style 1-topic/1000-partitions/4KB messages at fixed producer rates (128000 msg/s and 25600 msg/s) run repeatedly in CI against AutoMQ, Apache Kafka, and AWS MSK clusters on identical topic/producer/consumer configs.
claimed_speedup: At a fixed 500MB/s (128000 msg/s x 4KB, 1000 partitions): pub latency avg 3.4ms vs Kafka 4.2ms and P99 15.19ms vs 30.21ms (2024-06-13 run). Later 500MB/s runs gave P99 15.69 vs 37.65ms and 14.6 vs 40.48ms. At ~100MB/s (25600 msg/s): avg/P99 8.08/30.62ms vs Kafka 17.98/75.13ms (2024-06-24) and 6.81/25.36ms vs 12.3/72.54ms (2024-07-08). E2E latency was mixed: in the 2024-06-13 run Kafka had lower E2E avg (6.31 vs 6.54ms) and P95 (12.39 vs 15.91ms), while AutoMQ had lower E2E P99 (34.16 vs 42.31ms). name: Mino
workload: Six-stage automotive-style pipeline (Perception->Prediction->Planning->Control->Guardian->CANBus) exchanging 256B/64KiB/1MiB frames intra-host; Mino's zero-copy SHM/TCP transport was benchmarked head-to-head against a Protobuf+ZeroMQ pipeline (plus Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS) for one-way end-to-end latency and CANBus message rate, saturation mode, and separately a same-host 6-process 'mino_tcp' vs 'protobuf_zmq' network smoke test.
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data) same-host 6-process network smoke: Mino TCP p50 0.855ms vs Protobuf+ZeroMQ p50 10.33ms (~12x); pipeline small payload (256B): Mino SHM mean p50 1.815ms vs Protobuf+ZeroMQ mean p50 ~10.56ms (~5.8x); pipeline large payload (1MiB): Mino SHM mean p50 13.72ms vs Protobuf+ZeroMQ mean p50 ~26.85ms (~2x); medium payload (64KiB) latency also favored Mino SHM (mean p50 0.979ms vs ZeroMQ's ~1.97ms) though Fast DDS had slightly higher medium-payload throughput.
compiler_and_flags: bazel build --config=pipeline_comparison -c opt --jobs=4 (Bazel 7.4.1 via bazelisk 1.29.0; .bazelrc adds -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fno-omit-frame-pointer globally). The host toolchain is not named for the pipeline build; the same report says Debian 13's g++-14 ran the host sanity tests.
hardware: Debian 13 (trixie), 8 vCPU, 15.64 GiB RAM, x86_64 KVM guest (exact physical CPU model not disclosed)
tradeoffs: Solo-developer, ~2-month-old project (created 2026-07-26); README explicitly says 'not implemented yet' for parts of the typed Publisher<T> API; Linux-only for persistent SHM semantics (macOS is compile/non-persistent-SHM testing only); large-payload SHM run hit SIGBUS until /dev/shm was manually grown from 64MiB to 8GiB; LGPL-3.0 requires re-linkability for the Mino library itself.
caveats: The benchmark was designed, run and reported by the same solo author, so it is not independent. The physical CPU model is not disclosed, only a KVM guest with 8 vCPU and 15.64 GiB RAM, which falls short of full Tier A methodology. Saturation mode (publish-interval 0) means the percentiles include queuing delay, not idle one-hop latency. The baseline is Protobuf serialization over ZeroMQ ipc:// sockets at every hop, while Mino SHM transfers zero-copy handles to a generated typed frame and Mino TCP uses its own canonical wire codec. Part of the gap may therefore come from serialization and copying rather than transport alone. Only 2 rounds were run. The 12x network smoke figure comes from a single 50-message run, and buffering parameters (ZMQ HWM vs Mino SPSC capacity 64) are not semantically identical, as the README itself notes.

name: Prefix Filter
workload: Space usage, false-positive rate, operation throughput at varying load, and build time for 0.94*2^28 (~252M) random 64-bit keys at false-positive rate ~2^-8, single-threaded, on an Intel Ice Lake server (PVLDB 15(7), 2022)
claimed_speedup: Build time for n=0.94*2^28 (~252M) keys: the prefix filter is faster than every cuckoo filter configuration by more than 3.2x (abstract: 3.2-3.5x) and faster than the vector quotient filter (TwoChoicer) by 1.39-1.46x. Cuckoo filter insertions slow down more than 27x as load grows, so its build time is close to that of a plain Bloom filter BF-16[k=11]. Negative-query throughput is higher than CF-12 at every load up to 95% (+55%, +40% and +2.8% at 50%, 70% and 90% load). Positive queries at 100% load are 28-40% slower than CF-12-Flex and 46-60% slower than CF-12. The plain Bloom filter is the slowest filter for queries. The blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster than the prefix filter for all operations, but its false-positive rate is 3-6x higher. Space is 11.55-12.13 bits/key at a 0.37-0.39% false-positive rate (Table 3).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.0 on Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Sec. 7.1). The artifact repo's CMakeLists.txt builds the benchmark targets measure_perf, measure_built and measure_fpp with -Ofast -DNDEBUG, and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS is -march=native.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y (Ice Lake) @ 2.40GHz, 64GiB RAM, 48KiB L1d/1.25MiB L2 per core, 36MiB shared L3
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware for the fast path; is an incremental filter (supports insertion but the paper focuses on a fixed configured capacity); this is a mixed win, not a strict speed win across every metric.
caveats: The paper's 52%/79% figure is the cuckoo filter's query-throughput lead over the vector quotient filter at high load. It is not a lead over the prefix filter, so the earlier record misattributed it. The prefix filter beats CF-12 on negative queries at every load up to 95%, but it trails cuckoo filters on positive queries at full load (by 28-60%). The blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster than the prefix filter for all operations, at a much higher space and false-positive cost. The README requires an Intel CPU with AVX-512. All numbers come from single-threaded runs on one Ice Lake machine. The license is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md, although GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION. The paper is PVLDB 15(7) 2022 (the arXiv version is the full version). There have been no commits since 2022-09-12.

name: Xor Filter (xor_singleheader)
workload: Single-threaded membership-query time against space overhead for 10M and 100M random 64-bit keys, with 25% of queried keys present (fastfilter_cpp benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc). The binary fuse paper adds construction time per key and bits/key across set sizes up to 100M keys.
claimed_speedup: This record covers both filters in FastFilter/xor_singleheader. (1) Xor filters, JEA 2020 (arXiv 1912.08258, Table 3, 25% of queried keys present): at 10M keys, Xor8 takes 23 ns/query at 9.8 bits/key, against Bloom12 at 40 ns (12.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo12 at 31 ns (12.8 bits/key). Xor16 takes 27 ns (19.7 bits/key), against Bloom16 at 48 ns (16.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo16 at 32 ns (17.0 bits/key). At 100M keys, Xor8 takes 32 ns, against Bloom12 at 58 ns and Cuckoo12 at 38 ns. (2) Binary fuse filters, JEA 2022 (arXiv 2201.01174): the 3-wise filter reaches about 9 bits/key (12.5% above the lower bound) and the 4-wise filter about 8.6 bits/key (7.5% above). Xor uses 9.84 bits/key (23% above) and Bloom at least 44% above. Construction is more than 2x faster than xor filters, and xor and cuckoo construction are both slower. The 3-wise query speed is on par with xor and faster than Bloom filters. The 4-wise query speed is similar to cuckoo filters. The binary fuse figures come only from plots; the paper has no table.
compiler_and_flags: Xor paper: GNU GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native, 64-bit Linux executable. Binary fuse paper: GCC 10, -O3, plus -march=native on x64.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 @ 3.4GHz (Skylake) with 8MiB L3, the primary platform in both papers. The binary fuse paper also uses a secondary AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen 2), which has a 25% error margin.
stars_or_usage: 432 stars; used in production by Databend, ntop nDPI, InfiniFlow, and CockroachDB Pebble
tradeoffs: Immutable once built (no add/remove; must know the full key set upfront); needs a strong ~64-bit hash of the input keys; construction is slower than Bloom/blocked-Bloom (~110-130ns/key vs ~10-40ns/key at 10M keys per Table 2 of the same paper); naturally compressible with gzip/zstd, unlike Bloom/cuckoo.
caveats: This record covers both xor filters and binary fuse filters. The repo ships xorfilter.h and binaryfusefilter.h, and the README recommends binary fuse, which is smaller and faster to build than xor. Xor filter is itself a listed baseline in this category, so this entry's claim is measured against Bloom and cuckoo filters. The blocked Bloom filter is faster for queries (16 ns against Xor8's 23 ns at 10M keys) at 10.7 bits/key and about 0.94% false-positive probability. The 2020 paper found xor construction roughly half as fast as Bloom and cuckoo construction, and binary fuse removes most of that cost. The filters are static: no inserts after construction. The paper numbers were measured on the C++ implementations in fastfilter_cpp release 1.0, not on this C header, although the current harness can run the single-header code. All runs are single-threaded on one 2015-era Skylake CPU. The sample query-benchmark output in the README (98.765 ns/q, 0.123456 s) looks like placeholder text, not a measurement.

name: Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF)
workload: False-positive rate vs. memory budget on a malicious-URL dataset (485,730 URLs, 16.47% malicious) and other real-world datasets; standard Bloom filter vs. learned Bloom filter (LBF), sandwiched LBF, Ada-BF, and disjoint Ada-BF
claimed_speedup: Paper: Ada-BF/disjoint Ada-BF 'reduce the FPR by over 80% and save 50% of the memory usage over existing learned Bloom filters'. On malicious URLs at a 500Kb filter size, Ada-BF cuts FPR by 81% vs LBF/sandwiched LBF (disjoint Ada-BF: 84%); at FPR ~0.35% the memory drops from over 500Kb (LBF) to 300Kb (over 40% savings). On malware MD5, 0.2% FPR needs ~300Kb for LBF vs 150Kb for Ada-BF (50%), and all learned BFs cut FPR by over 98% vs the standard Bloom filter.
tradeoffs: Requires training/maintaining a classifier model alongside the filter; memory savings depend on how well the model's score distribution separates keys from non-keys, so gains are dataset-dependent
caveats: Reference Python research code with no LICENSE file (reference/study-only). Peer-reviewed at NeurIPS 2020 as 'Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF): Efficient Utilization of the Classifier with Application to Real-Time Information Filtering on the Web'. This is a numerical FPR-vs-memory comparison, not a speed benchmark: most headline gains are vs other learned Bloom filters, and the standard BF's bit budget is credited with the classifier size (146Kb on URLs). No CPU/compiler details apply. The repo also ships a PLBF.py baseline.

name: Better Choice Cuckoo Filter (BCF)
workload: Insert 1,048,576 items (12-bit fingerprints) using power-of-two-choices bucket selection, comparing average relocation count and insertion latency against the standard Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter design).
claimed_speedup: 35% fewer average relocations and 25% lower item-insertion latency vs standard Cuckoo Filter
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 0 @ 2.60GHz, Red Hat Enterprise Linux Server 6.2
tradeoffs: Only changes the insertion-time bucket-selection rule (pick the less-loaded of the two candidate buckets); lookup/delete paths are unchanged from a standard Cuckoo Filter, so read performance is unaffected while write performance and load factor improve.
caveats: The code is a modified copy of efficient/cuckoofilter, not a GitHub fork: same src/ files, CMake project named cuckoofilter_master, and the upstream conext benchmarks. The repo's LICENSE file is upstream's Apache-2.0 notice (Copyright 2013 CMU and Intel), which GitHub reports as NOASSERTION. The README adds a 2019 HUST copyright line but no other license. The evidence is the paper: Wang, Chen, Liao, Zhang, Jin, 'The Power of Better Choice: Reducing Relocations in Cuckoo Filter', ICDCS 2019, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDCS.2019.00043, which is paywalled. name: BuRR (Ribbon Filter)
workload: Space overhead, construction time and positive/negative query time (ns/key). Sequential runs use n=10^6 and 10^8 keys, and a parallel run queries 1280 filters of 10^7 keys from 64 threads. False-positive rates are about 1%, 10% and 0.05%. BuRR is compared against Bloom, blocked Bloom, cuckoo, Morton, quotient, xor, xor+ and fuse filters in the lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp harness (SEA 2022 best paper; the arXiv version is the extended one).
claimed_speedup: Space overhead over the information-theoretic minimum (arXiv 2109.01892 Table 2, false-positive rate about 1%, r=7/8): Xor 23.0%, Xor+ 14.4%, blocked Bloom 45-52% and Cuckoo12 40-46%. Plain Bloom is at least 44% by construction (1.44*log2(1/f)). BuRR ranges from 0.06% to 1.4% depending on ribbon width (0.21-0.48% at w=64). Speed: in the 64-thread parallel workload, BuRR and homogeneous ribbon Pareto-dominate plain Bloom filters. In that workload, BuRR 2-bit w=64 takes 215/215 ns for positive/negative queries and 190 ns/key to construct, against Xor r=8 at 386/392 ns and 586 ns/key. Sequentially, the faster BuRR variants are 'only moderately slower than Bloom and Xor filters'. For example, at n=10^8, BuRR 2-bit w=64 takes 82/74 ns for positive/negative queries against Xor's 41/41 ns, and constructs at 115 against 159 ns/key. The README's rounded figures are overheads 'as low as 0.1%' and below 0.5% for speed-oriented configurations.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 11.0 with -O3 -march=native on Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Experimental Setup). The BuRR Makefile bench target uses -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7702, 64 cores, 2.0 GHz base / 3.35 GHz boost, 1 TiB DDR4-3200
stars_or_usage: 52 stars; won Best Paper at SEA 2022 (20th International Symposium on Experimental Algorithms)
tradeoffs: Static/immutable retrieval structure (no keys stored, so it cannot enumerate members); construction cost scales worse than hash-table-based filters for very large n; a parallel-construction variant exists on a separate branch.
caveats: The main win is space, not speed. Sequential query latency is about 2x that of xor filters, and the blocked Bloom filter is fastest overall at about 50% overhead. BuRR beats xor and plain Bloom on speed mainly in the heavily loaded parallel benchmark. BuRR is a static retrieval/AMQ structure: no inserts after build. The comparison harness lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp is a fork of pdillinger/fastfilter_cpp, last pushed 2021-09-11. The README's '~20%' xor and '~10%' xor+ overheads round the paper's measured 23% and 12.8-14.4%. Building needs git submodules (tlx, ips2ra, DySECT, pcg-cpp, rocksdb).

name: Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter)
workload: 192MB filters holding ~120-128M pre-generated 64-bit random-integer keys; lookup throughput measured while varying the fraction of positive queries, and insert throughput measured across load factor, on a two-socket Intel Xeon testbed.
claimed_speedup: Lookup throughput (Fig. 5, read from the plot): CF is ~12 MOPS at 0% and 100% positive queries and dips to ~10.5 MOPS at 50%. The standard Bloom filter falls from ~8.3 MOPS (0% positive) to ~4.9 MOPS (100% positive), so the CF advantage runs from ~1.45x to ~2.4x (derived from page data, plot-read). Construction is 5.00M keys/sec (CF) vs 3.91M keys/sec (BF) with all filters at 192MB, at 12.60 vs 13.00 bits/item and the same 0.19% FPR (Table 3; ~1.28x, derived from page data). On space, semi-sorted cuckoo filters need fewer bits/item than space-optimized Bloom filters when the target FPR is below 3% (crossover 7.2 bits/item, Fig. 4 and Sec. 6).
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @ 2.27GHz, 12MB L3 cache, 32GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Supports deletion unlike standard Bloom filters, but load factor caps insert capacity (~95% full before insert failures); asymptotically worse in bits/item (O(log n)) than Bloom's O(1), though practically better for realistic table sizes with reasonably sized buckets; duplicate-heavy workloads (same item inserted >2b times) can fail insertion.
caveats: Peer-reviewed ACM CoNEXT'14 paper (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, Mitzenmacher). It states the hardware (2x Xeon L5640) but not the compiler or flags. The repo's benchmarks/conext-figure5.cc and conext-table3.cc only benchmark CuckooFilter, so the Bloom-filter baseline code is not public. The current benchmarks/Makefile flags (-O3 -march=core-avx2) postdate the paper and could not have run on the Westmere testbed. The CF only ties the paper's blocked Bloom filter at 0% positive queries (~12 MOPS each); its win is over the standard Bloom filter and grows with the positive-query fraction. Per Sec. 6, the <3% FPR space advantage is stated for the semi-sorting variant. The README has no numbers. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the Apache-2.0 text. Independent check: the Xor Filters paper (ACM JEA 2020, arXiv 1912.08258; i7-6700, GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native) measures a modified Cuckoo 12 at 31 ns/query vs Bloom 12 at 40 ns (10M keys, 25% find). In the same paper the original implementation measures 30 ns at 20.1 bits/key (Table 4).

name: Morton Filter
workload: Fan et al.'s reference cuckoo filter (plus semi-sorted CF and RSQF) vs a Morton filter with 128*1024*1024 slots and 8-bit fingerprints (3-slot buckets). The filters are filled to each load factor in steps of 0.05. Then 0.1% of total slots are inserted, deleted or looked up with 64-bit random keys. Results are the average of 5 trials (VLDB 2018 paper).
claimed_speedup: Paper vs Fan et al.'s reference cuckoo filter (CF): lookups 1.3x-2.5x faster (1.3x-2.5x for true negatives, Fig. 11; 1.6x-2.4x for true positives, Fig. 10), insertions 0.9x-15.5x (Fig. 12), deletions 1.3x-1.6x (Fig. 13). The README's 'up to 15.5x, 1.3x, and 2.5x' understates deletion; the paper says up to 1.6x. The MF uses about 11.71 bits/item at 0.95 load vs a 12-bit-fingerprint CF. The paper does not benchmark Bloom filters. Its point about using fewer bits than a Bloom filter below ~1-3% FPR is a general statement about cuckoo/quotient filters.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.4.0-6 with -Ofast -march=native (paper Sec. 6). The repo benchmarking/Makefile uses -Ofast -march=native -mpopcnt -std=c++11. The README recommends g++ 5.4 and reports a GCC 8.x performance regression as of March 2019.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1950X (2x8 cores, 32 MB L3), frequency fixed at 3400 MHz, 128 GB DDR4-2133, Ubuntu 16.04.4 LTS (Linux 4.11.0)
stars_or_usage: 90 stars; developed at AMD Research, published at VLDB 2018 with an extended version in the VLDB Journal (2019)
tradeoffs: Supports self-resizing (grow capacity without a backing structure) unlike vanilla cuckoo filters; requires only a multiple-of-two bucket count rather than a power of two; author explicitly labels the code 'academic-style prototype', not hardened for production.
caveats: The README says this is an academic prototype. The batch API works correctly only when the input is a multiple of 128. A later deletion correctness fix cut peak deletion throughput from about 38 to about 28 MOPS, so current code may not reproduce the paper's deletion numbers. Insertion speedup is 0.9x (slower) at some load factors. The repo has no commits since 2020-12-16.

name: Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter (PLBF)
workload: False-positive rate vs. space tradeoff on a synthetic dataset, a URL dataset, and the EMBER malware dataset, comparing PLBF against a theoretically-optimal Bloom filter, sandwiched learned Bloom filter, and Ada-BF
claimed_speedup: at matched space (400Kb/500Kb/3000Kb for synthetic/URLs/EMBER), PLBF achieves 22x, 26x, and 3x smaller false-positive rates than the sandwiching approach, and 8.5x, 9x, 1.9x smaller than Ada-BF; to hit FPR=0.001, sandwiching needs 8.8x/3.3x/1.2x the space of PLBF and Ada-BF needs 6x/2.5x/1.1x the space
tradeoffs: Needs a trained scoring model plus a dynamic-program solve for optimal partition thresholds; benefit shrinks when the model is weak (EMBER dataset shows only a slight improvement)
caveats: Peer-reviewed at ICLR 2021. The repo README says 'ICLR 2020', which is wrong; the CLBF paper cites it as ICLR 2021. The repo has only plbf_algo.py (threshold/FPR optimizer) and a README. It has no LICENSE file (reference/study only) and no experiment or benchmark code. The headline multipliers are against learned variants (sandwiched LBF, Ada-BF), not a raw Bloom filter. The 'optimal Bloom filter' curve is analytical (standard Bloom filter space / log2 e), and the standard-Bloom-filter comparison (Appendix E.1, Fig. 4) is shown only as a plot. The model is an sklearn random forest, sized by its pickle file. Last commit was in 2022-06, more than 3 years ago.

name: SIMD Blocked Bloom Filter (src/simd-block.h, Impala-derived)
workload: Single-threaded bulk construction and membership tests on 10M and 100M pseudo-random 64-bit keys (Murmur-finalizer hash), with 25% of queries on existing keys. Blocked Bloom (10.7 bits/key) is compared with standard Bloom filters at 8, 12 and 16 bits/key, using FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc.
claimed_speedup: Xor Filters paper (Graf & Lemire, ACM JEA 2020), testing the Impala AVX2 blocked Bloom that is also used in efficient/cuckoofilter, modified for flexible sizes. Membership tests take 16 ns/query vs 31 ns (Bloom 8) and 40 ns (Bloom 12) at 10M keys with 25% find, and 20 ns vs 53 ns and 58 ns at 100M keys (Table 3; ~1.9-2.9x, derived from page data). Construction takes 10 ns/key vs 40 and 60 ns/key at 10M keys, and 20 ns/key vs 70 and 90 ns/key at 100M keys (Table 2). The trade-off is 10.7 bits/key at 0.94% FPP vs 0.31% for Bloom 12.
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native (per paper)
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, 8 MB L3
tradeoffs: Higher false positive rate than standard Bloom at equal space (0.43% vs 0.19% at 13 bits/item, Table 3) because hashing items to one of many small per-block filters creates imbalanced "hot"/"cold" blocks even with strong hash functions; no deletion support.
caveats: The original record wrongly attributed the CoNEXT'14 paper's blk-BF numbers (Table 3's 7.64M keys/sec, the Fig. 5 '~4 MOPS' gap) to this code. The paper's blocked Bloom is its own 2014 implementation with 64-byte blocks and k=9. src/simd-block.h was added to efficient/cuckoofilter by Jim Apple in Dec 2016, two years later. This repo's own benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc header shows SimdBlock8 at ~55-75M adds/sec and ~58-75M finds/sec, vs Cuckoo12 at ~16-24M adds/sec and ~32-37M finds/sec. It includes no standard Bloom and no hardware (first-party, Tier C on its own). The peer-reviewed numbers come from a modified copy in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp src/bloom/simd-block.h, credited there as 'from apache/impala (via the cuckoo filter)'. The filter needs AVX2 (x86-only) and has a higher FPR per bit than a standard Bloom filter.

name: SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)
workload: RocksDB replacement of its Bloom filters with SuRF on a synthetic 100GB time-series dataset (2K simulated sensors, 128-bit keys); end-to-end open-range, closed-range, and worst-case (all-missing-key) point query throughput, SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper
claimed_speedup: RocksDB with SuRF vs RocksDB's Bloom filter at equal filter size: open-range (Open-Seek) queries 1.5x faster, and closed-range queries up to 5x faster (SuRF-Real, when 99% of queries return empty). On the worst-case all-miss point-query workload, the abstract says RocksDB is up to 40% slower with SuRF because of a higher false-positive rate (0.2% vs 0.1%). Fig. 12 point throughput is 32.9 Kops/s for Bloom, 19.8 for SuRF-Hash and 16.4 for SuRF-Real. So SuRF-Real is about 50% slower (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SuRF repo's CMake Release flags are -O3 -Wall -Werror -mpopcnt -pthread -std=c++11, with the compiler unspecified. The RocksDB end-to-end runs used the efficient/rocksdb fork, whose build flags were not checked.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6770HQ CPU, 32GB RAM, Intel 540s 480GB SSD
stars_or_usage: 554 stars; SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper; evaluated as a RocksDB Bloom-filter replacement
tradeoffs: SuRF trades a higher false-positive rate for the ability to answer range queries and approximate range counts, which plain Bloom filters cannot do at all; for pure point-query, moderate-FPP workloads the paper itself says 'the Bloom filter is usually a better choice than SuRF'; construction speed is comparable to Bloom filter's.
caveats: This is a mixed result, not a strict win. SuRF is 40-50% slower for all-miss point queries at equal filter size, and the paper says adding a few suffix bits per key closes the gap. Its wins (1.5x-5x) are for range queries only. The paper reports throughput in Kops/s, not latency. The end-to-end code lives in the efficient/rocksdb fork (last push 2018-12-20). The microbenchmarks (bench/workload.cpp vs bench/filter_bloom.hpp) ran on a Xeon E5-2680 v2. The GitHub license API says NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the plain Apache-2.0 text. bench/bloom.hpp is LevelDB-derived code under a BSD-style license.

name: Vacuum Filter
workload: Positive/mixed lookup, insertion, and deletion throughput plus bits-per-item vs. target false-positive rate, 64-bit random keys, varying table occupancy 0-100%, on a DELL workstation (PVLDB 13, 2020)
claimed_speedup: Abstract: about 25% less space on average and similar throughput vs cuckoo filters, and about 15% less space and >10x throughput vs Bloom filters, at the same false-positive rate. In memory: VF-ss is about 1.1x-1.8x faster than CF-ss for positive lookups. VFs have the highest lookup throughput below 90% occupancy, but CFs are slightly better at high occupancy. VFs have the highest insertion throughput below 65% occupancy, and deletion throughput is similar to CFs. On SSD with a 100 MB memory limit, VF lookups are 1.86x-2.13x faster than CF. Space: VFs save 2-5 bits per item vs the other methods in the average case (about 5 fewer bits vs CFs).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo makefile builds the test.cpp demo with g++ -Ofast -march=native -mpopcnt -std=c++14 (plus -pg -g).
hardware: DELL workstation, Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.00GHz, 30MB L3 cache, SK-hynix SC311-S 1TB SSD
tradeoffs: Built on top of / modified from Fan et al.'s cuckoo filter code; the fast implementation is a modified cuckoo filter rather than a from-scratch design; deletion throughput is only 'similar to' cuckoo filter, not better; insertion advantage narrows and eventually loses to cuckoo/vacuum crossover above ~65% occupancy where both slow down comparably.
caveats: The paper gives the CPU but no compiler or flags. The repo has no harness for the Bloom, Morton and CQF comparisons, only the test.cpp demo and Fan et al.'s inherited CF benchmarks under ModifiedCuckooFilter/. The top-level license is MIT, added 2024-11-23. ModifiedCuckooFilter/ is Apache-2.0 code derived from CMU/Intel's cuckoofilter. The throughput advantage over cuckoo filters is small or reversed at high occupancy.

name: Boost.Bloom (block / multiblock filter configurations)
workload: Insertion and successful/unsuccessful/mixed lookup of int keys (N=1M) comparing boost::bloom::filter's classical single-array configuration (filter<int,K>) against its block/multiblock/fast_multiblock32 configurations at equal bits-per-item budgets.
claimed_speedup: The quoted numbers belong to the block<uint64_t,K> configurations, not multiblock. GCC 14 x64, N=1M, same bits/element: at c=8, block insertion is 3.99 ns (5.07 ns for block<...>,1) vs 11.04 ns for the classical filter<int,K>, and lookup is 4.60-5.12 ns vs 12.08-19.38 ns. At c=16, insertion is 5.02/5.55 ns vs 20.28 ns and lookup 5.62-6.02 ns vs 18.12-22.04 ns. That is about 2.6-4x (derived from page data). fast_multiblock32 (AVX2) reaches 2.72-3.22 ns at c=8/12. At N=10M, c=16, the classical filter takes 85.98 ns to insert and 95.66 ns per successful lookup vs 16.90/18.69 ns for block, about 5x (derived from page data). Plain multiblock is slower than block, e.g. 9.18 ns insertion and 11.79 ns lookup at c=16, N=1M.
compiler_and_flags: g++-14 -m64 -march=native -std=c++2b -O3 -DNDEBUG (from boost_bloom_benchmarks/.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml). The page also tabulates Clang 18 x64, Clang 15 ARM64, VS2022 (/arch:AVX2) and x86 builds.

tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11. Block/multiblock variants trade a small FPR increase (at matched c) for large speed gains by confining all K bit-sets to one or few cache lines; classical filter<int,K> remains available for lowest FPR at a given c.
caveats: The benchmark workflow runs on a self-hosted runner ([self-hosted, linux, x64]) and never names the CPU model. The numbers are the project's own and have not been reproduced independently. The baseline is the library's own classical Bloom configuration. At equal bits/element, block filters trade FPR for speed: at c=16, N=1M, the FPR is 0.42% for block vs 0.045% for classical, about 10x worse. name: Cascaded Learned Bloom Filter (CLBF)
workload: Memory-vs-FPR (target F from 0.1 to 0.001) and memory-vs-reject-time trade-offs on the URL, Ember and Higgs datasets (14 datasets in the appendix), using XGBoost models and 10,000 held-out test non-keys. Baselines are all in C++: classical Bloom filter (fastfilter_cpp), PLBF (via Fast PLBF), Sandwiched LBF, G-PLBF, Ensemble LBF, PHBF and HABF.
claimed_speedup: At the same FPR, CLBF uses up to 17% less memory than the best PLBF configuration, for example on Ember at F=0.005. It cuts reject time by up to 14.6x vs PLBF under the default XGBoost setting, and by up to 65x across the appendix model variants. Construction takes 1.003x-1.23x longer than existing LBFs. A classical Bloom filter (fastfilter_cpp) is plotted as a baseline in Fig. 5, but no CLBF-vs-Bloom ratio is quoted. PLBF is described as the most memory-efficient LBF under a fixed model; G-PLBF matches CLBF on memory vs FPR.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0 with -O3, single-threaded (paper Section 6); repo builds with CMake Release inside an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker image
hardware: Linux, Intel Core i9-11900H @ 2.50 GHz, 64 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Adds a DP-based size/threshold optimizer at construction time (paper reports this is 0.3-24% of total build time); like other learned filters, needs a trained scoring model and benefits are dataset/model dependent
caveats: The record said there was no code, but that was wrong. The official implementation is https://github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF (Apache-2.0, C++, Docker-based reproduction scripts for CLBF and all baselines, 0 stars, created 2026-01). The repo_url should be set to it, but that field cannot be corrected here. The paper itself does not link the repo. The headline memory figure is against PLBF, not a classical Bloom filter. Reject time includes ML inference, so a plain Bloom filter may still reject faster. The source is arXiv v2 (2026-08-24), and no peer-review venue was confirmed.

name: ChainedFilter
workload: RocksDB (all SSTables in L0, default 64MB write buffer, 36-byte random keys and 64-byte values, 4M-16M items) P70/P99 point-query latency with ChainedFilter replacing the built-in Bloom filter, versus Bloom-only filters at 0x/1x/2x space; also external-memory accesses for Cuckoo Hashing, static-dictionary space and Learned Bloom Filter space
claimed_speedup: SIGMOD 2024 paper: up to 36% lower P99 tail point-query latency than RocksDB's built-in Bloom filter at the same filter space (|U|=16M existing-item queries: about 31us for Bloom vs under 20us for ChainedFilter); up to 31% fewer external memory accesses than raw Cuckoo Hashing; 26% extra space over the theoretical lower bound for an implicit static dictionary; 0.22 extra bits/item over the lower bound for lossless compression; up to 99.1% less filter space than the original Learned Bloom Filter
compiler_and_flags: g++ 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-6ubuntu2), -O3; the README says C++17, but the Self-Adaptive Hashing Makefile uses --std=c++11 -O3 -g
hardware: Intel Core i9-10980XE @ 3.00GHz (the paper says '36 Intel Core i9-10980XE CPU'), 24.8MiB L3, 128GB DRAM
tradeoffs: A general 'chain rule' framework composing several elementary filters rather than a drop-in single filter; the RocksDB integration is a case study, not a merged patch to upstream RocksDB

The 36% gain is for existing-key queries at |U|=16M; for non-existing keys at 16M, ChainedFilter latency rises depending on which SSTable reports the false positive. Last commit was 2023-04-27, more than 3 years ago.

name: Clubcard
workload: Encoding Mozilla's CRLite certificate-revocation-status dataset (816 million certificates, 795 issuers, 11.7 million revoked) as a set-membership filter, replacing the existing Bloom filter cascade used in production.
claimed_speedup: 8.5 MB (clubcard) vs 19.3 MB (Mozilla's CRLite Bloom filter cascade published 2024-08-29), which the README states as a 56% reduction in size. The IEEE S&P 2025 paper reports issuer-partitioned clubcards that are on average 54% smaller than Bloom filter cascades for the same data (2024-10-29 to 2024-11-11 snapshots).
stars_or_usage: 24 stars; clubcard-based CRLite has been the default revocation mechanism for all Firefox desktop users since Firefox 137 (Mozilla Hacks, Aug 2025) and is generated by Mozilla's CRLite backend
tradeoffs: Exact (no false positives for encoded set) membership filter built on Ribbon filters plus a two-level cascade; construction is offline/batch (not designed for online inserts like a classic Bloom filter). API and serialization format explicitly marked unstable ("work in progress").
caveats: This is a memory/size comparison from production snapshots, not a timing benchmark, so no CPU or compiler details apply. The baseline is Mozilla's own prior multi-level Bloom-cascade encoding of the same dataset, not a generic third-party Bloom filter. Part of the gain comes from partitioning revocations by issuer rather than from Ribbon versus Bloom: the README estimates an issuer-sharded Bloom cascade would be about 13 MB. The README warns that the API and serialization format are not stable. Peer-reviewed paper: Schanck, 'Clubcards for the WebPKI', IEEE S&P 2025.

claimed_speedup: Space: 2.5 MB (DCF) vs 10.8754 MB (DBF), labelled 4X. Time for 1M items: insert 1.08 s vs 1.69 s (1.5X), query 1.05 s vs 1.92 s (1.8X), delete 1.36 s vs 3.35 s (2.4X). Numbers and ratio labels are verbatim from the README results table; the README text summarizes this as 30-80% faster insert/query/delete and a 75% memory reduction.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -Wall with no -O flag (default -O0), for both DCF (makefile) and DBF (makefile_DBF); compiler version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-2430M @ 2.4GHz, Ubuntu 14.04.3 LTS
tradeoffs: Adds reliable item deletion plus dynamic capacity extension/reduction on top of standard Cuckoo Filters; requires OpenSSL for hashing and a compact/rehash operation to reclaim space from removed building blocks.

name: fastbloom
workload: Per-lookup latency (ns) of member and non-member checks on u64 keys in a 64 KiB (2^16-byte) filter holding 45,000 items (~8 hashes/item), measured with Criterion against other Rust Bloom filter crates (sbbf-rs-safe, bloomfilter, bloom, probabilistic-collections, solana-bloom). fastbloom uses foldhash, the others SipHash-1-3 (xxhash for sbbf). No insert benchmark is charted.
claimed_speedup: README headline: "2-20 times faster and magnitudes more accurate than existing Bloom filter implementations". Per-check latency charts on the page: non-member check fastbloom 1.36 ns (atomic 1.61) vs sbbf 5.16, bloomfilter 14.50, bloom 17.44, probabilistic-collections 21.29, solana-bloom 42.56 ns (~3.8x-31x, derived from page data); member check fastbloom 7.67 ns (atomic 7.38) vs bloom 27.26, bloomfilter 29.45, probabilistic-collections 35.19, solana-bloom 121.56 ns (~3.6x-16x, derived from page data), but sbbf is faster on member checks at 5.30 ns (fastbloom ~1.45x slower, derived from page data).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core Processor (3.70 GHz), 64-bit OS, x64
tradeoffs: Rust-only, no C API; speed comes from deriving many index bits from a single real hash (hash composition) instead of K independent hashes. Has an AtomicBloomFilter for lock-free concurrent use.
caveats: The claim is overstated: on the page's own member-check chart sbbf (5.30 ns) beats fastbloom (7.67 ns), so "2-20x faster than existing implementations" does not hold for every crate or operation. fastbloom was benchmarked with foldhash while bloom, bloomfilter and probabilistic-collections used SipHash-1-3, so part of the gap is the hasher (fastbloom's own default is SipHash-1-3). The benchmark repo has no license, no rustc version or flags are stated, the numbers exist only as labels on chart images, and it measures lookups only, with no insert throughput.

name: RocksDB Ribbon Filter
workload: Static-filter space overhead, construction time and query time at an FP rate around 1% for n=10^6 and 10^8 keys. Source: the Ribbon paper's fastfilter_cpp fork benchmark (bulk-insert-and-query.cc via ribbon-benchmark.sh), which runs a copy of RocksDB's ribbon_*.h code against RocksDB FastLocalBloom and other Bloom variants. Also the RocksDB blog's filter_bench figures (`./filter_bench -impl=2|3 -quick -m_keys_total_max=200 -use_full_block_reader`, 'Random filter' queries).
claimed_speedup: arXiv:2103.02515 Table 2, at an FP rate around 1% (r=7): Standard Ribbon w=128 (the 128-bit variant RocksDB ships) has 6-8% space overhead over the information-theoretic bound, depending on n. RocksDB's FastLocalBloom blocked Bloom has 49.8% and another blocked Bloom has 52.0%. The cost is CPU: at n=10^6, Ribbon takes 166 vs 21 ns/key to build and 58 vs 10 ns/key to query; at n=10^8 it is 235 vs 72 and 140 vs 36 ns/key. The RocksDB blog (2021-12-29) gives ~30% space savings for 3-4x CPU (typical 7 bits/key Ribbon vs 10 bits/key Bloom at the same FP rate). It also says 100M keys in one filter still save 27% vs 30% at 100K keys. Its filter_bench figures are 140 vs 32 ns/key to construct (~4.4x, derived from page data) and 600 vs 500 ns/key to query (~20% slower, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.4.1, g++ -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=skylake-avx512 (paper Table 2); not stated for the blog's filter_bench numbers
hardware: Single-socket Intel Xeon D-2191 (Skylake DE), 64GB RAM (paper Table 2); not stated for the blog's filter_bench numbers
stars_or_usage: 32.1k stars; Ribbon filter shipped in production RocksDB since v6.15
tradeoffs: Higher construction CPU and ~3x more temporary memory during build (~230 bits/key vs ~75 for Bloom); relatively worse (more CPU) at low false-positive rates; RocksDB recommends Ribbon only for filters kept in memory beyond roughly an hour
caveats: Tier A rests on arXiv:2103.02515. The paper has no journal reference on arXiv and no Crossref record, so the earlier claim that it 'appeared at ESA 2021' could not be verified and is dropped. The paper benchmarks a 2021 copy of RocksDB's ribbon_*.h code (Facebook copyright headers) inside the pdillinger/fastfilter_cpp fork (last pushed 2021-04-27). That is neither RocksDB's in-database filter path nor its current code. The memory win costs CPU: Ribbon construction is 3-8x slower and queries are several times slower than RocksDB's FastLocalBloom (Table 2), so RocksDB recommends a Ribbon+Bloom hybrid policy for long-lived levels. The blog's filter_bench numbers state no hardware or compiler.

name: Windowed Cuckoo Filter (WindowFilter, implements 'Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters')
workload: Bit-packed Bloom filter, standard Cuckoo(2,4) filter, and overlapping-window Cuckoo(2,2) filter compared on bytes/item, false-positive rate, lookup/insert latency, and max load factor
claimed_speedup: Windowed cuckoo (2,2): 1.5958 bytes/item vs Bloom's 1.8034 (README: about 12% less memory) and Cuckoo(2,4)'s 2.1299 (about 25% less) at similar FPR (2^-10 target); lookup 60.28 ns vs Bloom's 81.59 ns and Cuckoo's 61.19 ns (essentially tied with cuckoo).
